notes: Oh, the joys: This Hebrew term (’ashrey) is used twenty-six times in Psalms. Some translations render it as “blessed,” but a different term (barak) is used in contexts of blessing (Psalm 5:12; Psalm 45:2; Psalm 107:38). • The godly do not permit themselves to live under the influence of sinners. Those who do not fear the Lord are wicked (Psalm 36:1); they are the enemies of those who love God, those who do right, and the poor and oppressed (see Psalm 10:2-13; Psalm 37:14). The wicked might appear pious (Psalm 50:16) and sometimes enjoy temporary prosperity (Psalm 37:35), but sorrow (Psalm 32:10) and destruction (Psalm 1:4-6) await them when their deeds catch up with them (Psalm 9:16). • Those who go astray (Psalm 25:8) in rebellion against the Lord (Psalm 78:17) are sinners; they commit heinous crimes such as adultery and murder (cp. Psalm 51:1-19). • join in with: This expression (literally sit in the seat of) depicts a life in bondage to sin (cp. Psalm 1:2; Psalm 26:3-7; Deuteronomy 6:7). • Mockers hate the Lord, scorn his wisdom, and insult anyone who attempts to correct them (Proverbs 9:7-8). They seek only the “wisdom” that justifies their actions. These brash people have little regard for the Lord, his plans, or his children (see Psalm 86:14; Psalm 119:51, Psalm 119:69, Psalm 119:78, Psalm 119:85, Psalm 119:122). These three terms (wicked, sinners, mockers) apply to all kinds of ungodly people.
The Lord gives true happiness to all who reject evil and delight in him.

This wisdom psalm sets the tone for the whole Psalter. The psalmist strongly contrasts the happiness of the godly with the condemnation of the wicked; in the end, the way of wisdom will triumph. This idealization of the godly person (as in Psalm 8:1-9) highlights the Lord’s expectations of his people and especially of the coming Messiah (Psalm 2:1-12). The people of Israel did not live up to this ideal, and neither did the kings of David’s dynasty. Not even the best of them could bring in the triumph of righteousness described in Psalm 1:1-6, Psalm 2:1-12, Psalm 72:1-20. In the New Testament, the apostles’ use of the Psalter to describe the life and ministry of Jesus the Messiah confirms that Jesus alone fulfills the ideal of the godly person presented in the psalms. Only Jesus could please God and secure redemption, happiness, and peace. Psalm 1:1-6 introduces the hopeful anticipation of the final hallelujah (Psalm 150:1-6), when the Lord will remove all evil from his creation and prosper his children.

The first two psalms are an introduction to the entire Psalter. Psalm 1:1-6 introduces the Lord’s instruction in wisdom, while Psalm 2:1-12 introduces God’s rule over a rebellious, sinful world. Together, these psalms invite people to leave the way of folly that leads to destruction and to enter the way of God that leads to wisdom and salvation. The New Testament affirms that God will rule the nations through Jesus Christ, his appointed agent (Hebrews 1:5; Revelation 12:5; Revelation 19:15).

Psalm 1:1-6 and Psalm 8:1-9 form an inclusio (set of literary bookends) that describes what God expects of the ideal person (cp. Psalm 19:1-14; Psalm 33:1-22; Psalm 104:1-35; Psalm 145:1-21), contrasts the godly person with the wicked, and extols the godly person’s dignity. Jesus the Messiah (Psalm 2:1-12)—the sovereign Lord (Hebrews 2:6-8; see 1 Cor 15:27) and perfection of humanity—embodies this ideal.

The law (Hebrew torah) of the Lord is the full revelation of God’s instructions (see study note on Deut 4:44). • Meditating is a process of inner reflection that can be positive (Psalm 1:2; Psalm 63:6; Psalm 77:12; Psalm 143:5) or negative (see Psalm 2:1; Psalm 38:12). The Lord’s word is the object of godly meditation (Psalm 119:48). • Day and night includes all times, whether one is walking, standing, sitting, or sleeping (see Deuteronomy 6:7).
Well-watered trees endure and bear abundant fruit (cp. Jeremiah 17:8).
The future belongs to the godly.
The coming time of judgment (Psalm 1:5) will carry off the wicked and their deeds (Psalm 35:5; Psalm 83:13; Isaiah 17:13; see study note on Jer 13:24).
The wicked cannot abide the scrutiny of the Lord’s judgment; they are already condemned (see Psalm 5:5; Psalm 7:6; Psalm 101:7).

The Lord’s care for the righteous and the demise of the wicked both demonstrate the Lord’s principle of retribution (see Galatians 6:7-10). The brief and futile lives of the wicked will end, whereas the Lord and his saints will triumph (see Psalm 9:5, Psalm 9:6, Psalm 9:18; Psalm 10:16; Psalm 37:20; Psalm 73:27; Psalm 92:9; cp. Psalm 142:4; Isaiah 57:1). • The godly (see Psalm 5:12; Psalm 14:5) are joyful (Psalm 1:1) because the Lord protects and cares for them, hears them when they cry out for justice, and secures their future (see Psalm 121:3-4). • A person’s path is their life and character.
plans: The Hebrew verb rendered “meditate” in Psalm 1:2 here suggests an attitude of opposing the Lord in speech (Isaiah 59:13) or in thought (Psalm 38:12; Proverbs 24:2).
Their futile paths lead to death (Psalm 1:4, Psalm 1:6), but fallen human beings unite in opposing the true God and his Messiah.

This royal psalm pertains to the Lord’s appointment of a king descended from David. It celebrates the mission of all the kings in David’s line, and it introduces the hope of an ideal ruler who will accomplish the Lord’s goal of bringing all nations into submission (Psalm 2:11) or to destruction (Psalm 2:9). The New Testament identifies Jesus as this descendant (see Acts 13:33; 1 Cor 15:25-27; Hebrews 1:5; Hebrews 5:5; Revelation 19:15).

The kings hate the Lord’s established order in the world, so they desire to be independent of him (see Psalm 36:4). They scheme about dominating the Lord’s people (Psalm 31:13; see Psalm 83:1-4). Their goal is to subvert the Lord’s rule in the world by overthrowing his anointed one (or his messiah); the Lord chose the kings of David’s dynasty to establish his kingdom throughout the earth. The New Testament confirms that Jesus, the appointed and anointed Son of God (Acts 4:26; Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5; Hebrews 5:5), fulfills the role in which these earlier kings failed.

break their chains: These kings believe that acknowledging the true God and his chosen ruler will result in their enslavement (Isaiah 28:22; Isaiah 52:2; cp. Lamentations 3:7; Romans 1:1; 1 Cor 7:22; Titus 1:1).
rules in heaven: The Lord’s place in the universe is so certain that he scoffs at humans who boast that they can rebel against his power and authority (see Psalm 37:13; Psalm 59:8).

The Lord finds the human threat insignificant. He provided a solution long before their rebellion. He will end their agitation through the appointment of a human agent, a descendant of David’s line who will rule the nations.
my chosen king: The Lord establishes his anointed ruler.

Today I have become your Father: People in the ancient Near East commonly accepted a father-son relationship between gods and kings. In Israel, the Lord adopted kings as his sons. God set David apart as his most excellent and exalted son (Psalm 89:27). All descendants of David were the Lord’s representatives or agents. As an eternal member of the Godhead (John 1:1) and a descendant of David (Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5; Hebrews 5:5), Jesus is the true Son of God.
The Lord adopted the king of David’s dynasty to conquer rebellious nations by force (see Psalm 89:26-27).

In an example of the suzerain-vassal relationship between the Lord and Israel’s king (see Deuteronomy Book Introduction, “Literary Form”), the Lord invites the king to ask for favors (see Psalm 21:2, Psalm 21:4). • All nations will be subject to David’s descendant, the Messiah.

The Lord gives his anointed ruler the power to conquer the nations as his inheritance (Isaiah 11:4; Revelation 2:27; Revelation 12:5; Revelation 19:15), breaking their rebellion, resistance, and independence.
It pleases the Lord when his people submit to him and seek his protection. The wise accept the Lord’s rebuke and desire to repent.

rejoice: Rulers must welcome the Son as their true and only King. • Submit to God’s royal son (or Submit to God’s royal Son, or kiss the son): Kissing was an expression of submission (Hosea 13:2). • The Lord gives joy to all who fear him (Psalm 1:1-2) and trust him (Psalm 18:30; Psalm 34:22; Psalm 119:1-3).

Psalm 3:1 This sad episode in David’s life (see 2 Sam 15–18) helps readers keep the promises of Psalm 2:1-12 in perspective. The Lord granted victory to his anointed king (Psalm 2:1-12), but the manner and timing of this victory remained in God’s hands.

The psalmist’s many enemies speak brashly (Psalm 4:6; Psalm 12:4; Psalm 40:15) and question the Lord’s ability to rescue (Psalm 10:11; Psalm 22:7-8; Psalm 71:10). Their words haunt him because it seems that the Lord will not answer his prayer. • These enemies wield great power (cp. Psalm 2:1-3); unlike Psalm 2:1-12, this psalm does not resolve the crisis.

This psalm laments that the expectations raised by Psalm 1:1–2:12 have not been met. But even when beset by enemies, godly people need not question the Lord’s just dealings. Rather, they can confidently trust his goodness and expect God to rescue them.

This group of psalms moves readers from the orderly world of Psalm 1:1–2:12 to a disoriented one. The Lord’s anointed cries out while facing enemies, ferocious opposition, evil schemes, and the Lord’s apparent distance.
The psalmist contrasts the contention of his enemies (Psalm 3:2) with the Lord’s provision. The Lord is a shield for his people; he turns their defeat and shame into victory and glory.
The psalmist’s eyes turn from his enemies to the Lord.

By refocusing on the Lord (Psalm 3:3-4) in the midst of his crisis, the psalmist can rest, confident of his safety (see study note on 4:8). The Lord cares for his servant; he protects him and keeps his mind and heart from fear (Psalm 37:17; Psalm 54:4; Psalm 119:116; Psalm 145:14).

The psalmist’s peaceful confidence in the Lord’s protection and care shields him from evil and gives him a new sense of reality (Psalm 23:4; Psalm 27:1, Psalm 27:3; Psalm 46:1; Psalm 56:4, Psalm 56:11; Psalm 91:5-6; Psalm 118:6).
The psalmist does not seek revenge; instead, he waits for the Lord’s vengeance. • Arise: The psalmist calls upon the Lord to take action now.
Waiting for the Lord’s answer allows for growth in patience and for the refinement of living faith (Psalm 38:15).
This individual lament includes a prayer for rescue (Psalm 4:1), a rebuke of the adversary (Psalm 4:2-3), an exhortation to the godly (Psalm 4:4-5), and an expression of confidence (Psalm 4:6-8).
The opponents of the godly place their hope in delusions, treachery, and idolatry. • my reputation (or my glory): The honor of the psalmist, or possibly of the Lord, is at stake.

Angry feelings are not sinful, but letting anger control you leads to sin (see Psalm 37:7-8; cp. Ephesians 4:26-27, Ephesians 4:31-32). • Instead of acting on their emotions, the godly think about their circumstances overnight. They might be disturbed as they sleep, but silence opens their hearts to trust in the Lord (Psalm 4:5).
Offer sacrifices in the right spirit: Redirecting emotions toward the Lord prevents a godly individual from doing too much self-reflection (Psalm 40:6-8; Psalm 51:17).

your face (or the light of your face): The psalmist seeks God’s favor and peace (Numbers 6:25-26), which can transform darkness into light (see Psalm 27:1). Confident trust in the Lord is an antidote to anger, resentment, jealousy, and materialism.
Peace comes from God’s blessing and protection (Psalm 4:6; see Psalm 37:11).

The request hear me appears in several prayers as a call for God’s attention during a time of trouble (Psalm 39:12; Psalm 84:8; Psalm 143:1), as does pay attention (Psalm 17:1; Psalm 54:2; Psalm 130:2). The needy ask their God, “Are you listening?”

This morning prayer (Psalm 5:3) expresses unwavering confidence in the Lord’s help and protection. The psalmist asks for and awaits God’s response (Psalm 5:1-3). He describes the schemes of the wicked in detail but does not get lost in his circumstances. The psalmist also knows that the wicked cannot coexist with God (Psalm 5:4-6, Psalm 5:9; see Psalm 1:5). He keeps returning to the Lord (Psalm 5:7-8, Psalm 5:10; see Psalm 5:1-3), and then he prays for the godly community (Psalm 5:10-12; see Psalm 3:8).

The psalmist begins and ends each day with prayer, awaiting new expressions of God’s fidelity and goodness (Psalm 143:8). • wait expectantly: The psalmist does not demand God’s grace but places hope in it (see Micah 7:7; Habakkuk 2:1).

the proud: Mockers (see study note on 1:1), the wicked (Psalm 73:3; Psalm 75:4), and the arrogant (Psalm 10:2) use their mouths to twist truth and challenge the faith of the godly. • The Lord allows only the godly into his presence (see Psalm 1:5). His holiness and justice do not tolerate oppression or those who do evil. • you hate: The Lord rejects proud sinners (see also Psalm 11:5).

God promises his unfailing love—his covenant goodness and faithfulness—to his people (see Psalm 25:6; Psalm 69:16; Lamentations 3:32). • your house: The godly long to come into God’s presence with reverence and awe (see Hebrews 12:28).

God guides those who are obedient, submissive, and patient in waiting for him to lead, provide, and protect them (Psalm 27:11; Psalm 43:3; Psalm 143:10), not those who expect God simply to endorse their own decisions. • Following the right path of wisdom leads to the Lord (Psalm 27:11; Psalm 61:2; Psalm 139:24).
The psalmist again describes the vile acts of the wicked, who cannot stand in God’s presence.

The psalmist prays for the justice and retribution that God promised against the wicked (Psalm 1:6)—those who have rebelled against the Lord. • The wicked lay traps to kill (Psalm 38:12) or deceive (Psalm 140:4-5).

A blessing rests on all who take refuge in God (see Psalm 18:30). • Joy and praise make good companions. The godly rejoice when they see evidence of God’s rescue. They sing joyful praises as a new song (see Psalm 33:3). When the Lord restores peace to this world, puts down evil, and rewards the righteous, they will have lasting joy (Psalm 9:2-4; Psalm 53:6; Psalm 90:14-15; Psalm 118:24). • The children of God, who find refuge in him, love his name. To love his name is to love his very character.
The psalmist extends his concern beyond himself to all the godly. • A shield, here an image of God’s protection, deflects spears and arrows from its bearer.
don’t rebuke me . . . or discipline me: The psalmist does not explicitly connect God’s discipline with sin here (cp. Psalm 39:8-11), but it might be implied.
The psalmist asks for God’s favor and restoration at a difficult time.
The occasion for this lament might have been sickness or a mental or spiritual depression from which the psalmist sought healing.

In his longing for God’s response to his prayer, the psalmist grew physically weak (Psalm 6:6; see Psalm 77:3; Psalm 119:81; Psalm 142:1-3; see also Psalm 101:1-8). Fasting might have played a part in his agony, but this is not mentioned.
The experience was so painful that the psalmist might as well have been dead, or perhaps he feared for his life.
from the grave? Hebrew from Sheol? In the Old Testament, Sheol is the abode of the dead. It is not necessarily associated with punishment.

The psalmist is exhausted to the depths of his being from the anguish of his spiritual distance from the Lord (Psalm 22:1; Psalm 31:9-10; Psalm 102:5). • When eyes dim, the body is failing (see Psalm 13:3; Psalm 31:9; Psalm 38:10; Matthew 6:22).
In a closing note of triumph, the psalmist reasserts his confidence in the Lord.
Persecutors (a common term for “enemies”) intentionally seek out people in order to destroy them (Psalm 31:15; Psalm 56:1-2; Psalm 71:11; Psalm 143:3).

This psalm consists of a lament (Psalm 7:1-2), an oath of innocence (Psalm 7:3-5), an appeal to God’s justice (Psalm 7:6-9), an affirmation of God’s just kingship (Psalm 7:10-16), and a concluding hymn of praise (Psalm 7:17).
Like a lion, a wicked enemy relentlessly and violently pursues its prey (Psalm 10:9; Psalm 17:12; Psalm 22:13, Psalm 22:21; Psalm 35:17; Psalm 57:4), but God promises victory (Psalm 91:13).
The psalmist does not claim to be without sin, but he knows that he does not deserve the brutal attacks of his opponents (see Psalm 35:7).
The psalmist swears to his innocence, making himself vulnerable to scrutiny (Psalm 7:9.
trample: Cp. Psalm 44:5; Psalm 60:12; Psalm 91:13; Psalm 108:13. • into the ground . . . in the dust: Disgrace and shame can lead to death and the grave (Psalm 143:3; see Psalm 13:3-4).
God’s judgment brings justice, despite the chaos created by adversaries (see Psalm 7:11).
With this appeal to God for justice in the world, the psalmist also submits to God’s examination.

The judgment is against the defendants (the nations) and in favor of the righteous plaintiff (the psalmist; see Psalm 43:1). • Although not innocent of all sin, the psalmist is a person of authentic integrity (see Psalm 15:2; Psalm 25:21; Psalm 41:12; Psalm 78:72; cp. Job 1:1, Job 1:8; Job 9:20, Job 9:22).
God examines the mind and heart of each person (see Psalm 11:3-4; Psalm 26:2; Psalm 139:1, Psalm 139:23).

The psalmist moves from his own situation (Psalm 7:1-9) to speak for all the godly who long for redemption (Psalm 7:10-16). He depicts God as the righteous King who vindicates his subjects when they cry out for rescue.
The honest Lord cannot be bought or bribed, nor does he abuse his power (Psalm 9:4; cp. Psalm 82:1-8).
sword . . . bow . . . deadly weapons . . . flaming arrows: As the Divine Warrior, God goes on the offensive on behalf of himself and his people.
Evil begins with small words or steps, and gives birth to increasingly worse deeds as time goes on (see Isaiah 59:4-5).

I will thank . . . sing praise: The laments in Psalm 3:1–7:17 usually move from lament to praise, as does the Psalter as a whole. • Most High: This is an ancient designation for God (see Genesis 14:19). • God is just and reliable, so his order prevails in this world.

The Lord (Hebrew Yahweh), the covenant God of Israel (Exodus 3:15), also holds the title of Lord (Hebrew ’adonay), the king of the earth. • The word translated majestic (sometimes translated “mighty”) can describe kings (Psalm 136:18), heroes (Psalm 16:3), mountains (Psalm 76:4), or waves breaking on the seashore (Psalm 93:4). While all are awe-inspiring and mighty, the created order pales in comparison with the Lord. • A person’s name embodies their reputation. • The earth and the heavens reveal the Lord’s splendor. All creation worships and praises the Lord (Psalm 66:4; Psalm 113:3; Psalm 145:21).

Psalm 8:1-9 opens the second segment of Book One (Psalm 8:1–14:7). The psalmist celebrates God’s creation and the dignity of the ideal human being (see Psalm 1:1-6). Instead of the world of enemies, wicked people, and distorted justice that is presented in Psalm 3:1–7:17, this psalm promotes an image of the world as God originally created it. A weary person can envision a place of dignity in God’s world.

silencing: The loud noise of the oppressors contrasts with the praise of God. In the end, the praise of God will overwhelm the sound of evil (Psalm 31:18; Psalm 63:11; Psalm 101:5; Psalm 143:12). • Those who oppose God seethe with vindictive anger (Psalm 2:1-3; Psalm 44:16; cp. Psalm 149:6-7).

The nations around Israel worshiped heavenly objects as deities. The sun, moon, and stars are indeed immense and glorious, but they are merely the work of your fingers, a reason to praise the Almighty.
In light of God’s awesome glory, it might seem that people would be insignificant to him. However, he has crowned them with glory and honor and placed them over all creation.

human beings (literally son of Adam): The Hebrew idiom son of man (or son of Adam) means a human being. Through the influence of Daniel 7:13-14, it became a title with divine overtones in the New Testament. See Hebrews 2:6-8, where this passage is quoted.

Yet you made them only a little lower than God: Humans bear God’s image; the Lord has endowed humans with dignity and charged them to rule (Genesis 1:26-27). Hebrews 2:6-8 applies these words to Jesus Christ, the ideal human who fully realized God’s purposes.

gave them charge of everything: The psalmist is still referring to humans in general. Paul applies these words to Jesus as the perfect man who has made the created order—even death (1 Cor 15:25-27)—subject to God and his glory. The New Testament connects these themes of creation and salvation with Jesus Christ (John 1:1-2, John 1:14; Colossians 1:16).

Wild animals, including birds and fish, remind readers of God’s creation of the animal world in Genesis 1:1-31. Contrary to beliefs among Israel’s neighbors in the ancient Near East, animals are not sacred.

The verb translated praise is translated “thank” in Psalm 7:17, suggesting a close connection between Psalm 7:1-17 and Psalm 9:1-20 (see Psalm 7:17; Psalm 8:1-2). With all my heart expresses the psalmist’s deep devotion and commitment (Psalm 86:12; Psalm 111:1; Psalm 119:10; Psalm 138:1). • I will tell: These stories educate the next generation (Psalm 78:4; Psalm 145:4); when they are not remembered, a generation might easily depart from the Lord (Psalm 78:11, Psalm 78:32). • The marvelous things include the Lord’s judgments on the enemies of his people (Psalm 9:4) and his care for the oppressed (Psalm 9:9). The wonders in creation, in redemption, and in revelation reveal his character and show his power (Psalm 89:5; Psalm 111:4; Psalm 119:18, Psalm 119:27). His powerful manifestations evoke public praise (Psalm 9:1; Psalm 26:7; Psalm 75:1).

This hymn celebrates the Lord’s kingship and victory over evil. It might also serve as a response to the laments of Psalm 3:1–7:17. Some believe that Psalm 9:1-20 and Psalm 10:1-18 should be read together as one psalm in two parts because Psalm 9:1-20 includes a title and Psalm 10:1-18 does not, and although several letters are missing or inverted, the two psalms connect as an acrostic of the Hebrew alphabet (other such alphabetic acrostics are Psalm 25:1-22, Psalm 34:1-22, Psalm 37:1-40, Psalm 111:1–112:10, Psalm 119:1-176, Psalm 145:1-21). The ancient Greek and Latin translations treat 9 and 10 as one.
filled with joy . . . sing praises: The psalmist often connects joy with praises, as one leads to the other (Psalm 5:11-12; Psalm 32:11; Psalm 67:4; Psalm 90:14; Psalm 92:4).
retreated . . . staggered: The Lord overpowers even powerful enemies (see Psalm 27:2). Israel also experienced judgment when it resisted the Lord (Psalm 107:12).
The psalmist celebrates God’s judgment of the wicked, which is a testimony to the Lord’s reliable promise to establish his kingdom on earth (Psalm 1:6; Psalm 2:1-12).
The throne represents the Lord’s royal authority.

God created the heavens and the earth with a word (Genesis 1:1-31), and he can bring nations to an end with a word (see Psalm 2:5). Evil and those who do evil will come to an absolute end (Psalm 69:28; Psalm 109:13; Revelation 21:4).
The godly do not put their hope in corruptible human government but in God’s everlasting rule of justice and fairness (see Psalm 96:1–100:5).

The Lord provides shelter in dangerous circumstances and refuge from powerful and oppressive people. The Psalter includes many similar images of the Lord, such as fortress (Psalm 18:2; Psalm 31:2), rock (Psalm 18:2; Psalm 42:9), strength (Psalm 18:1), and strong tower (Psalm 144:2). These images occur frequently in the royal prayers (see Psalm 9:9; Psalm 18:30). • Even oppressed, afflicted, and marginalized people (Psalm 10:17; Psalm 74:21) can enjoy divine protection. • The times of trouble (Psalm 10:1; Psalm 20:1) stand in contrast with appointed times when the Lord openly bestows his favor upon the afflicted (Psalm 69:13; Psalm 102:13; see Psalm 107:6).

Alienation from the Lord might be part of an individual’s experience (Psalm 22:1; Psalm 42:9; Psalm 119:8), yet the psalms affirm that the Lord will not abandon his people (Psalm 16:10; Psalm 37:25, Psalm 37:28).

The psalm writers often connect the idea that God reigns (or sits, or is enthroned) with a place, such as heaven (Psalm 2:4; see Psalm 47:9), Jerusalem, “between the cherubim” (Psalm 80:1; Psalm 99:1), “on high” (Psalm 113:5), or “at my right hand” (Psalm 110:1). Since the Lord rules the world, all people must know of his unforgettable deeds of salvation (see Psalm 9:1; Psalm 64:9; Psalm 66:16; Psalm 105:1).

Recognition that the Lord’s judgment falls on some of the wicked (Psalm 9:3-6) and that God promises to judge all evil (Psalm 9:7-10) motivates praise. The psalmist calls on the godly community to join him.

The Lord avenges and saves his servants (Psalm 18:46) by righteously judging his enemies on earth (Psalm 58:11). The godly do not seek revenge; they wait for the Lord to vindicate them (Psalm 94:1-2; Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19).

The psalmist returns from a vision of the glorious future to the reality of facing his enemies (Psalm 9:3). • The jaws (literally gates) are a vivid image of the powerful grip of death (see Psalm 13:3-4). • Jerusalem’s gates provide an intentional contrast to the “gates” of death.
Hope requires waiting for the Lord’s rescue or justice (Psalm 25:3, Psalm 25:5, Psalm 25:21). The godly find hope, rest, and quietness as they await the Lord (see Psalm 1:6; Psalm 27:14).

The psalmist ends his lament with a prayer for the Lord’s intervention and divine vengeance. • mere mortals . . . merely human: Humans who have received authority and glory sometimes become oppressive and assume glory for themselves (see Psalm 8:4; Psalm 10:18).
The opening questions set the mood. The Lord does not seem to hear the prayers of his people (Psalm 22:1, Psalm 22:19; see 2 Kgs 4:27; Isaiah 1:15).

The lament of Psalm 9:13-20 continues in Psalm 10:1-18 (see study note on Pss 9–10), but the mood changes from confident assertion to anguished questioning. The psalmist prays for rescue, believing that the Lord, as a just king, takes care of the needy.

The wicked brazenly defy God with their acts and speech (Psalm 17:10; Psalm 31:18; Psalm 59:12; Psalm 73:8; Psalm 123:4). Although the Lord will deal with them (Psalm 31:23), they disturb the righteous (see Psalm 5:4-6) prior to their condemnation and judgment.
Wicked and oppressive people might prosper, leaving ugly consequences. Evil can be as dramatic as the psalmist portrays it here, or it could be more subtle.
Unlike those who have evil desires, the godly wait for justice (Psalm 10:17).
God is dead: See Psalm 10:11; Psalm 14:1.
Despite their evil ways (Psalm 5:9; Psalm 28:3; Romans 3:14), the wicked expect a future free of trouble such as the righteous will enjoy.
The wicked rely on outright violence (Psalm 11:5; Psalm 37:32) and deception (Proverbs 12:6; Proverbs 23:27-28).
With confidence that the wicked will be held responsible for their deeds and that the Lord will care for the helpless, the psalmist prays intensely for rescue from evil.
Because the Lord cares for the afflicted, he will take note and punish evildoers (see Psalm 72:14; Psalm 116:15).
The psalmist strongly invokes a curse as he prays (see “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note). • Arms represent an ability to wage war (Psalm 18:34; Psalm 44:3).
As the true and just king, God will bring the wicked to an end, as he promises (Psalm 1:6).
The psalmist expresses his confidence in the Lord.
Mere people misuse their power and enslave the very people God wants them to serve (see Psalm 9:19-20; Luke 22:25-26).
God provides protection (or refuge; see Psalm 5:11; Psalm 9:9; Psalm 25:20) when the foundations of justice collapse. • The mountains provide another place of refuge (see Psalm 121:1).

The psalmist affirms his faith in the righteous God. Even though the world appears hopelessly chaotic, both the godly and the wicked can count on God’s justice. The godly can depend on him as a refuge and shelter.
The wicked live in the shadows and create gloom for the godly (Psalm 82:5; Psalm 139:11; Psalm 143:3; Proverbs 4:19).
In the inevitable battle between the evil and the godly, the wicked cannot tolerate the righteous, so they victimize them. This seems to leave the godly with nothing but questions.
The wicked create a world of darkness (see Psalm 82:5).
The righteous King rules from heaven, where his throne is untouched by human corruption (see Psalm 2:4). He examines everyone and sees everything that happens on earth (see Psalm 14:2-3).
hates: See Psalm 5:4-6; Proverbs 6:16-18. • Wicked deeds result in destruction and violence (Psalm 58:2; Psalm 73:6; Psalm 74:20).
God rained blazing coals and burning sulfur on Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:1-38) as symbols of judgment (Psalm 18:8; Psalm 120:4; Psalm 140:10).
The godly are assured of the Lord’s favorable presence when they see his face (see Psalm 23:6).
Evil becomes so pervasive that the godly pray for rescue (Isaiah 57:1; Micah 7:2; cp. Psalm 1:6; Psalm 37:20; Psalm 58:7; Psalm 104:35).
This community lament seeks the Lord’s help against the prevalence of evil. Because of the Lord’s answer, the godly can face the future knowing that God protects them.
The words they say reveal the character of the wicked. They deceive and overpower the godly and arrogantly question the Lord’s purposes.
The godly can rely on the Lord’s promises, but not on the lies of the wicked (Psalm 12:2-4). • Seven times means totally or completely.
The godly know that the Lord cares, even though the wicked continue to oppress them. The Lord sees the corrupt and foolish people who praise evildoers (see Psalm 9:19-20; Psalm 14:2-6).
How long? The fourfold repetition expresses agitation and deep anguish (Psalm 79:5).
The psalmist’s piercing cry for help becomes a confident song of hope.

A sense of anguish and sorrow closes off any perspective of hope (Psalm 6:3). Unless the Lord answers the psalmist’s prayers (Psalm 22:1), death seems inescapable, torturous, and slow (Psalm 6:6; Psalm 32:3; Psalm 55:4; Psalm 61:2; Psalm 102:5; Psalm 116:3). The psalmist hardly knows how to pray; he longs for God’s redemption (Psalm 25:17-18; Psalm 31:10; Psalm 38:8; Psalm 39:2).
The psalmist’s affliction feels like death (Psalm 22:15; Psalm 55:4; Psalm 88:15; Psalm 94:17; Psalm 116:3).
Only the Lord can bring enlightenment and relief. The psalmist longs for the Lord’s vindication so that his foes will not rejoice.
The psalmist no longer hears the ridicule of his foes. Instead, because of his trust in the Lord, he is full of joy.

Also known as fools, the wicked speak to themselves, think, scheme (Psalm 10:4, Psalm 10:6, Psalm 10:11), and make claims; however, because they do not heed God’s revelation, they possess no understanding (Psalm 14:1; Psalm 39:8; Psalm 53:1; Psalm 74:18, Psalm 74:22).
Paul uses phrases from the Greek translation of this passage in his description of the depravity of all people (Romans 3:10-12).

This wisdom psalm contains some characteristics of lament and prophetic speech. The ideals of Psalm 8:1-9 have run aground on the reality of foolish human attitudes and sinful actions. With the exception of vv Psalm 5:1–6:10, this psalm parallels Psalm 53:1-6.

From heaven (Psalm 33:13; Psalm 80:14; Psalm 102:19), the Lord sees the wicked, who stand out as vile sinners (Psalm 11:3-5). The entire human race lacks wisdom and fails to live up to the glory originally given to them (Psalm 10:4-11; see Romans 1:1–3:31).
The evil live at the expense of others (Psalm 27:2; Psalm 44:11; Psalm 53:4; see Isaiah 5:8) and have no reverence or knowledge of God (Psalm 79:6).
Though the wicked perish (Psalm 1:5-6), God is with the godly.
The psalmist prays for the renewal of God’s relationship with his people. • Jacob is a synonym for Israel (see Genesis 35:9-10).

Only the godly may reside in the Lord’s presence (Psalm 5:4). As his guests, they experience his hospitality and protection. • sanctuary (or tent): In David’s time, God’s sanctuary was a tent (the Tabernacle; see 1 Sam 21:6; 2 Sam 6:17; 7:6; 12:20; 1 Chr 6:32).

In this wisdom poem, the psalmist contrasts the lifestyle of the godly with the actions of fools (Psalm 14:1-7). The questions in this psalm invite readers to examine themselves and to look away from problems with the wicked. The question of who dwells in God’s presence leads into a description of godly character qualities (cp. Psalm 24:3-6; Isaiah 33:14-16).

The psalms in this section affirm integrity and purity (Psalm 17:15; Psalm 18:20-26; Psalm 19:13-14). They refer to people as dwelling in God’s presence (Psalm 16:9-11; Psalm 17:15) and as not being shaken (Psalm 15:5; Psalm 16:8).
The godly speak truthfully and act faithfully in their relationships. Unlike the wicked, they are open and transparent (Psalm 12:2-4).

The Lord prohibited Israel from charging interest to people in need (Exodus 22:25-27). • The assurance of God’s presence keeps the godly from destruction (Psalm 16:8; Psalm 46:5; Psalm 125:1). Their circumstances might shake them temporarily, but they ultimately stand firm (Psalm 30:6; Psalm 94:18; Psalm 112:6).
The psalmist feels safe because the Lord alone offers security (Psalm 16:5-6), guidance (Psalm 16:7-8), and the joy of his presence (Psalm 16:9-11).

In this psalm of confidence, the poet moves quickly from a short petition (Psalm 16:1), to expressions of passionate commitment to God and his people (Psalm 16:2-6), to a conclusion of confident praise (Psalm 16:7-11).
I said to the Lord: The various writers of the psalms pray, lament, and praise the Lord throughout the Psalter, and the Lord answers them (see Psalm 12:5-6).
The psalmist dissociates himself from ungodly worship, rituals, and words (see Psalm 15:3-5).
The cup of blessing represents God’s provision for all the psalmist’s needs (Psalm 23:5; see Psalm 116:13; cp. Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17).
The land is God’s gift for his people (Deuteronomy 18:8).

God’s instruction brings life (Psalm 16:11; see Psalm 5:8; Psalm 23:1-3; Psalm 32:8; Psalm 73:24). • The psalmist so deeply depends on the Lord for strength and joy that he senses that God is right beside him (Psalm 16:11; see Psalm 73:23; Psalm 109:31; Psalm 110:1, Psalm 110:5; Psalm 121:5). • Peter quoted Psalm 16:8-11 in his sermon on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:25-28).

Knowing that not even death can separate him from the Lord strengthens the psalmist’s confidence. He fears a separation (see Psalm 13:3-4), but he remains confident of seeing the Lord (see Psalm 11:7).
The psalmist expresses his confidence that life continues beyond death. The apostles applied this text to the resurrection of Jesus (Acts 2:25-33; Acts 13:35).
with you: See Psalm 16:7-8; Psalm 110:1.

comes from honest lips: Deception characterizes the wicked. The godly reject such deceit as a failure of character and pray for rescue from such people (Psalm 5:6; Psalm 43:1; Psalm 120:2). They love honesty, truth, and integrity (Psalm 15:2-3; Psalm 24:4; Psalm 101:7).
The psalmist pleads for God’s protection and vindication, affirms his own integrity, and prays that the Lord will prevail against his fierce enemies.
Though he is not perfect, the psalmist commits himself to the Lord. He does not want to sin through deception, flattery, or gossip (see Psalm 10:7; Psalm 15:2-3; Psalm 17:1).
The psalmist declares his innocence (Psalm 17:1) and commits himself to integrity by being open to God’s examination.
This prayer for God’s care returns to the petition begun in Psalm 17:1-2 for redemption from evil.

as you would guard your own eyes (literally as the pupil of your eye): This metaphor expresses God’s care and affection for the psalmist (see Deuteronomy 32:10). • The shadow of God’s wings is a place of his protection from enemies and adversity (Psalm 36:7; Psalm 57:1; Psalm 61:4; Psalm 63:7; Psalm 91:4).

The psalmist confidently prays for the Lord’s victory, knowing that God possesses more power than the evildoers. The psalmist finds his joy in the Lord’s inheritance (Psalm 16:5), whereas the wicked search for joy in this world.
see you face to face: The psalmist does not allow temporary concerns raised by adversaries to stand in the way of his experiencing a real and lasting relationship with the Lord.

Psalm 18:1 David was a faithful servant of the Lord, charged with the responsibility of establishing God’s kingdom on earth (see Psalm 78:70; Psalm 132:10; Psalm 144:10). • The Lord rescued David from all his enemies when he enabled David to conquer them (see 2 Sam 8:1-14).

This royal drama of divine rescue (also found with minor variations in 2 Sam 22:1-51) encourages readers who are following the laments and requests for rescue in Psalm 16:1-11 and Psalm 17:1-15. The psalmist describes the dramatic nature of God’s rescue in three different ways (Psalm 18:7-15, Psalm 18:16-19, Psalm 18:30-36). The psalm also extends hope that a future Son of David will be totally victorious over evil (Psalm 18:43-50; cp. Psalm 2:1-12).

A shield is an image of protection, salvation, and victory (Psalm 7:10; Psalm 18:2, Psalm 18:30, Psalm 18:35; Psalm 84:11; Psalm 91:4; Psalm 115:9, Psalm 115:10, Psalm 115:11; Psalm 119:114; Psalm 144:2). It evokes a response of trust, waiting, and godly confidence.
God deserves praise for his greatness and faithfulness (Psalm 48:1; Psalm 96:4; Psalm 145:3).
God dwells in his sanctuary, the heavenly temple (Psalm 102:19; see Psalm 14:2-3). He knows everything, sees everyone, and will vindicate the godly (see Psalm 11:3-7).

The destabilization of the whole earth will be a means of God’s judgment (Psalm 77:17-18; Psalm 96:9; Psalm 97:4; Psalm 99:1; Psalm 104:32; Isaiah 29:6; Micah 1:3-4; Nahum 1:2-6; Haggai 2:7, Haggai 2:21).

The psalmist depicts the Lord’s descent from heaven to earth with phenomena such as earthquakes, flames, smoke, darkness, and rain. Creation shudders at God’s marvelous coming as the Divine Warrior (see Psalm 97:2-5) and Judge (see Psalm 50:1-6).

his nostrils . . . his mouth: The psalmist likens God to an angry person or a fierce creature (see Job 41:12-22). • The terrifying images of smoke, flames, and glowing coals express God’s wrath against sin.
The Lord’s sovereignty extends over all of nature (see Psalm 104:2-4; Psalm 148:5-6).
a mighty angelic being (Hebrew a cherub): See study notes on 1 Chr 28:18; 2 Chr 3:10-13.
Because God loves and delights in the psalmist (see Psalm 18:1), he will save him (Psalm 37:23; Psalm 41:11; Psalm 91:14-16).

The psalmist affirms that loyalty is rewarded. He puts his trust in the Lord (see Psalm 16:1) and commits himself to living with integrity (see Psalm 1:1-6, Psalm 15:1-5, Psalm 24:1-10; see also Psalm 19:12-14).

kept the ways of the Lord: The psalmist faithfully obeys God’s instructions (see Psalm 25:8-10). • not turned . . . to follow evil: The psalmist rejects the way of folly (see Psalm 1:1-6 and Psalm 14:1-7) and chooses the way of wisdom (see Psalm 1:1-6 and Psalm 15:1-5).
The faithful God remains true to his character. He loves faithfulness, blamelessness, and purity, and he hates the perverse (see Psalm 1:6).
The pure have clean hands (see Psalm 18:20-24). • to the crooked you show yourself shrewd: The Lord knows each person’s character, and he justly responds to them in kind.
proud: The Lord hates pride (Psalm 101:5; Psalm 131:1; see Proverbs 6:16-17; Proverbs 21:4; Proverbs 30:13).
light a lamp: The Lord renews the psalmist’s life, helping him overcome the darkness of adversity (see Psalm 112:4; Psalm 119:105).
scale any wall: God helps his servants fight their battles.

perfect: God’s character has integrity (see Psalm 18:26). • God promises to protect his people, and he does so. • Seeking God’s protection entails trust and faith. Regardless of his feelings or external circumstances, the psalmist makes a deep commitment to the Lord. He experiences joy (Psalm 5:11; Psalm 64:10) as he awaits the Lord’s rescue (Psalm 57:1).
The psalmist experiences God’s rescue and provision of victory.
The psalmist’s victories come from the Lord. He completely depends on God.
A wide path represents freedom and safety (see Psalm 4:8; Psalm 119:35).
With help from the Divine Warrior, the psalmist experienced victory over his enemies.
Placing a foot on the necks of the enemy represents total victory (see Joshua 10:23-26).

With God’s victorious help, the psalmist achieved military and political success, thus fulfilling the history of David’s dynasty (Psalm 2:1-12). The previous laments find some resolution in this psalm.
The psalmist again reflects on the Lord’s victories. God’s marvelous rescue and the king’s victory are cause for celebration.
God vindicates his servant and so fulfills his mission (Psalm 2:1-12; see Psalm 47:3; Psalm 144:2).
The psalmist’s vision of praise . . . among the nations motivated Paul in his mission to the Gentiles (Romans 15:9).
God appointed David, his anointed ruler, to bring order into God’s world (see Psalm 2:1-12). Both David and his descendants received this responsibility.
The glory of God refers to the splendor or manifest presence of the Creator (Psalm 113:4). • God (Hebrew ’el): El is an ancient designation for God that signifies his creative power.

The created order is an arena of God’s wisdom, and the heavens are the place of God’s dwelling (Psalm 2:4; see Psalm 8:1; Psalm 57:5; Psalm 89:6; Psalm 115:3). From heaven, God observes humanity (Psalm 11:4; Psalm 14:2; Psalm 33:13; Psalm 53:2; Psalm 80:14; Psalm 102:19) and comes to the rescue of his servants (Psalm 18:6-8, Psalm 18:13; Psalm 20:6; Psalm 57:3; Psalm 76:8; Psalm 144:5). The heavens remain unaffected by human failures and rebellions (see Psalm 2:1-4). They display God’s qualities of fidelity, righteousness (Psalm 36:5; Psalm 50:6; Psalm 57:10; Psalm 85:11; Psalm 89:2, Psalm 89:5; Psalm 97:6; Psalm 108:4), and wisdom (Psalm 136:5; see Psalm 119:89-90). The heavens reveal the Lord’s glory (see Psalm 19:1) and give evidence of his presence and handiwork.

God’s wisdom is manifest in heaven (Psalm 19:1-4), in nature (Psalm 19:4-6), in his instruction (Psalm 19:7-11), and in the life of the psalmist (Psalm 19:12-14). Like Psalm 8:1-9, this hymn uses creation to motivate reflection—it is a peaceful oasis after the drama of the lament and victory psalms. The psalm begins with creation as a source of wisdom, then moves to God’s word as the perfect source of wisdom, and ends with the human need for redemption.

God’s wisdom does not need to be spoken. Through creation, it is seen, felt, and experienced. Paul applied this text to condemn Israel for its lack of receptivity to Jesus Christ (Romans 10:18). • The sun is part of God’s creation, but it is not a deity, as people of other nations in the ancient Near East commonly believed.

God’s instructions to humans reveal his character and wisdom. God’s instruction is precious and pleasant (Psalm 119:103). It nourishes the person (Proverbs 16:24; Proverbs 24:14) and is of more value than objects of human worth (Psalm 81:13-16).
The psalmist knows his faults, so he prays to remain faithful and commits himself to the Lord.
An individual who commits deliberate sins does so with an insolent (Psalm 86:14) or arrogant (Psalm 119:21, Psalm 119:69) attitude. • The great sin is rebellion (see Psalm 32:1).
words of my mouth . . . meditation of my heart: The psalmist desires to please God in everything he says and thinks (see Luke 6:45; Romans 12:1-2).

The title God of Jacob affectionately expresses God’s ancient relationship with his people (see Psalm 46:7, Psalm 46:11; Psalm 75:9; Psalm 76:6; Psalm 81:1, Psalm 81:4; Psalm 84:8; Psalm 94:7; Psalm 114:7; Psalm 146:5). • keep you safe from all harm: See Psalm 59:1-2.
The community prays for the king’s protection and victory.
This royal prayer for God’s victory (Psalm 20:1-5) leads to confidence in God’s rescue (Psalm 20:6-8) and a communal request for God’s response (Psalm 20:9).

This sequence of psalms expresses the experience of moving from confidence and commitment (Psalm 20:1–21:13), through anguish and abandonment (Psalm 22:1-31), and finally to comfort, insight, and hope (Psalm 23:1–24:10).
Gifts and burnt offerings express submission to the Lord (cp. Psalm 40:6).
make all your plans succeed . . . answer all your prayers: These requests could be those stated in Psalm 21:3-6 (cp. Psalm 27:4).
Troops carried a victory banner to battle, under which they gathered and roused one another to action (see Isaiah 11:10, Isaiah 11:12).
God chose his anointed king to be ruler (see Psalm 2:7).
An individual member of the community (Psalm 20:1-5) responds with a word of assurance and confidence in God’s help.
chariots and horses: These were instruments of war (see Psalm 33:16-17; Psalm 76:6; Psalm 147:10; Isaiah 30:16; Isaiah 31:1-3).
God’s people thank him for giving victory to the king.
The king has experienced his heart’s desire—God’s protection and blessing (see Psalm 20:5; see also Psalm 2:8).
success and prosperity: See Proverbs 10:6.
The king returned victorious from battle and received honor from the people. His greatest honor came from God, who gave him blessings, life, and his presence.

God offers a rich quality of life (Psalm 61:6-7; Psalm 91:14-16; Psalm 128:4-6) characterized by his presence (Psalm 16:11; Psalm 23:6; Psalm 27:4; Psalm 36:9), joy (Psalm 16:11), goodness (Psalm 23:6; Psalm 34:14-15), and protection (Psalm 41:2; Psalm 61:7).
God’s eternal blessings also bring fullness of life in the present (see Psalm 133:1-3).
The king enjoyed victory not because of his strength or intrinsic goodness but because God honored his faith.
As long as even a single enemy opposed the king’s authority, God’s kingdom was not fully present. This prayer requests victory over all evil in the world.

The flaming furnace and fire portray the severity of God’s judgment on the wicked. In the Old Testament, this image often refers to hell (Psalm 11:6; Psalm 18:8; Psalm 50:3; Psalm 68:2; Psalm 78:21; Psalm 79:5; Psalm 80:16; Psalm 89:46; Psalm 97:3; Psalm 104:4; Psalm 140:10; see Isaiah 66:24).
children . . . descendants: Evil will end when God destroys all opposition to himself (Psalm 109:13; cp. Psalm 18:50; Psalm 22:30-31; Psalm 25:13; Psalm 102:28).
Rise up (or be exalted, as in Psalm 57:5, Psalm 57:11; Psalm 108:5) expresses communal praise and joy in God’s greatness and power.
A deep sense of alienation from God overwhelms the psalmist (see Psalm 10:1).
The psalmist alternates between reflections on his present dire circumstances and memories of the Lord’s past faithfulness; he ends with a prayer for rescue.

All previous laments pale in comparison with this outcry against the enemy and God’s abandonment. The psalm contains two main sections: the lament (Psalm 22:1-21) and praise for redemption (Psalm 22:22-31), which leads naturally to Psalm 23:1-6. The apostles saw in this psalm an expression of the sufferings of Jesus Christ, who ultimately fulfilled the purpose of David’s humiliation, rejection by people, and divine abandonment (Matthew 27:35, Matthew 27:39, Matthew 27:43, Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34; John 19:23-24, John 19:28; Hebrews 2:12).
God, the holy King, is set apart from all his creation, but he chooses to reveal himself to Israel. • God greatly desires that his people offer praises to him.
Both the Lord and people reject the psalmist. He vividly describes his anguish (Psalm 22:1-2); he lives like a lowly animal.
Everyone mocks the psalmist’s confidence in the Lord (see Psalm 3:2; Matthew 27:43), which shames him (Psalm 44:13-14; Psalm 74:10; Psalm 89:50; Psalm 109:25).
The Lord took care of the psalmist before he could do anything for himself (see Psalm 71:6; Psalm 139:13).
The psalmist reflects on his past relationship with God (see Psalm 22:3-5). The Lord has been his very life.
Bashan, a region known for its herds and vegetation, produced strong bulls (Psalm 68:30).
The psalmist returns to expressing his anguish and suffering (see Psalm 22:1-2, Psalm 22:6-8). His trouble comes from human beings who act like beasts.
The psalmist’s sense of being poured out like water expresses a meaningless, transitory existence that leaves him depleted.
Facing adversity is as horrible as dying of thirst (see Psalm 137:6). • Jesus may have had this verse in mind when he said, “I am thirsty” (John 19:28).
The wild pack of dogs represents fierce and unscrupulous people.

I can count all my bones: The psalmist’s enemies have utterly shamed him by taking his garments. Jesus also suffered this disgrace (see Matthew 27:35). • stare at me and gloat: Enemies make the psalmist the object of their scorn (see Psalm 35:24, Psalm 35:26; Psalm 38:16; Psalm 55:3; cp. Psalm 59:10). • throw dice: Literally cast lots. The casting of lots was sometimes a way for godly people to find God’s direction (Leviticus 16:8; Numbers 27:21; Acts 1:24-26). Here, the lots are thrown simply as a game of chance. The soldiers threw dice for Jesus’ clothing after the crucifixion (Matthew 27:35; Mark 15:24; Luke 23:34; John 19:24).
The psalmist faces his troubles by praying for God’s rescue. Only the Lord has the strength to ward off dogs, lions, and oxen.
The sword makes evident the lethal intent of the enemy.

I will proclaim your name: The writer to the Hebrews ascribes these words to Jesus (Hebrews 2:12). • my brothers and sisters: Literally my brothers. In the New Testament quotation, the Greek translation picks up the broader meaning as “my brothers and sisters.”
The psalmist praises the Lord and calls for the godly to join him. He tells of God’s goodness to the needy, including himself.
The godly respond with awe (see Psalm 22:25).
Unlike his response to the wicked (see Psalm 21:8-12), God cares about the needy and hears their prayers (Psalm 51:17; Psalm 69:33; Psalm 102:17).
The great assembly might include all nations (Psalm 22:27; Psalm 26:12; Psalm 35:18).
The psalmist vows to praise the Lord, the great King of the earth (Psalm 22:27-28) who cares for the needy. God alone deserves praise.
God knows his people’s needs and addresses them (Psalm 63:5; Psalm 81:16; Psalm 103:5; Psalm 107:9; Psalm 132:15; Psalm 145:16; Psalm 147:14).

families of the nations: All clans and tribes of humanity (see Genesis 12:3; Revelation 5:9-10) will live in submission to the Lord (Psalm 96:1-3; see Psalm 2:1-12, Psalm 72:1-20; Isaiah 2:2-4; 1 Cor 15:25-27).
The universal kingdom belongs to God alone (Obadiah 1:21).
The Lord invites all people, rich and poor (Psalm 22:26), to the banquet as long as they worship him.

Future generations will join those from the past who praised the Lord (Psalm 22:3-5). The descendants of the godly will receive blessings (Psalm 22:30-31), unlike the offspring of the wicked (Psalm 21:10).

The Lord’s acts of redemption (Psalm 40:9; Psalm 50:6; Psalm 71:15, Psalm 71:16, Psalm 71:24; Psalm 97:6) demonstrate that he is righteous (see Psalm 4:1). His righteousness provides the character required for rule, judicial decisions, and relationships. This virtue leads to harmony and order (see Psalm 50:6).
The Lord promises to take care of his children (Psalm 34:9-10; Isaiah 51:14). He demonstrated this ability to Israel in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 2:7) and in the Promised Land (Deuteronomy 8:9).
People in the ancient Near East commonly viewed their rulers as shepherds.

This psalm of trust and confidence in the Lord has been a favorite of God’s people for generations. It expresses assurance of God’s presence in the midst of adversity. It evokes images of the Good Shepherd (Psalm 23:1-3; see Ezekiel 34:12; John 10:11) and of the messianic banquet (Psalm 23:5-6; see Isaiah 25:6; Revelation 19:9).

These psalms develop the importance of integrity (Psalm 25:4-7, Psalm 25:12-14, Psalm 25:21; Psalm 26:6, Psalm 26:11; Psalm 27:7-12), God’s shepherding care (Psalm 23:1; Psalm 28:9), God’s guidance (Psalm 23:2-3; Psalm 25:5; Psalm 27:11), God’s goodness (Psalm 23:6; Psalm 25:7-8; Psalm 27:13), and living in his house (Psalm 23:6; Psalm 26:8; Psalm 27:4, Psalm 27:8).

Sheep rest after they have eaten their fill (Zephaniah 3:13; see Isaiah 11:7; cp. Isaiah 13:20; Isaiah 27:10). • The Lord leads the sheep for their own benefit (see Psalm 5:8). • Sheep only drink from still water, so the shepherd seeks out peaceful streams for his flock.

Cp. Psalm 19:7; the Lord’s word renews my strength. • The Lord guides by rescuing his people from evil (Psalm 23:4-5; see Psalm 31:3), bringing them back to himself (Psalm 5:8; Psalm 61:2), caring (Psalm 48:14; Psalm 139:10), ruling (Psalm 67:4), counseling (Psalm 73:24), protecting (Psalm 78:53; Psalm 107:30; Psalm 143:11), and instructing them in wisdom (Psalm 27:11; see Proverbs 4:11). • The Lord’s name guarantees the relationship; he guards his reputation against any accusation of his abandoning his people or allowing them to sin (see Psalm 25:11; Psalm 31:3; Psalm 106:8; Psalm 143:11).
The shepherd used his rod and staff to fend off danger.

A feast demonstrates the Lord’s care and mercy toward his people (see Psalm 22:26, Psalm 22:29). Although enemies can watch, they cannot trouble the guests. • The ritual of anointing the head with oil showed guests honor (Psalm 92:9-11), hospitality, and refreshment (Psalm 104:15; Psalm 133:2).

The Lord expresses his unfailing love through the goodness of his presence and other benefits that he alone provides (Psalm 69:16; Psalm 86:17; Psalm 109:21; see Psalm 18:6; Psalm 61:4). He actively bestows care that is greater than the temporary trials imposed by enemies (Psalm 7:1).
The Lord created and now rules the earth and everything in it (see 1 Cor 10:25-26). He sees all its people (Psalm 33:14), regardless of their status (Psalm 49:1-2).
The kingdom belongs to the Creator, the Great King (cp. Psalm 22:27).
The shepherd of Psalm 23:1-6, who is also the King of the whole world, takes possession of Zion.
God created everything in an orderly and stable manner (see Psalm 89:11; Psalm 102:25; Psalm 104:5).

These questions invite readers to look away from their problems with the wicked and to examine themselves (see Psalm 15:1). • God’s holy place is the holy mountain, a reference both to Jerusalem and to heaven.
The citizens of the King’s realm include all who seek him. The Lord invites them to enter his presence.

Those with pure hands have not shed blood or injured relationships between people (see Psalm 9:12; Psalm 15:2-5). • Those with pure hearts commit themselves fully to the Lord, as evidenced in strength of character, transparency, and selflessness (Psalm 51:10; Psalm 73:1; see Matthew 5:8).
The Lord of Heaven’s Armies reigns from his home, the Temple in Jerusalem (Psalm 84:3-5). He excludes sin and sinners (Psalm 24:3-6) but protects all who dwell in Zion.
The psalmist commits himself to the Lord instead of to idols (see Psalm 24:3-4).
The psalmist expresses confidence that the godly will be vindicated and his enemies will not succeed (see Psalm 25:15-22).

This individual lament includes instruction in wisdom and a community lament; it begins and ends with an affirmation of trust in the Lord (Psalm 25:1-3, Psalm 25:15-22). The psalmist prays for guidance (Psalm 25:4-7) and encourages the godly to practice a lifestyle of wisdom (Psalm 25:12-14). In addition to the enemies who trouble him, the psalmist confesses his sins (Psalm 25:7, Psalm 25:11, Psalm 25:18) as part of his anguish. Trust develops with understanding God’s character: He is compassionate, faithful, and good (Psalm 25:8-10).
Enemies would rejoice by singing a victory song.
The right path, the path of wisdom (see Psalm 5:8), means being open to instruction that leads to life (Psalm 27:11; Psalm 43:3; Psalm 73:24; Psalm 119:12).

In this prayer for guidance, compassion, and forgiveness, the psalmist turns to the Lord for instruction in wisdom. He confesses his past failures and acknowledges that his hope lies with his merciful Savior.
Biblical hope does not mean wishing for an event to turn out favorably. Hope trusts the Lord’s will and gives the courage to face disappointments (Psalm 33:22; Psalm 130:5).
compassion: See also Psalm 51:1; Psalm 57:1; Psalm 103:8.
The Lord keeps his people close to himself.

The psalmist again asks forgiveness for his many sins (Psalm 25:7; Psalm 32:1-5). The sins of Israel’s kings demonstrated the weaknesses inherent in David’s dynasty and the reasons for its failure in Old Testament Israel (see Psalm 89:1-52).
Those who fear the Lord will receive further instruction and experience God’s presence (Psalm 25:14) and blessing (Psalm 25:13).

prosperity: See Psalm 23:6. • inherit the land: Unlike the wicked, who will perish (Psalm 1:6), the godly have a secure future. In the end, God will bless them, and their blessings will endure (see Psalm 37:9, Psalm 37:11, Psalm 37:22, Psalm 37:29, Psalm 37:34; Isaiah 57:13; Matthew 5:5).
the traps of my enemies: See Psalm 5:9-10; Psalm 31:4; Psalm 140:5; Proverbs 3:26.
The psalmist expresses confidence in the Lord, commits to a life of integrity, and prays for rescue.

The psalmist can find no relief (see Psalm 4:1; Psalm 13:1-2) as his problems go from bad to worse. He associates his anguish with sin, but he does not elaborate on the nature of his sin (see Psalm 25:7, Psalm 25:11).
Knowing that the Lord hates violent people (see Psalm 11:5), the psalmist pleads with God to deal with these enemies.
Just as it opened, the psalm closes with a commitment of trust and hope (see Psalm 9:18; Psalm 25:5).
The psalmist opens himself to divine examination of his life, especially in the areas of his character and devotion.
In this individual lament, the psalmist prays for redemption on the basis of his own innocence and the Lord’s justice.
For God’s truth to become part of one’s character requires a habitual commitment.
Because of his devotion to the Lord (Psalm 26:1-3), the psalmist dissociates himself from evil people (see Psalm 1:1).
Ritual purity required the worshiper to wash their hands, symbolic of separation from evil and evildoers (see Psalm 73:13). • The altar symbolizes God’s presence (Psalm 43:4).
The psalmist demonstrates his loyalty to the Lord through pious rituals, praise, and acknowledgment of the Lord’s presence in the Temple.
The sanctuary symbolized the manifest presence of the Lord (see Psalm 18:6).
Don’t let me suffer: The end of the godly cannot be the same as that of the wicked.
The psalmist’s footing on solid ground represents salvation (cp. Psalm 143:10). • publicly: Or in the great assembly at the Temple (Psalm 26:6-8; Psalm 22:25).
Light expresses the Lord’s goodness (Psalm 27:13; see Psalm 4:6; Psalm 23:6; Psalm 31:19; Psalm 38:10; Psalm 43:3; Psalm 56:13).

The psalmist acknowledges the Lord at the center of his life (Psalm 27:1). Because of God’s presence, he engages his adversaries with confidence. They cannot intimidate him or penetrate his inner security.

This psalm mixes two genres—a psalm of confidence (Psalm 27:1-6) and an individual lament (Psalm 27:7-14)—held together by the theme of longing for the Lord’s presence. The psalmist focuses on the Lord; his circumstances are secondary. The strength of the psalmist’s faith is expressed in his openness to the Lord’s instruction, timing, and priorities.
The psalmist’s enemies seek to devour him by living at his expense (see study note on 14:4).
remain confident: See Psalm 25:2; Psalm 26:1.

Searching for and enjoying the Lord’s presence provides the psalmist’s foundation for confidence and security. He lives in the assurance of God’s protection and looks forward to offering sacrifices of thanksgiving and praise (see Psalm 18:6).
sanctuary (or tabernacle): This early shrine was the Israelites’ place of worship before the Temple was constructed.
hold my head high: A sign of victory. • The granting of the request of Psalm 27:4 prompts sacrifices with shouts of joy.

Unlike the wicked (Psalm 10:4), who only want a temporary advantage (Psalm 78:34-36), the godly search for the Lord as a thirsty person searches for water in the desert (Psalm 63:1; Psalm 105:4; Psalm 119:2, Psalm 119:10; Matthew 6:33). They act wisely (Psalm 34:10, Psalm 34:14) while waiting for the Lord to resolve their crisis (Psalm 34:4; Psalm 69:6; Psalm 77:2; Psalm 119:58).
The psalmist requests the Lord’s mercy, presence, and instruction. God is the psalmist’s greatest good; enemies and other circumstances are peripheral.

The psalmist expresses confidence and hope in the Lord’s presence. To live in faith means to wait patiently in recognition of the Lord’s goodness. Such a life is not always pleasant for the godly (Psalm 42:2-3; Psalm 43:5), but their future is secure (Psalm 37:9; Psalm 130:7; see Psalm 9:18).
if you are silent: The psalmist appeals to the Lord to take action (Psalm 35:22; Psalm 50:3; Psalm 83:1; Psalm 109:1).
The psalmist urges the Lord to listen; his urgency flows out of the tension between his deep relationship with the Lord and the adversity he faces.
In this individual lament, the psalmist pleads for justice and mercy. He expresses confidence in the Lord’s strength and faithfulness, and he intercedes for the Lord’s people.
It was common to lift up one’s hands in a gesture of devoted prayer (Psalm 63:4; Psalm 134:2).
The psalmist curses his enemies, asking God for retribution and vindication.
The wicked do not acknowledge the difference between the sacred and the common, so they have no respect for the Lord’s creation, redemption, or revelation.
The psalmist anticipates rescue because of his confidence in the Lord’s justice.
my strength and shield: The Lord protects the psalmist (see Psalm 59:9, Psalm 59:17).
The poem closes with intercession for the Lord’s people. • Bless Israel, your special possession: See Psalm 29:11; Psalm 133:3.

The psalmist issues a call to honor the Lord for his power (cp. Psalm 96:7-8). • you heavenly beings: Angels or deities who, some believed, held special powers. The psalmist did not believe in other deities but called on people who thought they were real to look to the Lord as the only God.
This nature hymn in praise of the Creator declares that the Lord holds all power over nature. God uses the same unsurpassed strength to care for his people.

The word translated voice (Hebrew qol) can also mean “noise” (1 Kgs 1:45) or “thunder” (Joel 3:16). The Lord’s voice is awe-inspiring, and it dominates whatever rumblings people might attribute to other deities.
The cedars of Lebanon were known for their size and quality (see Isaiah 2:13).
Lebanon’s mountains and Hermon are high mountains to the north of Israel. • The Lord can cause even immense mountains to shake at his command (see Psalm 114:4).
The wilderness of Kadesh was located south of Judah. God’s voice can be heard throughout the land, from the north (Psalm 29:6) to the south.
The image of powerful floodwaters connects with the Genesis flood (Genesis 6:17). The Lord reigns as king over the whole created order; no one contests his kingdom.
The ruler of nature blesses his people with peace (see Psalm 28:8-9; Psalm 37:11; Psalm 133:3).

I will exalt you is a call to lift up the Lord’s name in praise and thanksgiving (Psalm 34:3; Psalm 81:1; Psalm 99:5, Psalm 99:9; Psalm 107:32; Psalm 118:28; Psalm 145:1; see Exodus 15:1; Isaiah 25:1). • you rescued me: God pulled the psalmist from death (Psalm 30:3). • In his justice and care, God refused to let the psalmist’s enemies triumph (see Psalm 26:9; Psalm 27:12; Psalm 28:3; Psalm 31:8).
The psalmist praises God for his triumph over adversity, which he likens to salvation from the grave.

This individual thanksgiving psalm opens in praise to the Lord for his salvation (Psalm 30:1-3), then contrasts God’s favor with his anger (Psalm 30:4-7), and ends with a transformation from mourning to dancing (Psalm 30:8-12).
The godly should celebrate the Lord’s acts of rescue with song and praise (Psalm 33:21; Psalm 97:12; Psalm 103:1; Psalm 105:3; Psalm 145:21).

Nothing can stop me now! The psalmist confesses his presumptuous attitude (cp. Psalm 32:3-4). • secure as a mountain: In the psalms, this phrase creates a powerful image of stability and of God’s control (see Psalm 11:1; Psalm 18:7; Psalm 36:6; Psalm 46:2; Psalm 72:3; Psalm 76:4; Psalm 83:14; Psalm 97:5; Psalm 114:4, Psalm 114:6; Psalm 125:2). • I was shattered: The absence of God’s favor destroys the security of the proud (cp. Psalm 104:27-30).

The psalmist faced death (also in Psalm 30:1-3)—perhaps literally, perhaps figuratively. But when he turned to the Lord, the Lord rescued him and turned his mourning into joyful dancing. Only God’s favor can permanently and powerfully overcome human failure and the depths of despair.
The Lord offers refuge to anyone who comes to him for protection. The psalmist trusts in and submits to the Lord. See also Psalm 71:1-3.

The psalmist encourages the godly to find refuge in the Lord and wait for his salvation. Despite having had a death-like experience, he testifies to the Lord’s faithfulness. This psalm foreshadows the suffering of Jesus (Luke 23:46).
The psalmist issues an urgent call for the Lord to pay attention to his desperate situation (Psalm 71:2; Psalm 88:2; Psalm 102:2).
I entrust my spirit into your hand: Whether he lives or dies, the psalmist will trust his Lord. Jesus uttered these words on the cross just before he died (Luke 23:46).
Trust in the Lord requires confidence that he has our best interests at heart.
A safe place literally means a broad place, in contrast to a “narrow” or constricted place of distress (see Psalm 18:19).
In this prayer for mercy, the psalmist wedges a description of the intensity of suffering and the pain of rejection between two affirmations of trust (Psalm 31:6, Psalm 31:14).
wasting away from within: This is a powerful description of how despair takes a toll on our physical well-being.
Hope does not confide in frail and changeable human beings but only in the Lord. The sufferer entrusts himself to God while waiting for the Lord’s justice.
My future is in your hands: To relinquish control of timing is one way to express submission.
The psalmist, who did not deserve to be disgraced, invokes the principle of retribution (see study note on 1:6; see also “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note).
Since the godly are under the Lord’s protection and shelter, evil has no power over them.
The psalmist thanks the Lord for answering his prayer (Psalm 31:1-18) and rescuing him.
Praise the Lord: The psalmist expresses his joy at the experience of God’s goodness and love. Throughout his ordeal, the Lord has cared for him.

Out of his own pain and renewed awareness of the Lord’s goodness, the psalmist turns to others who suffer. He holds out the promise of God’s loving care for those who persevere in hoping for the Lord.
The Lord’s forgiveness restores people to fellowship with him, clears them of guilt, and gives them great joy. Paul quoted this text when explaining justification by faith alone (Romans 4:4-8).

This wisdom psalm of confession and thanksgiving encourages and exhorts the godly to learn from the psalmist’s experience of sin, denial, confession, and forgiveness. This psalm was one of the seven psalms of penitence used in the early church (also Psalm 6:1-10, Psalm 38:1-22, Psalm 51:1-19, Psalm 102:1-28, Psalm 130:1-8, Psalm 143:1-12).
The psalmist acknowledges his own sin (see Psalm 19:12-13; Psalm 25:7, Psalm 25:11, Psalm 25:15-22) and his resistance to confessing sin. The Lord pressed him hard until he confessed his guilt.
The psalmist attributes his suffering directly to the Lord’s hand of discipline (cp. Psalm 38:2; Psalm 39:10).
God has forgiven the guilt and rebellion of Psalm 32:1. The Lord’s nature is to reconcile and forgive (Psalm 78:38; Psalm 85:2; Psalm 130:4), but he requires confession and repentance.
The godly will learn from the psalmist’s experience to pray for forgiveness before it is too late.
The Lord promises to be his people’s hiding place (Psalm 31:20). Instead of being overwhelmed by terror (Psalm 31:13), the psalmist is surrounded by songs of victory.
God interrupts the psalmist’s teaching with a message that invites the godly to receive the Lord’s wisdom (see Psalm 5:8; Psalm 23:3; Psalm 25:4-6).
The senseless person is not wise. Rejecting the Lord’s counsel ruins life and makes one like an animal (see Isaiah 1:3; James 3:3).
Difficulties common to all of life will ensnare the wicked, whereas the Lord promises to protect the godly with his care.
The psalmist exhorts the godly to praise the Lord with melodies, with a new song, and with skillfully-played music.

This hymn of creation (see also Psalm 8:1-9, Psalm 19:1-14, Psalm 104:1-35, Psalm 145:1-21) might be a continuation of Psalm 32:1-11. It exhorts readers to praise God (Psalm 33:1-3), to recognize the power of his word in creation (Psalm 33:4-7), and to fear the Creator (Psalm 33:8-11). It offers hope to forgiven sinners (Psalm 32:1-11) that they can live a new life in the fear of the Lord and under divine protection.
God’s word displays his character and his power.
The nations surrounding Israel thought that the sea had divine power, but it is under God’s control, within boundaries that he set (see Psalm 104:8-10).
The power of the Lord extends to all the nations (see 2; Psalm 96:1-3).
Fear of the Lord begins with awe for God and for his powerful word. His word created everything and continues to order and sustain creation. He frustrates the plans of people who oppose his will.
The plans and schemes of the mighty will not prevail, except by God’s will (see Isaiah 8:9-10).
God’s word still orders creation and will do so forever. • God’s intentions are marvelous (Psalm 40:5; Psalm 92:5).
People who fear God are chosen as his inheritance (see Psalm 33:13-19); this excludes rebellious people (Psalm 78:62).
From the heavens, the Lord searches out and cares for anyone who fears him (see Psalm 14:2-3).
army . . . great strength . . . warhorse: Even military might is under God’s control (see Psalm 33:10-11; Ecclesiastes 9:11).
God watches over all who live by his counsel (Psalm 32:8). He protects, rescues, and remains close to them (Psalm 34:15-22).
The godly respond to this magnificent vision of God’s power in creation and in the affairs of the world with an affirmation of trust, commitment, joy, and hope as they pray and wait for God’s rescue.
Using a play on words, the psalmist contrasts his people’s sure hope (Hebrew yakhal) in the Lord with the supposed strength (Psalm 33:17; Hebrew khayil) of the horses of the wicked.
Psalm 34:1 Abimelech is another name for Achish (see 1 Sam 21:10-15). The body of the psalm makes no explicit connection to this event.
The psalmist exhorts the helpless to join him in praise.

This wisdom psalm includes a thanksgiving hymn (Psalm 34:1-7) that celebrates the Lord’s care for and protection of godly sufferers. It also includes an invitation to wisdom (Psalm 34:8-14) and an exposition of wisdom concerning the Lord’s care for the needy and the suffering of the wicked (Psalm 34:15-22).
The psalmist narrates his experiences of answered prayer.
The angel of the Lord represented the Lord’s presence during the wilderness journey. He protected Israel from the forces of Egypt (Exodus 14:19-20), and he will guard all the godly (Psalm 91:11).
The godly encourage everyone to seek wisdom, to fear the Lord, and to place themselves under the protection of the Lord’s angel.
Fear of the Lord includes reverence and respect, and it motivates a life of wisdom (see Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10).
Anyone who listens, even children, can become wise followers of God.
Wisdom contains three components: fearing the Lord (Psalm 34:11), doing good (Psalm 34:14), and rejecting evil (Psalm 34:13).
Peter quotes this passage in his instructions for peaceful living (1 Pet 3:10-12).
Godly people control their words; speaking evil and telling lies are foolish (see Psalm 10:7; cp. Psalm 17:1).
The way of peace leads to harmony and order, whereas evil destroys them (see Psalm 37:11).

The Lord distinguishes between wise and foolish people; he shows his concern for the wise by rescuing them from trouble (Psalm 34:15, Psalm 34:17-20), but he destroys the foolish (Psalm 34:16, Psalm 34:21).

Those who are brokenhearted possess a spirit of deep contrition and dependence on the Lord. God accepts this spirit as a proper sacrifice (Psalm 51:17). The wicked hate the brokenhearted (Psalm 109:16), but the Lord heals them (Psalm 147:3; see Isaiah 57:15; Isaiah 61:1).
The godly might suffer, but the Lord will reward them in the end. Similarly, the wicked might prosper for a time, but ultimately they will perish (Psalm 1:6; Psalm 34:15-16).
Bones represent a person’s entire being (see Psalm 6:2). • not one of them is broken: John applied this statement to Jesus at the crucifixion (John 19:36).
In this lament, the Lord’s troubled servant calls for God to see his circumstances and vindicate him.
The psalmist longs for the Lord’s salvation. The language seems vindictive, but it arises from a desire for justice and for the Lord to care for the needy and oppressed.

A path that is dark and slippery suggests instability and untimely doom under the Lord’s judgment (see Psalm 69:23; Psalm 73:18; Psalm 82:5; Psalm 107:10; Psalm 143:3). • The angel of the Lord is an agent of judgment as well as salvation.
Nothing in the universe can compare with the Lord (see Psalm 86:8; Psalm 89:6, Psalm 89:8; Isaiah 40:18, Isaiah 40:25).
Malicious witnesses want nothing but violence (see Psalm 11:4-6; Psalm 54:3).
The psalmist presents the Lord with the reasons for his suffering. Evil has many faces. He is tired and worn out, and he knows that only the Lord can help him.
The psalmist’s attackers snarl to express their bitter envy.
John applied this claim of innocence (see also Psalm 69:4) to Jesus (John 15:25).

In this prayer for vindication, the psalmist’s crisis looms so large that a resolution must be found in the Lord. The psalmist has taken the high road, believing that vengeance belongs to the Lord. God’s patience hardens the hearts of the wicked and gives them reasons to justify their evil lifestyle.
Aha! . . . Look: Both words translate the same expression of glee (Hebrew he’akh).
The psalmist calls on the Lord to judge the wicked and to rescue the godly and bring them joy.
no fear of God: Paul includes this phrase in his description of the depravity of all people (Romans 3:18).
Fools despise what is wise and good as they pursue evil.

This lament contrasts the world of folly devised by the wicked with the world of wisdom created and sustained by the Lord. The wicked care only about themselves, whereas the Lord cares for all of creation. He will intervene to bring about justice in his world. The righteous will enjoy his protection, but the wicked will perish.
God’s all-encompassing goodness surpasses that of the created order. God graciously meets his people’s practical needs.
As the source of wisdom, the Lord is reliable and incomparable. His faithful care extends to all parts of the created order.
All creatures live by God’s grace (1 Tim 4:10).
God invites all humanity to the banquet in his house (cp. Proverbs 9:1-6).
Light represents salvation and celebration (Psalm 18:25-29; Psalm 27:1; cp. Psalm 35:6).
Since God’s wisdom extends to all of creation, it protects the godly.
The psalmist remains confident that the disorder caused by the wicked (Psalm 36:1-4) will end when they meet their demise.
envy: The jealous desire to have what others enjoy leads to further sin (Psalm 73:3; Proverbs 3:31; James 1:14-15; James 4:1-2).

The wise respond to evil by trusting in the Lord. Trust includes five dimensions: (1) renouncing irritability and envy (Psalm 37:1-2); (2) delighting in the Lord (Psalm 37:3-4); (3) submitting to the Lord (Psalm 37:5-6); (4) practicing patience in hope (Psalm 37:7); and (5) avoiding anger (Psalm 37:8-9).

This psalm elaborates on the problems posed in Psalm 36:1-12: How should the godly respond to the reality of evil? When will the Lord bring justice? Why does he permit the wicked to destroy his created order? Psalm 37:1-40 offers clear responses that reduce the tensions of life (Psalm 37:1-9, Psalm 37:34) and promise that the meek will have a future (Psalm 37:10-11, Psalm 37:39-40). The alternating contrast between the godly and the wicked emphasizes the futility of folly (Psalm 37:12-24, Psalm 37:27-33). The personal observations of the psalmist add a human touch (Psalm 37:25-26, Psalm 37:35-38). He encourages viewing the inheritance of the land from a long-range perspective: The earth belongs to the Lord, who will give it to those he blesses—the lowly and godly who trust in him, put their hope in him, and follow him (see Psalm 37:9, Psalm 37:11, Psalm 37:22, Psalm 37:29, Psalm 37:34; see also Isaiah 57:13; Matthew 5:5).
Finite existence is part of the human condition (see Psalm 90:5-6; Psalm 92:7; Psalm 102:4, Psalm 102:11; Psalm 103:15; Psalm 129:6; Isaiah 40:7-8).
To do good means cultivating a devotion to wisdom (see Psalm 34:14; Proverbs 3:5-7).
The antidote to irritability and envy (Psalm 37:1) is trust in the Lord.
To take delight in the Lord means aligning with the Lord’s way in order to enjoy him.
Justice occurs when the Lord’s will triumphs and the godly experience his rescue (Isaiah 45:8; Isaiah 51:5-6; Isaiah 58:8, Isaiah 58:10-11).
Be still: We should let the Lord be God rather than taking matters into our own hands.
Irritability and anger quickly corrode character.
The wicked will not possess the land; those who trust in the Lord will. The Lord promises an inheritance because he is committed to caring for his people.

The Lord is the author of peace (Psalm 85:10)—he brings peace to a chaotic world (Psalm 29:11; Psalm 37:11; Psalm 85:8; Psalm 147:14). His wisdom guides the lowly into the way of peace (Psalm 119:165; Matthew 5:5).
The wicked snarl to express their bitter envy. They plot to bring an end to the godly, but the Lord derides them because they cannot succeed (Psalm 2:4).
The wicked seek to destroy the Lord’s order, but he defeats them.
The weapons of the wicked will turn against them (cp. Psalm 7:12-13).
Being wise with modest means is better than having prosperity and power and being wicked (Proverbs 15:16; Proverbs 16:8, Proverbs 16:19; Proverbs 17:1; Proverbs 28:6).
The Lord cares for the blameless in this life and for eternity, but the wicked will perish.
Smoke depicts the temporary nature of life (Psalm 68:2; Psalm 102:3).
To borrow and never repay is a behavior of a crooked lifestyle. • Generous givers freely share what they freely receive from the Lord (see Psalm 111:5; Psalm 112:5).
The rectitude and strength of a godly person’s life comes from the Lord (see Proverbs 4:12; Proverbs 14:15; Proverbs 16:9; Proverbs 20:24).
The Lord does not abandon his children or their descendants.

The godly are wise; they do good and reject evil. The Lord cares for them, protecting them and ensuring that they receive their rightful portion of the land as their inheritance. The wicked might try to ambush the godly, but they will not succeed.
The godly base their counsel on the Lord’s wisdom.
They have made God’s law their own: The godly internalize God’s wisdom and instructions (see Psalm 119:11; Jeremiah 24:7; Jeremiah 31:31-34).
The wicked might appear to be flourishing like a tree (cp. Psalm 52:8; Psalm 92:12-13), but they eventually die and are forgotten (Psalm 37:2).
The Lord provides strength for his people.
Psalm 38:1 asking God to remember him: The meaning of this phrase is uncertain (also in Psalm 70:1).
The psalmist’s sins had triggered the Lord’s anger and rage, resulting in the arrows and blows of discipline and rebuke; as a result, his whole body is sick.
