These verses form a prelude to the psalmist’s confession (Psalm 38:18) and describe his woeful condition.
This psalm is a lament and prayer for healing. The psalmist’s suffering is associated with his unconfessed sin. He confesses his sin and entrusts his case to the Lord.

Sin can lead to sickness and even death (1 Cor 11:30). Whether the psalmist actually felt physically ill or his sickness was a metaphor for emotional turmoil, he knew that it came from God and threatened his life (see Psalm 32:3; Psalm 39:10).
The psalmist’s burden results from sin (see Psalm 40:12; Psalm 41:4; cp. Genesis 4:13).
The severity of God’s punishment brings anguish that affects every part of the psalmist’s being.
The psalmist longs for a restored relationship with God, but he feels alienated. He finds himself lost and alone as his friends disappear.
The psalmist suffers quietly before his opponents (see Isaiah 53:7).
The Lord alone will resolve the conflict (Psalm 9:18; Psalm 27:14; Psalm 37:9, Psalm 37:34).
No longer able to endure his suffering and teetering on the verge of collapse (cp. Psalm 15:5), the psalmist confesses his sin (see Psalm 32:5).
That the psalmist’s enemies hate him without reason compounds his pain.

Asking the Lord to act quickly in times of great need is common in the Psalter (Psalm 22:19; Psalm 31:2; Psalm 40:13; Psalm 69:17; Psalm 70:1; Psalm 71:12; Psalm 79:8; Psalm 102:2; Psalm 141:1; Psalm 143:7). However, wisdom and experience teach that God’s people must often wait for him to act (Psalm 27:14; Psalm 37:7; Isaiah 8:17; Isaiah 40:31).
Psalm 39:1 Jeduthun was a levitical singer appointed by David along with Asaph (1 Chr 9:16; 16:38; 25:1).
Suffering in silence only intensifies the psalmist’s anguish, pain, and inner turmoil.
This prayer for rescue reflects the psalmist’s discouragement, which comes from having a limited perspective on his situation.

how fleeting my life is: This perspective comes out of suffering (see Psalm 78:39; Psalm 89:47-48; Psalm 90:3-10). The human lifetime is but a moment to God (Psalm 90:4), as temporary as a breath (see Psalm 39:11; Psalm 144:4).

Because of his suffering and sin, the psalmist concludes that life is meaningless and fleeting (see Job 7:7-10; Isaiah 40:6-8). He had expected a wicked life to have those qualities (see Psalm 37:2, Psalm 37:20; Psalm 103:15-16), but now whether a person is godly or not seems to be irrelevant.
The idea that rebellion brings on suffering is a common thread in Psalm 32:1-11, Psalm 38:1–41:13.
The psalmist links suffering with God’s discipline, assuming that it is punishment for his sin.
The Lord uses discipline to correct his children (Psalm 38:1, Psalm 38:3, Psalm 38:7; Psalm 40:12; see Proverbs 3:11-12; Hebrews 12:5-6).
A guest (or foreigner) had no rights of land ownership (see Leviticus 25:23). The patriarchs had lived as guests in Canaan (Psalm 105:23).
Unlike the psalmist’s earlier request that God stay close to him (Psalm 38:21-22), his present desire for God to leave him alone echoes Job’s disposition (Job 7:17-19).
The psalmist thanks the Lord for his rescue and testifies that God can be trusted.

This psalm includes a thanksgiving song (Psalm 40:1-10) followed by a lament (Psalm 40:11-17). The thanksgiving song includes the reason for the thanksgiving (Psalm 40:1-5), an affirmation of commitment (Psalm 40:6-8), and a public testimony of God’s character (Psalm 40:7-10). The lament concerns the psalmist’s troubles because of his sins (Psalm 40:11-12) and is followed by two prayers for vindication (Psalm 40:13-15, Psalm 40:17).

The Lord delights in the attitude and character of the person making an offering more than in the offering itself. • Now that you have made me listen, I finally understand: Greek text reads You have given me a body. In Hebrews 10:5-7, the writer quotes from the Greek version of Psalm 40:6-8. He casts the words as something Jesus said as he left heaven and came into the world.
As is written about me in the Scriptures: Moses had recorded God’s requirements for Israel’s kings in Deuteronomy 17:14-15.
The psalmist prays that the Lord will be true to his character when answering this plea for mercy.
The psalmist is troubled by both his adversities and his own sins and prays for rescue. • This passage is repeated almost verbatim as Psalm 70:1-5.

The poor who suffer hardship have special protection under God’s law (Leviticus 14:21; Leviticus 19:10); they receive God’s justice and godly rule (Psalm 72:13; Psalm 82:3-4). The word translated poor is often a synonym for the godly (Psalm 113:7; see Zephaniah 3:12).
In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist prays for healing (Psalm 41:4, Psalm 41:10), laments his distress (Psalm 41:5-9), and expresses confidence in the Lord’s blessing (Psalm 41:1-3, Psalm 41:11-12).
when they are sick: This illness might be physical or spiritual (see Psalm 6:2; Psalm 38:1-22).

The psalmist applies the blessing to himself (Psalm 41:12). Apparently he has taken care of the poor (Psalm 41:1), but he has sinned against the Lord in other ways. Out of his pain, he cries for healing while confessing his sin. The Lord alone can grant the restoration that brings true joy (Psalm 30:2; Psalm 107:20-21).
How soon will he die? The psalmist’s opponents regard his suffering as a divine judgment (cp. Psalm 1:6).
The psalmist’s enemies disguise themselves as friends, while his friends openly become his enemies.

the one who shared my food: Eating together was a sign of unity (Acts 2:42). Refusing to eat with someone indicated hostility (1 Cor 5:11). Jesus experienced the same kind of betrayal (John 13:1, John 13:18).
The psalmist knows that the Lord has forgiven him and will bless him.
This doxology closes Book One (Psalm 1:1–41:13). Cp. Psalm 106:48.

Psalm 42:1 The descendants of Korah were members of a Levitical choir appointed by David to serve as Temple singers (see 1 Chr 6:22-38; 9:19-34; 2 Chr 20:19). Their ancestor Korah was the apostate who had rebelled against Moses and whom the earth swallowed up (Exodus 6:24; Numbers 16:1-50).

The psalmist’s longing for God comes from being geographically distant from the Temple as he remembers the past. • The verb translated longs is found only here and in Joel 1:20 (“cry out”); in both cases it refers to extreme thirst in a waterless desert (see Psalm 63:1; Psalm 143:6; see also Psalm 84:2).

These psalms, like Psalm 9:1-20 and Psalm 10:1-18, form a unit comprising a lament with a bittersweet refrain of hope (Psalm 42:5, Psalm 42:11; Psalm 43:5). In many Hebrew manuscripts these two psalms are combined as one. The historical context is uncertain; these psalms might be the voice of God’s people in exile, confessing their loyalty to God as he punishes them for their prevailing apostasy. The psalmist longs for fellowship with God such as he enjoyed in Jerusalem (Psalm 42:4); his memories only make him more discouraged. As the psalmist cries out to God, he recalls God’s love and faithfulness (Psalm 42:8), which moves him to plead for vindication (Psalm 43:1-4).

Having tears for food speaks of great grief (Psalm 80:5; Psalm 102:9; see Psalm 6:6; Psalm 56:8; Psalm 119:136; Psalm 126:5). • The wicked try to hold God to their timetable and deny his power to intervene.
The psalmist recalls leading a great procession as a member of the Levitical choir, possibly during the high holy days.
The psalmist feels depressed, but it does not incapacitate him. He remembers that the living God is his Savior. This verse is repeated in Psalm 42:11 and Psalm 43:5.
The psalmist encourages himself with questions and answers.
Mount Hermon is a high mountain range northeast of Israel. The source of the Jordan is by Dan at the foot of Mount Hermon. • Mount Mizar might be a peak in the Mount Hermon range.
The raging seas, waves, and surging tides conjure images of God’s wrath (see Psalm 88:7).
The psalmist sees rays of hope. A life oriented to God includes songs of joy and praying for justice and vindication (Psalm 42:9-10; Psalm 43:1-4).
The psalmist brings his many doubts, discouragements, and questions directly to God.
The psalmist turns to the Lord for rescue from his troubles, for guidance, for restoration, and for vindication.
tossed me aside: Other psalms similarly ask whether God has rejected his people (Psalm 44:9, Psalm 44:23; Psalm 60:1, Psalm 60:10; Psalm 74:1; Psalm 77:7; Psalm 88:14; Psalm 89:38; Psalm 108:11).

In this prayer for God’s redemption, light and truth are viewed as guides (see Psalm 18:25-29; Psalm 27:1; Psalm 85:10-13; Psalm 89:14-18; see also Psalm 119:105; John 3:19; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thes 5:5-7). • The Temple on the mountain in Jerusalem symbolized God’s holy presence among his people (Psalm 15:1; Psalm 43:3; Psalm 99:5, Psalm 99:9; Psalm 132:7).
This verse is repeated in Psalm 42:5, Psalm 42:11.
we have heard . . . of all you did: The story of redemption encompasses the story of God’s favor and power in his past acts of rescue (see Psalm 78:1-4; see also Psalm 105:1–106:48).

This national lament after defeat in battle continues the tone of the previous two psalms, including reflecting on an unspecified moment in Israel’s history and calling on God for salvation. The people recite God’s past acts of rescue (Psalm 44:1-3), acknowledge God’s power to save (Psalm 44:4-8), describe their humiliation in exile (Psalm 44:9-16), claim their innocence and lament the injustice of their current situation (Psalm 44:17-22), and cry for vindication (Psalm 44:23-26).
God drove out the pagan nations during the conquests recorded in Joshua.
Though the Israelites used swords and other weapons (Psalm 44:6), they would have lost their battles without the light of the Lord’s favor (see Psalm 18:25-29; Psalm 27:1; Psalm 89:15).
God’s people feel confident about his mighty acts; he was with them in the past, and he is their king in the present.
The people have experienced defeat (Psalm 44:9-12), so they understand suffering and disgrace (Psalm 44:13-16).
scattered us among the nations: This probably refers to the Exile (see Psalm 51:18-19; Psalm 89:38-51; Psalm 106:40-47; Psalm 137:1-9).
Paul quotes this verse as a parenthetical aside in his list of things that cannot separate us from Christ’s love (Romans 8:36).
Wake up: Biblical authors often call for God’s attention in a crisis (Psalm 35:23; Psalm 44:23; Psalm 73:20; Psalm 80:2; Mark 4:38).
In the end, God’s people can turn to the Lord and trust him for rescue. Their petition for God to remedy their situation is as strong as their lament about God’s rejection.
Psalm 45:1 The tune “Lilies” is no longer known (see also Psalm 69:1-36).

This psalm celebrates a royal wedding; it might have been sung on many occasions and not just at one wedding. As God’s representative, the king carried the responsibility of dispensing justice and maintaining order in God’s world (see Psalm 2:1-12).

This general description of the king’s symbolic status anticipates his permanent legacy (Psalm 45:16). That the Lord has blessed him and charged him to bear God’s attributes is symbolized by his handsome appearance and gracious words.
Glory and majesty belong to the Lord (Psalm 96:6; Psalm 111:3).
The psalmist expounds on the royal splendor the king showed when fighting his enemies.
As God’s agent of truth, humility, and justice (see Psalm 72:1-2, Psalm 72:4, Psalm 72:7), the king can carry out awe-inspiring deeds (Psalm 65:5; Psalm 96:4).
Justice characterizes God’s rule, as it should characterize the king’s administration.

The king is like a god among humans; he is anointed by God, he has received a mighty throne, and he dispenses justice as he rules forever. • The writer to the Hebrews applies Psalm 45:6-7 to Jesus as he argues that the Son is greater than the angels (Hebrews 1:8-9).
Fine spices mixed with oil create distinctive perfumes. • The king’s palaces were wood paneled with ivory inlays (cp. Psalm 6:4; Amos 3:15).
Marriages often sealed diplomatic connections between kings; the women became part of the harem (see 1 Kgs 11:1-3).

The bride is a representative of the king. Powerful people and nations try to gain her favor in order to get close to the king. This is a great honor, and she is encouraged to give herself fully to her new position.
The princess of Tyre: Israel traded with Tyre, a powerful city-state. The noblest woman of the city bears a wedding gift to her counterpart, the new queen, who represents an honored kingdom.
Psalm 46:1 sung by soprano voices: Hebrew according to alamoth (“maidens”; see also study note on 1 Chr 15:20). In worship, a choir or a group of instrumentalists performed this hymn.
Even when faced with natural disasters, the citizens of Zion express no fear.

This psalm of Zion celebrates God’s special presence in Jerusalem (see also Psalm 48:1-14, Psalm 76:1-12, Psalm 87:1-7, Psalm 122:1-9), inviting confidence in the Lord because the citizens of Zion enjoy his protection.
Like the streams flowing through Eden, this river brings the water of life, restoration, and healing (Psalm 36:8-9; see Genesis 2:10; Ezekiel 47:1-23; Revelation 22:2).
The strong city where God dwells protects its inhabitants. They enjoy the river flowing inside the city. This river contrasts with the turbulent waters (the powers of the nations) outside the city.
From the very break of day: In the ancient Near East, enemies attacked cities during the day; even during the most dangerous times, the Lord will protect the place where his name dwells.

People and nations live in chaos, characterized by opportunism (Psalm 83:2), busyness (Psalm 39:6), and noise. These people shake, totter, and crumble, unlike the city of God (cp. Psalm 15:5). In contrast, when the godly feel disturbed, they cry out for God’s help (Psalm 42:5, Psalm 42:11; Psalm 43:5; Psalm 55:17).
This refrain reminds readers of the identity of the God of Zion. • among us: Hebrew ‘immanu, part of the name Immanuel, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 8:8; Matthew 1:23).
Israel saw the Lord’s glorious works in the wilderness (Psalm 107:24; Psalm 111:2), but the wicked, who have no concern for them (Psalm 28:5), are left desolate (Psalm 73:19).
This invitation to trust in the Lord offers a perspective on God’s interactions with human powers.

A message directly from the Lord confirms the authenticity of the psalmist’s vision (see also Psalm 12:5-6; Psalm 32:8). • know that I am God: The Lord will do what he promises (Isaiah 45:3; Isaiah 49:23; Isaiah 60:16). • God will be exalted (Psalm 47:1-9; Isaiah 6:1); he will judge the nations and rescue his people (see Psalm 57:11; Psalm 89:13; Psalm 108:5-6; Psalm 118:16).
People clap their hands in praise and recognition of marvelous deeds (Psalm 47:3-4; see Psalm 98:8; Isaiah 55:12; cp. Nahum 3:19).
As the sovereign king over the nations, God requires praise.

This psalm celebrates God’s kingship over all the earth; it tells of God’s victory in dealing with Israel and the nations. Both Israel (Psalm 47:3-4) and the nations (Psalm 47:9) participate in God’s kingdom.
The Lord made Israel victorious, especially under David (see Psalm 18:40-50). God’s mighty deeds of redemption manifest his love for Israel.

Jacob’s descendants: Jacob was the father of all Israelites (Genesis 32:28); the name Jacob often represents the nation of Israel. • God loves and commits himself to Jacob (see Psalm 78:68; Psalm 127:2; see Romans 11:28).
trumpets: Or rams’ horns (see Psalm 81:3). At times, rams’ horns were sounded in celebration (Psalm 98:5-6; 2 Kgs 11:14; 1 Chr 15:28).
The psalmist portrays the Lord as returning to heaven, having accomplished his victories. For a portrayal of his descent, see Psalm 18:9-16.
People from all the earth (see Psalm 96:1-3) will worship God.

This song of Zion (see also Psalm 46:1-11, Psalm 76:1-12, Psalm 87:1-7, Psalm 122:1-9) explicitly views Jerusalem (Zion) as the city of the Great King where the godly find protection (Psalm 48:1-3). God rules from Zion in faithfulness, righteousness, and justice, and he inspires his subjects with confidence and joy (Psalm 48:9-11). They commit themselves to seeing the glory of Zion for themselves so that they can tell the next generation about it (Psalm 48:8, Psalm 48:12-14).
God dwells in Zion to protect it from all enemies (see Psalm 46:5).
The ships of Tarshish, built for long voyages, represent human accomplishment (see also 2 Chr 9:21; Isaiah 2:16). Their destruction might be the event mentioned in 1 Kgs 22:48.
The psalmist joyfully celebrates the Lord’s presence in the midst of the community, reflecting on the faithfulness, righteousness, and justice of God’s rule.
towers . . . fortified walls . . . citadels: These structures provide a visual tour of Zion’s strength.

No one is like God (Psalm 35:10; Psalm 71:19; Psalm 86:8; Psalm 89:6, Psalm 89:8; Psalm 113:5; see Isaiah 40:18, Isaiah 40:25). He is the shepherd King (Psalm 95:7) who will guide (see Psalm 5:8; Psalm 23:2) the sheep of his flock (Psalm 77:20).
Anyone who will listen can gain wisdom (Proverbs 1:5, Proverbs 1:8, Proverbs 1:33).
The wisdom teacher invites everyone to the hall of wisdom; he promises to instruct with a proverb and a riddle.

In this wisdom psalm, a wise teacher warns against enemies, whom he portrays as living a rich lifestyle and caring only for themselves (Psalm 49:5-9). They cannot keep anyone alive, least of all themselves, even in their memories (Psalm 49:10-12). Like fattened animals, they are led to slaughter (Psalm 49:14-20).
The teacher used both proverbs and riddles for instruction in wisdom (see Proverbs 1:5-6).
If enemies who live for material rewards cannot sustain themselves, how can they give life to others?
The teacher brings wisdom through irony. Everyone dies, and even those with estates named after them will be forgotten.
The teachers of false wisdom cannot rescue themselves from death. Only God has that power.
The wicked might have rich, luxurious lives, but they forget that they cannot avoid death.
The whole universe must pay attention when God approaches to bring justice into the world.
God appears as judge to remind the godly and the ungodly in turn that outward performance of sacrificial rituals and recitation of the law are worthless without thankfulness, repentance, and justice.

The Lord is coming to bring righteousness. This hope encourages his faithful people, but those who have been unfaithful will not experience blessing when the heavens above and earth below testify against them (cp. Deuteronomy 30:19; Deuteronomy 31:28; Deuteronomy 32:1; Isaiah 1:2). The Lord comes to restore order to the world (Psalm 5:8; Psalm 22:31; Psalm 33:5; Psalm 40:9; Psalm 50:6; Psalm 71:16; Psalm 97:6).
The psalmist delivers a message against those who regard the sacrificial rituals as more important than having a proper heart attitude.
Unlike pagan gods, God does not need food; instead, he wants his people to serve him with a right heart (Psalm 50:14-15).
I own the cattle on a thousand hills: God has no needs; he possesses everything.

Thankfulness means looking beyond self-interest to express gratitude for God’s blessings (see Psalm 51:15-17; Psalm 54:6). • True sacrifice requires offering one’s self to the glory of God (Psalm 50:23; Romans 12:1-2).
God’s response to his people’s cry is to rescue them.
This message is against the wicked, who only pretend to listen to God.
my discipline . . . my words: The wicked may observe rituals, but they reject more important matters such as justice, mercy, and faithfulness (cp. Matthew 23:23-24).
Because he is patient, God remained silent.
God will tear the wicked apart like a lion tearing its prey (Isaiah 5:29; Isaiah 31:4; Ezekiel 19:3; cp. Psalm 7:2; Psalm 22:13).
The wicked will experience God’s justice, while the godly will see God’s everlasting salvation.

A prayer for God’s mercy and kindness is part of the genre of lament. Sometimes the plea comes from the psalmist’s acknowledgment of his weakness and sin, as here (see also Psalm 6:2; Psalm 9:13; Psalm 25:16; Psalm 31:9; Psalm 41:4, Psalm 41:10). At other times, it arises from the psalmist’s commitment to the Lord (see Psalm 26:11; Psalm 27:7; Psalm 119:29, Psalm 119:58, Psalm 119:132). In each case, God’s mercy brings an inner renewal.
The repentant offender has nothing to offer God. He needs God’s favor, mercy, forgiveness, and blessing before he can experience renewal and restoration.

This moving prayer for restoration asks for God’s favor, mercy, forgiveness, and cleansing. Out of a broken spirit, the psalmist confesses and accepts responsibility for his sin (Psalm 51:3-6), then petitions God to remove his guilt and renew him inwardly (Psalm 51:7-12). The psalmist then recommits himself to a lifestyle of wisdom and joy in the service of God and others (Psalm 51:13-17).

These psalms of David share a common thread in their reflection on the experience of evil. In Psalm 51:1-19, the psalmist confesses the evil he has done and asks God’s forgiveness. Psalm 52:1–64:10 lament specific evils that David experienced. A song of praise (Psalm 65:1-13) brings David’s laments to an end.
Wash me . . . Purify me: The psalmist prays for cleansing and release from the guilt of his sin (Psalm 51:7; see Psalm 26:6; Isaiah 1:16, Isaiah 1:18; Isaiah 4:4).
The psalmist accepts the consequences of his sin against God. He knows that there is nothing good in him unless God renews his life.

Against . . . you alone: This is hyperbole—the psalmist knows he also sinned against human beings (2 Sam 11:2-4, 15-17), but his offense against God is more important. He expects God to rebuke him and will accept whatever verdict God renders (see Romans 3:4).
I was born a sinner: The psalmist is not making excuses but is acknowledging the depth of his sinfulness. From the time we are conceived, we all share in the human condition of sinfulness.
Purify me from my sins (literally Purify me with the hyssop branch; see Exodus 12:22; Leviticus 14:4; John 19:29; Hebrews 9:19): The psalmist depends on God to purify and renew him (see Isaiah 1:18).
Regaining joy is a gracious gift from God. • you have broken me: The psalmist’s whole being feels broken (Psalm 6:2; cp. Psalm 34:20).
A loyal spirit yields the inner qualities of constancy and perseverance.
God’s Spirit renews and recreates the human spirit.
your Holy Spirit: Only the power of the Holy Spirit can change the human will to make it “loyal” (Psalm 51:10) and “willing to obey” (Psalm 51:12).
As he learns from his sin and its consequences, the psalmist wants to teach others.
shedding blood: This idiom includes any injustice, not just homicide (Psalm 9:12; Psalm 58:10; see 2 Sam 11:14-26; cp. Isaiah 1:15-17).

rebuild the walls of Jerusalem: These verses were probably added as a prayer for national restoration after the Exile (see Psalm 42:1–43:5); the entire community in exile identified with the spirit of the psalm.
Sacrifices offered in the right spirit come from a heart that is right with God and with others (see Psalm 15:2-5; Psalm 24:3-6; Psalm 50:14; Matthew 5:23-24).
Psalm 52:1 This psalm refers to an incident in 1 Sam 21:1-10; 22:9-10. The accuser, Doeg the Edomite, is a paradigm of evil.

Liars foolishly deceive themselves by thinking that they can be heroes by their words. They believe themselves innocent of any charges of evildoing, though they love evil and cause destruction. Those who speak curses, sarcasm, bitterness, arrogant boasting, and deceptions (Psalm 31:18; Psalm 34:13; Psalm 59:7, Psalm 59:12; Psalm 120:2-3; Psalm 140:3, Psalm 140:9) bring about chaos, alienation, and destruction (James 3:5). Their sharp words cut like swords and daggers (Psalm 55:21; Psalm 57:4; Psalm 64:3), the fangs of a snake (Psalm 140:3), or a razor.

Wicked people use words to destroy relationships and communities. They foolishly think that they can be heroes by their words (Psalm 52:1-4), but their fate suddenly overtakes them (Psalm 52:5-7). In contrast, the godly renew their commitment to the Lord (Psalm 52:8-9) and find their future secure in him.
Deceptive speech changes one’s character.
God will strike the wicked down like a pagan altar, idol, or unclean vessel (Exodus 34:13; Leviticus 11:35; 2 Kgs 10:27).
God’s judgment on the wicked will come suddenly and forcibly. The godly rejoice in God’s justice, not in the misfortunes of the wicked.
In Hebrew, the verbs here translated see and be amazed sound almost alike.

The psalmist commits himself to a life of trust in the Lord. • An olive tree lives a long time when cared for (Psalm 1:3; Psalm 128:3). The psalmist desires to be close to the Lord, his Savior and the source of his blessing (Psalm 18:6; Psalm 23:6).
Paul uses the Greek translation of this passage in his description of the depravity of all people (Romans 3:10-12).
This psalm parallels Psalm 14:1-7, differing only in verse 5.
scatter the bones: Israel’s enemies would suffer shameful defeat and lack the peaceful rest of a decent burial (cp. Psalm 141:7; 2 Kgs 9:10; Jeremiah 8:1-2; Ezekiel 6:5).
Psalm 54:1 This psalm refers to the account of 1 Sam 23:19-20, when the Ziphites were bent on violence.

In this individual lament, occasioned by violent and godless people (Psalm 54:3), the psalmist turns to God in prayer and maintains his focus on God’s help (Psalm 54:4). He prays for God to save him from evil and to judge his enemies (Psalm 54:5, Psalm 54:7).

The strangers were alienated from the covenant community (see Psalm 109:11; Proverbs 5:10). • Proud and violent people hold no regard for God or for other people (see Psalm 35:11, Psalm 35:25; Psalm 86:14; Proverbs 11:16).
A voluntary offering is a sacrifice of praise. Sacrifices of praise are the kind of offering God most desires (see Psalm 50:14-15, Psalm 50:23).
In anticipation of God’s response, the mood of the psalm changes from gloom to thanksgiving.
The occasion for this prayer is an attack by an enemy.

The psalmist is faced with adversaries whose leader is a former friend (Psalm 55:12-14), and he is overwhelmed with anguish. He turns to the Lord in prayer and commits himself to the Lord for redress (Psalm 55:22-23). Jesus experienced similar suffering when his friend (Judas) betrayed him. He also experienced the answer to the psalmist’s prayer: (1) by taking the place of the wicked and receiving their judgment (Isaiah 53:7-9), and (2) by committing himself to the Father, who rescued (Luke 23:46) and rewarded him (Isaiah 53:10-12).
In the experience of deep anguish, the psalmist confesses that his adversity has become unbearable and he seeks an escape.
The psalmist’s enemy was once a friend; memories of that close relationship bring him pain (see Psalm 31:11).
God is good and faithful, but the psalmist’s enemies and so-called friend are deceitful and wicked.
The psalmist commits all his cares to the Lord.
To die young means that one fails to experience God’s full blessing (cp. Proverbs 3:2, Proverbs 3:16).
Psalm 56:1 David was seized by Philistines concerned about his loyalties and brought before King Achish (1 Sam 21:10-15).
This individual lament moves from petition to confidence two times (Psalm 56:1-4, Psalm 56:5-13).
mere mortals: Or mere flesh, in contrast to the immortal and infinitely more powerful God (see Isaiah 2:22).
The psalmist specifies his charge against his attackers as he prays for their evil to cease.
The psalmist makes a play on the Hebrew words translated sorrows (Hebrew nod) and bottle (Hebrew no’d).
mere mortals (Hebrew ’adam): The psalm also uses two other words for man: ’enosh (“people,” Psalm 56:1) and basar (“mere mortals,” Psalm 56:4). All express the ideas of mortality and finitude.
The light of God’s goodness and salvation will replace the darkness of death (see Psalm 18:25-29; Psalm 27:1).
shadow of your wings: As a bird protects its young, God protects the one who trusts in him (see Psalm 17:8).

The psalmist’s cry for mercy and protection quickly turns into an affirmation of trust and confidence in the Lord (Psalm 57:1-4). When the wicked fall into their own traps (Psalm 57:6), the psalmist will praise the Lord (Psalm 57:7-10).

God Most High (Hebrew Elohim-Elyon) is a generic title for God, who is more powerful than all real or imagined supernatural beings (see Psalm 91:1; Psalm 97:9; Genesis 14:18-22). • who will fulfill his purpose: Or who will end my [trouble], or who deals kindly with me.

These verses are a prayer for rescue from powerful enemies. The metaphor of fierce lions describes human enemies; the psalmist feels unable to escape them without God’s intervention (see also Psalm 35:11-21; Psalm 124:6).
This verse is repeated in Psalm 57:11 and Psalm 108:5. • God’s glory—his manifest presence that excludes all evil (Psalm 8:1; Psalm 19:1-4; Psalm 24:7)—will fill the whole created order (Isaiah 6:3).
The psalmist is confident that God will end the night of evil (cp. Psalm 56:13).
This section is repeated with a few modifications in Psalm 108:1-5.
God’s glory extends to the whole universe, as will praise for his unfailing love and faithfulness.

rulers (or gods): This designation was used for high officials and administrators of justice (Psalm 82:1, Psalm 82:6). Elsewhere, it might refer to angelic creatures (Psalm 89:7) or to the gods of the nations (Psalm 82:1; Daniel 11:36).
The administrators of justice were furthering their own interests rather than those of the needy. The absence of justice gradually resulted in a violent society.

The administration of justice is a mark of good government. God expects nothing less from his people. The psalmist condemns Israel’s leaders for abusing their power, and he calls on the Lord to rain down his curses upon the wicked. The demonstration of divine justice will reassure the godly that God is just.
All human beings are born sinners (see Psalm 51:5); however, whereas the wicked indulge their sinful nature, the godly fight against it (Romans 7:19-23; James 4:1-10).
Venom here means poisonous speech (see Psalm 140:3).
The psalmist calls on God to break the destructive power of the wicked.
When moving over dry ground, snails dry up.
God’s judgment will come suddenly. The certainty of vindication brings joy to the godly.
Vindication is the reward of those who live for God.
Psalm 59:1 the time Saul sent soldiers to watch David’s house: See 1 Sam 19:11-18.
Protect me (or place me on high): When surrounded by evil, the godly pray for God to set them apart for himself and protect them.
The psalmist laments the power of enemies who conspire with other nations.
The psalmist asks God to show the treacherous, deceptive, and wicked traitors no mercy (see Psalm 25:2).
The wicked threaten like vicious dogs, but the Lord responds with scorn.
The psalmist prays that the wicked will be forced to endure the same agonizing pain they have caused.
The wicked will go unsatisfied, but the psalmist will praise the Lord’s power and unfailing love.

Psalm 60:1 useful for teaching: This psalm was taught to young people as part of their education. • regarding the time: See 2 Sam 8:13-14. • Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah refer to the Arameans of northwest Mesopotamia and Syria (see study note on Gen 24:10). • The tune “Lily of the Testimony” is unknown today.
When God’s people experience his discipline, they affirm their loyalty and await God’s answer.
The psalmist laments a national defeat and cries out to God for rescue.

wine (Hebrew yayin) that sent us reeling: Yayin, the generic Hebrew term meaning “wine,” is often associated with drunkenness (2 Sam 13:28; Isaiah 5:11; Isaiah 28:7-8; cp. Psalm 104:15; Deuteronomy 14:26; Isaiah 55:1); it symbolized God’s judgment of the wicked (Psalm 75:8; Jeremiah 51:7).

God raised a banner over his people to serve as a rallying point and as a source of pride and confidence. • The fear of God that leads to wisdom (Psalm 111:10) is not weakness; it provides the perspective and strength required to do what is right.
The psalmist prays for rescue based on the special relationship between God and his people.
This section is repeated verbatim in Psalm 108:6-13.
Shechem and Succoth represent Israel’s heartland.
The Lord responds with a message of promise. He shares his land with his people as spoils of war.

Destroying a defeated invader’s capital (the fortified city) would help to ensure that they would not attack again. The capital of Edom was Bozrah, located to the southeast of Israel. Only God could grant victory.
The lamenting psalmist petitions God to protect him and lead him into his presence (Psalm 61:4-5). He prays for God to extend and protect the king’s rule and makes vows to praise God.
In these royal prayers, the psalmist longs for God’s presence. All three psalms concern themselves with the king’s security.
the ends of the earth: This expression has the connotation of a cry that comes from a place far away from God. • The psalmist’s heart is overwhelmed with deep anguish.

The poet longs for God’s presence and seeks entrance into God’s home on earth for divine protection and care. To be received into God’s sanctuary (literally tent) is the greatest good (see Psalm 15:1; Psalm 23:6; Psalm 24:3-6). The Hebrew word translated sanctuary recalls the Tabernacle and the tent that David built for the Ark (1 Chr 15:1). See also study note on John 1:14. • The shelter of your wings symbolizes God’s protection and care (see Psalm 9:9; Psalm 17:8).

you have heard my vows: The psalmist’s vows might also be a part of ceremonial sacrifices (Psalm 66:13-15; Psalm 76:11; Psalm 116:14, Psalm 116:18). He praises and thanks God for his rescue. • The inheritance refers to the promise of the land (see Psalm 60:1-12), the sacredness of the Temple, the joy of God’s presence (Psalm 119:111), or any similar reward (Psalm 16:6; Psalm 37:9, Psalm 37:11, Psalm 37:18, Psalm 37:22, Psalm 37:29, Psalm 37:34; Psalm 127:3).
Psalm 62:1 Jeduthun: See 1 Chr 25:1; also in Psalm 39:1-13 and Psalm 77:1-20.

This psalm expresses confidence in the king and offers prayer for him. The king rests in God despite his difficulties. Although his deceptive and powerful adversaries push hard against him, he remains undaunted. He encourages himself and his people to trust in God and to see their human adversaries from God’s perspective, where they appear frail, fleeting, and deceptive (Psalm 62:9).
The enemies desire to topple the king with lies and cunning.
My high position refers to the royal throne.
The psalmist encourages himself and others to place their hope in God.
not what they appear to be: People often try to look stronger and better than they are.
Unlike God, humans are transient beings. Even when they thrive, their prosperity is fleeting.
The crime of extortion means using intimidation and threats to make others give up what is theirs, while stealing is taking what belongs to others.
Strength and unfailing love remain in balance only in God. He cares for his people by ridding the world of evildoers (see Psalm 1:6).

Together, soul and whole body refer to a person’s entire being. • parched and weary land: When David was living in the desert, he also found himself in a spiritual wasteland, separated from God’s people and the sanctuary.

The king longs for God’s presence so vividly that he eats, drinks, and sees God’s goodness. Though worn out and harassed by the wicked, the king sees God, and this animates him with praise. God becomes his life (Psalm 63:3), while the wicked perish (Psalm 63:9).
The psalmist remembers that he had found God to be present in his sanctuary (see Psalm 18:6; Psalm 61:4; Psalm 62:5, Psalm 62:11-12).
better than life itself: The highest quality of life is found in relationship with God (see Psalm 4:7; Psalm 63:5; Proverbs 16:8).
Meditating on God requires focused awareness, concentration, thought, and reflection (see Psalm 1:2).

The psalmist reflects and meditates on God’s presence through the night. In the absence of light, God is the light. The quietness of the night and the longing for dawn provide time to focus on the true significance of life with the Lord.
The wicked were plotting to destroy the psalmist’s life through deception and lies, but they would meet their end. • The depths of the earth refers to the place of the dead.

Wild jackals are associated with desolation and abandonment (Isaiah 13:20-22; Isaiah 34:10-15; Jeremiah 9:11; Jeremiah 49:33; Jeremiah 51:37; Lamentations 5:18; Malachi 1:3). The wicked will not receive honor in death; their bodies will be left to scavenging animals (Ecclesiastes 6:3; Jeremiah 22:18-19; Jeremiah 36:29-30).
These verses form a prayer for rescue from bold and powerful liars.

This lament decries the destructive plots and arrogant attitude of the wicked (Psalm 64:1-6). The psalmist turns to God in prayer and takes heart in God’s justice because whatever the wicked do will be undone by the righteous judge. The godly will rejoice and grow in wisdom as they reflect on God’s mighty acts.
their tongues . . . bitter words: Liars use their speech to kill. This description might also refer to practicing magic.
The enemies create a perfect plan to harm the innocent without getting caught. • Human beings will sink to unthinkable depths with evil words, acts, or plans (Psalm 83:3; see Jeremiah 17:9).
What God does is righteous. God undoes what is wicked and pays the wicked back with what they planned for others.
God alone deserves praise and is worthy to have vows made to him.
Praise is the appropriate response to God’s majestic deeds in redemption (Psalm 65:3-5) and in nature (Psalm 65:5-13).
This psalm recounts the reasons why all people should praise and revere God for his almighty power and merciful care for his universe.
All of us means all humans.
you forgive: God graciously removes the guilt of sin (see Psalm 32:5).

those you choose to bring near: This includes people from Israel and from other nations. • Only those whom God sees as blameless live in his holy courts (Psalm 15:1-5 and Psalm 24:1-10). • At the Temple, God’s earthly palace, all nations can gather to experience God’s holy presence. No structure can separate humans from God (see Revelation 21:22).

God brought order to the mountains, the raging oceans, and the pounding waves (see Psalm 95:4-5; Psalm 104:6-9). • The psalmist compares the chaotic forces of nature with the rebellion of the nations (see Psalm 2:1-12; Psalm 33:6-11; Psalm 46:6).
All over the world (Job 38:13; see Psalm 50:1-3), people should stand in awe of the Lord.

The river of God and all rivers demonstrate God’s victorious power and goodness through the order in nature and the regularity of the harvests (see Psalm 1:3; Psalm 36:8; Psalm 46:4; Ezekiel 47:6-12; Zechariah 14:8; Revelation 22:1).
The created order provides clear evidence of God’s power (Psalm 65:6-8). He shows his love by maintaining nature. Everything praises the Lord as all the parts fit together harmoniously.
Nature bursts out in praise of the Creator (see Psalm 79:13; Psalm 96:11-13; Psalm 148:3-5, Psalm 148:7-12; Isaiah 55:12-13).
The psalmist exhorts nature to join in a mighty chorus to praise God’s glory, name, and power.
This anonymous psalm includes two hymns (Psalm 66:1-12, Psalm 66:13-20) that praise God for his redemption.
The glory of his name represents the perfection of God’s character.
God conquers his enemies (see Psalm 18:44; Psalm 59:11; Psalm 81:15).
The story of the Exodus and God’s victory over the sea evokes responses of astonishment (Psalm 66:5) and worship (Psalm 66:6). God works miracles . . . for people in order to redeem them for himself.
God’s power brings redemption. The same word occurs in Psalm 65:6 for God’s power in creation (see also Psalm 80:2).
The orderly lives of the redeemed reflect the order of God’s world. The Lord protects them from evil and purifies them.
God guides his people into wisdom and away from folly (Psalm 17:5; Psalm 37:31; Psalm 121:3).
You have tested us, O God: As the silversmith heats silver to remove the dross, God’s discipline removes sin from his people (see Psalm 12:6).
God decrees and permits the many trying circumstances his people experience.
Then you put a leader over us: Or You made people ride over our heads. This expression possibly refers to a foreign ruler who kept the Israelites in submission.
Vows often included sacrifices of thanksgiving, including burnt offerings (see Psalm 20:3; Psalm 40:6; Psalm 50:8; Psalm 51:19).
The private testimony in the conclusion of the psalm parallels the public praise of its opening (Psalm 66:1-4).
Confession leads to restoration (see Psalm 32:5).
This prayer is based on the priestly blessing found in Numbers 6:24-26. God’s goodness to Israel affects his reputation among the nations (see Psalm 96:1-3).

In this anonymous prayer for God’s blessing, the psalmist addresses the knowledge and worship of God among the nations (cp. Psalm 64:9; Psalm 65:8). The prayer requests that God’s name be kept holy and that his kingdom come (cp. Matthew 6:9-13).

God’s international reputation leads to his praise among the nations (see Psalm 138:4), whose turmoil and rebelliousness will cease when they join Israel in praise of God. • One God rules over all, and the nations will give thanks for God’s just rule (see Psalm 67:4).
God brings the ultimate justice that human beings desire (Psalm 96:10; Psalm 98:9).

Bountiful harvests are evidence of God’s blessing (Genesis 26:12; Isaiah 30:23). • all over the world: See Psalm 2:8; Psalm 96:1-3. • All will fear him, joining with Israel to acknowledge the God of Israel.
These verses form a prayer for God to rise up and scatter his enemies, as he did when Israel entered the Promised Land (cp. Numbers 10:35-36; Joshua 6:1–12:24).

This prayer for God’s victorious rule traces God’s march from Sinai to Zion (Psalm 68:7, Psalm 68:16-18, Psalm 68:24). He rescued the nation of Israel from Egypt, guided it through the wilderness, brought it into the Promised Land, and established his kingdom. He is a caring and victorious God, whose nature is unchanging. Therefore, the godly hope and rejoice in the prospect of God’s universal dominion.
Both smoke and wax represent a transitory existence (Psalm 22:12-18; Psalm 37:20; Psalm 102:3).
The lot of the godly contrasts with that of the wicked (see Psalm 1:6).

him who rides the clouds: This is an ancient description of Baal, a Canaanite deity. The psalmist applies it to the Lord as the true “Rider of the Clouds” (see Psalm 68:33; Psalm 104:3). God wields power over the clouds and the rain.
The psalmist praises God’s powerful and compassionate reign.

God, the Father of all marginalized and needy people, shows them compassion and protects their rights (see Psalm 10:14, Psalm 10:18; Psalm 69:33; Psalm 82:3). • Like his dwelling, the Lord is holy. The supreme example of the holy God coming down to rescue humanity is Jesus Christ.
God released Israel from slavery in Egypt (Exodus 20:2; see Psalm 69:33), and he still sets the prisoners free. • The sun-scorched desert represents alienation from God and separation from blessing.
The earth trembled as in an earthquake (see Exodus 19:18). • the heavens poured down rain: Wells in the desert and rain showers in Canaan supplied an abundance of water.
a great army (or a host of women) brings: The Hebrew suggests women singers caroling the good news of victory (see Psalm 68:25; Exodus 15:20).
The seminomadic pastoral people who lived among the sheepfolds were surprised to receive silver and gold carvings from the battle.

The Almighty (Hebrew Shaddai) is an ancient designation for God (see Psalm 91:1; Genesis 17:1). • The identification of Mount Zalmon is uncertain; it was possibly a mountain in Bashan (see Psalm 68:15).

Bashan is a plateau northeast of Jerusalem and east of the Sea of Galilee that was known for its woods and pastureland (see Psalm 22:12; Isaiah 2:13). The mountains might have included Mount Hermon to the north of the plateau or Mount Zalmon, which might be Jebel ed-Druze on the east.

Why do you look with envy? Bashan is physically much more impressive than the mountains around Jerusalem, but it was not the home of the Lord. Only Mount Zion enjoyed the privilege of providing God’s dwelling place.
Chariots, the ultimate weapon of the armed forces in the psalmist’s day, are an image of the Lord’s power to grant victory (Psalm 20:7; Psalm 44:3).

When you ascended to the heights: The Most High established his reign victoriously in Zion. • a crowd of captives . . . gifts: This is an image of a victorious ruler leading the victory march after battle. Paul applied this image to Jesus Christ (Ephesians 4:8-13).
Like a caring father or a shepherd, God carries his people in his arms (see Psalm 55:22; Psalm 68:5-6).
The Divine Warrior cares for his people like a shepherd; the people praise him.
God will smash the heads of his enemies: Cp. Genesis 3:15.
God will deal with all enemies, whether from high places (represented by Bashan) or low (the depths of the sea).
A great company joins together in the pilgrimage to Zion.
The people pray for God’s success and for victory over the enemy nations (Psalm 68:1-3).
The conquered kings will bring gifts to the Lord.
Hostile and rebellious people delight in warfare and insurrection (see Psalm 2:1-3).
The term kingdoms of the earth includes all nations and power structures.
The psalmist calls for the people to praise God, who is victorious over his enemies.
When the Lord demonstrates his power, majesty, and strength against the nations, he strengthens his people (see Psalm 96:4-6).

Psalm 69:1 to the tune “Lilies”: Psalm 45:1-17 also notes this tune, but Psalm 45:1-17 celebrates the glory of kingship, whereas Psalm 69:1-36 is the cry of a tired king who feels abandoned by the Lord.
The psalmist sees himself as almost drowning but still surviving chaotic forces and alienation from God (see Psalm 42:7; Psalm 69:14, Psalm 69:15; Isaiah 8:8).
In this individual lament, the poet expresses his vulnerability, humiliation, and overwhelming pain, asking God to vindicate him for the sake of the righteous.

These last four psalms of Book Two contrast with the psalms describing God’s mighty acts in creation and in redemption, capped by God’s march to Zion (Psalm 65:1–68:35). Psalm 69:1–71:24 portray the king’s anguish, and Psalm 72:1-20 responds with a prayer for God to bless the king.
John applied this lament to Jesus (John 15:25).
The psalmist confesses his sins and prays that God’s response to him will encourage others in similar conditions to place their hope in the Lord.
Mistreated and abandoned by family, friends, and community, the psalmist turns to the Lord for comfort, relief (Psalm 69:13-18), and redress (Psalm 69:22-28).

Though the psalmist concerns himself with God and all that is holy, insults have been his earthly reward. This verse was later applied to Jesus’ anger at the Temple’s money changers (John 2:17) and to his undeserved suffering (Romans 15:3).
When the psalmist denies himself normal comforts to seek God in prayer, the wicked ridicule him.
The psalmist’s only recourse is to pray for rescue and relief from his enemies.
Alone and misunderstood, the psalmist confesses that he cannot bear his doubts. His heart has been broken by his problems.
sour wine for my thirst: This description applies to Jesus’ suffering (Matthew 27:34, Matthew 27:48; Luke 23:36; John 19:28-29).
The psalmist wants God to transfer his suffering (Psalm 69:3) to his enemies. Paul applied these words to the unbelieving Jews of his day (Romans 11:9-10).
Peter quoted this verse after the death of Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:20).
Erase their names from the Book of Life: Cp. Psalm 1:5-6; Psalm 9:5; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 20:15; Revelation 21:22-27.
The psalmist prays that his pain will turn to praise.
Making a vow often included a sacrifice (Psalm 20:3; Psalm 51:19; cp. Psalm 50:13-14; Psalm 51:16).
despise: See Psalm 22:24; cp. Matthew 25:36; Hebrews 13:3.
The psalmist prays for Zion, offering a new petition from a new circumstance. He applies the prayer (Psalm 69:1-33) to the desperate condition of Judah (see Psalm 51:18-19).
God’s people will inherit the land because the wicked will perish (see Psalm 37:8-9).
Psalm 70:1 asking God to remember him: The meaning of this phrase is unknown (also found in Psalm 38:1).
This psalm, nearly identical to Psalm 40:13-17, contains an urgency (Psalm 70:1, Psalm 70:5) that fits with the surrounding psalms (cp. Psalm 69:17; Psalm 71:12).
The poet has learned to acknowledge God as the reliable rock who will do what is right toward him and his oppressors. See also Psalm 31:1-3.

This untitled lament by an aging believer is more of a confession of confidence and hope than the cry of someone abandoned by God. The psalmist experienced God’s power and protection in his youth (Psalm 71:5-8) and now prays for rescue from the adversaries who stalk him in his old age (Psalm 71:9-13). Even in the midst of his peril, he continues to tell of God’s past faithfulness and looks forward with hope to a time when he can testify to the next generation that God is faithful and righteous.
The psalmist has trusted God throughout his life (see Psalm 22:9).
The poet prays for continued fellowship with God (see Psalm 9:10; Psalm 51:11). In his weakness, he needs the Lord’s strength even more (see Psalm 143:7).

The aging believer turns to the Lord for hope. As questions from his adversaries get under his skin and his own strength fails, he asks God to answer his prayers. He does not seek answers to prayer for himself but so that he can tell the story to the next generation.
In their plotting, the psalmist’s enemies take counsel and scheme together (Psalm 2:2; Psalm 21:11; Psalm 31:13; Psalm 35:4; Psalm 63:9-10).
The psalmist contrasts his own goodness with his enemies’ evil; he centers his life in the Lord, even during hard times (see Psalm 9:17-18; Psalm 27:13-14).
God’s righteous character provides encouragement and strength in the midst of suffering. The wounded psalmist confesses faith in God’s ability to transform his misery and weakness into abundant life.
lift me up from the depths: The psalmist hopes for the renewal of an abundant earthly life. This later became grounds for belief in the resurrection of the dead.

Being assured of God’s comfort also assures the poet of God’s presence, care, and goodness (Psalm 23:4, Psalm 23:6; Psalm 86:17). God’s comfort enhances the psalmist’s sense of being alive (see Psalm 119:50).
As he awaits God’s rescue, the psalmist prepares himself to declare with instruments and voice that God is faithful and righteous.
love of justice . . . righteousness: Kings in the ancient Near East were expected to represent justice; the standard for Israel’s kings was much higher because the Lord was their model.
The blessings of justice create a balance in nature, resulting in harmony, prosperity, and fertility.

This royal psalm closes Book Two, with Psalm 72:18-20 functioning as an epilogue to all of Book Two. The psalmist reflects on the prospects of David’s royal line and on Zion (see Psalm 46:1-11, Psalm 48:1-14). He prays that Israel’s kings will be good and prosperous, extending the Lord’s blessing on his people throughout the whole earth. The surpassing righteousness and dominion sought in this prayer foreshadow the coming of Jesus, the Son of David.
The administration of justice transforms the earth into fruitfulness, abundance, harmony, and goodness (see Isaiah 32:16-17).
A just ruler will defend the poor against injustice, rescue them from violence, and bring their oppressors to account for their wrongdoing.

May they fear you: In Hebrew, this clause seems to be a response to the enforcement of justice. The Greek version reads May they endure, which makes this a prayer for longevity (Psalm 21:4; Psalm 72:15, Psalm 72:17).

The administration of justice is refreshing like spring rain, enabling the godly to flourish (see Isaiah 45:8) like flowers. • until the moon is no more: This phrase means forever (see Psalm 89:36-37).

from sea to sea: This phrase represents the whole world. • Solomon’s kingdom extended from the Euphrates River in the east to the Philistine territory in the west (1 Kgs 4:21; see Psalm 80:8-11; Psalm 89:19-25), where the Mediterranean Sea appeared to be at the ends of the earth (see Psalm 2:8). Everyone will bow before this king, including the desert nomads (Psalm 72:9), his enemies, and all the kings of the world (see Micah 7:17).

The anointed king will rule over the whole world. Even hostile nations will submit to him. In the ancient Near East, bearing gifts to the king acknowledged his success and his reputation (see 1 Kgs 10).

The western kings of Tarshish came from a major colony in the western basin of the Mediterranean. The eastern kings of Sheba came from an area in southern Arabia, home of the queen of Sheba (1 Kgs 10). • Seba was probably located somewhere south of Egypt, perhaps on the western shore of the Red Sea across from Sheba. • The gifts offered to the king represented a tribute and a token of submission.

All kings and all nations must submit to the messianic king. The hope expressed in Psalm 2:10-11 will be realized (see Psalm 96:1-3; 1 Cor 15:25) when other leaders and peoples bow before and serve this king.
To rescue the poor means to bring an end to the rule of their oppressors.
The anointed king will rescue the needy. He is not only the judge but also a father to the poor (Psalm 10:14, Psalm 10:17; Psalm 68:5).
Like a father, the king feels pity for those in need (see Malachi 3:17).
The people will bless him, fulfilling God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3; see Psalm 133:3).
The just kingdom will be long-lasting and universal. The summary combines the themes of abundance of crops, longevity, tribute of the nations, and the prayer of the nations.
the trees of Lebanon: Lebanon was renowned for its lumber (see study note on 2 Chr 2:8).
This doxology concludes Book Two of the Psalter.

This parenthetical note ends Book Two, which consists mostly of prayers of David. Books Three to Five were probably compiled after Book Two; they include additional psalms of David (Psalm 86:1-17, Psalm 101:1-8, Psalm 103:1-22, Psalm 108:1–110:7, Psalm 122:1-9, Psalm 124:1-8, Psalm 131:1-3, Psalm 133:1-3, Psalm 138:1–145:21).
People whose hearts are pure are renewed by God’s Spirit (Psalm 51:10), commit themselves to lives of godliness, keep away from anything that is sinful, and enjoy God’s presence (see Psalm 24:3-4).

This wisdom psalm examines the injustice of the prosperity of the wicked. The psalmist affirms that God is good to the godly but his own experience differs (Psalm 73:2-12). Nearly overcome by his doubts (Psalm 73:13-16), the psalmist meets the Lord in the sanctuary and gains a perspective that stretches beyond his life and renews his confidence in God (Psalm 73:17-26). His disturbing doubts stir a greater passion for truth. He knows that he can trust God and that God will rescue him (Psalm 73:27-28).

The apparent prosperity of the wicked (Psalm 73:1-28) and God’s apparent rejection of his people (Psalm 74:1-23) raise questions about his justice. God is sovereign over the whole world, and he determines the time for judgment (Psalm 75:1-10).

The poet sees the prosperity of the wicked as unfair (see Psalm 72:7) and resents it. • The psalmist’s feet were slipping from the way of wisdom and godliness (see Psalm 17:5; Psalm 37:31), but God kept him from falling off the trail entirely (Psalm 38:16; Psalm 66:9; Psalm 94:18; Psalm 121:3). • when I saw them prosper: Cp. Psalm 72:3, Psalm 72:7.
The psalmist presents a caricature of the bliss of the wicked (cp. Psalm 1:1-6).
The proud adorn themselves with pride and cruelty rather than wisdom (Proverbs 1:9).
The proud boast, claiming that they own everything and are not subject to anyone (see Psalm 2:1-3).

These rhetorical questions expect a discouraging “yes” for an answer. The psalmist wonders if godliness has become a meaningless ritual (see Malachi 3:14-15). • My heart refers to his whole being. • The psalmist’s pain comes from discipline and rebuke (Psalm 39:11; Proverbs 1:23, Proverbs 1:25; Proverbs 12:1).
Recognizing the ramifications of his discouragement and doubt, the psalmist turns to the Lord and receives special insight.

If the psalmist had verbalized his suspicions about the futility of godly living, he would have discouraged God’s people and given God’s enemies an opportunity to blaspheme (cp. John 13:20). Instead, the psalmist internalizes the problem and reflects on it.

At this time, God’s sanctuary was the Temple in Jerusalem. There, in God’s presence, the psalmist receives special insight (cp. Psalm 18:6). • God deals with the wicked over the long term. He waits patiently and gives them time to repent (Ezekiel 33:11; 2 Pet 3:9); those who do not repent will get what they deserve.
The psalmist’s feelings about the prosperity of the wicked had given him a bitter spirit.
The Lord leads the godly through their troubles and changes their misery into splendor.
Nothing in heaven or on earth is better than being near God.
God rejected his people because their sin aroused his anger (Psalm 106:34-46). • Like a tender shepherd, God cares for his people, the sheep of his pasture (Psalm 23:1-6; Psalm 100:3).
In the aftermath of Jerusalem’s fall, it seemed that God had forgotten his special covenant relationship with his people.
The psalmist laments the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem (586 BC) with vivid imagery, questions, fresh memories, and a direct appeal for the Lord to act (Psalm 74:19-23).

The Lord chose and redeemed Israel from Egypt in the Exodus (cp. Exodus 15:13). • your own special possession: This is another expression for “your people” (Psalm 28:9; Psalm 78:62; Psalm 94:14; Psalm 106:40).
Like a guide, the psalmist points out to the Lord what took place during the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
my king from ages past: The psalmist acknowledges God’s power and his historical bond with Israel (Psalm 5:2; Psalm 44:4; Psalm 84:3).
Leviathan: See Psalm 104:26; Job 3:8; Job 41:1, Job 41:12, Job 41:22, Job 41:31; Isaiah 27:1. Here, the creature’s multiple heads suggest a mythical monster.
springs and streams to gush forth: God provided water in the desert for his people (see Psalm 68:8-9; Exodus 17:6); he dried up the Red Sea (Exodus 14:21) and the Jordan River (Joshua 3:17).
The poet urges God to act.

This hymn of thanksgiving includes two direct messages from God that provide assurance of his justice (Psalm 75:2-3, Psalm 75:10). The Lord rebukes arrogant people who defy him, promising to forcibly humble them (Psalm 75:4-8). Together, the community and the psalmist respond with thanksgiving for God’s character (Psalm 75:1, Psalm 75:9).
The Lord will bring justice in his own time.
The wicked arrogantly defy the heavens—the dwelling place of God. Through their boasting they insist that they are wiser than God.
No creature has the right to rebel against its Creator.
The Lord alone is the Judge, with the power to exalt and humble (see 1 Sam 2:7; Luke 1:52).
Psalm 76:1 to be accompanied by stringed instruments: The Greek version reads for the Assyrian.
God’s victory over Zion’s enemies foreshadows his worldwide victory over all his enemies.

This psalm appears to celebrate a victory. The victory might have been recent, such as over the Assyrians (see note on Psalm 76:1; see also Isaiah 37:1-38); or the psalm might be recalling God’s great acts of rescue in the past.
God brings an end to the attacks of his enemies (see Psalm 46:9).
The victorious king’s splendor, glory, and majesty are greater than anything in the created order (Psalm 8:1; Psalm 29:4; Psalm 111:3).
The psalmist praises God for his achievement and for his glorious majesty.
The word translated feared (Hebrew nora’) is a wordplay on the word translated “glorious” in Psalm 76:4 (Hebrew na’or).
The needy await their victorious God, while the wicked stand in fear of him.
The night provides a special opportunity for prayer and meditation (Psalm 77:6, Psalm 77:11; see Psalm 6:6; Psalm 16:7; Psalm 17:3; Psalm 30:5; Psalm 63:6; Psalm 119:55, Psalm 119:62, Psalm 119:148).

The psalmist laments that God has turned away from him, even though he feels innocent. He reflects on his situation (Psalm 77:3, Psalm 77:6, Psalm 77:12) and finds hope (see Psalm 25:5) in remembering God’s past deeds (Psalm 77:11).

I think of God: God’s people inevitably face difficult times, but recalling his mighty acts at the beginning of their relationship assures them of God’s commitment. • Feeling overwhelmed, the psalmist is unable to deal with the crisis (Psalm 142:3; Psalm 143:4).
As the psalmist meditates at night, he feels so disturbed that he cannot sleep or speak. He has pleasant memories of the past, but he cannot look beyond the present moment into the future.
Feeling rejected (see Psalm 43:2), the psalmist asks if the situation is permanent.
The psalmist questions his status before God.
The psalmist fears that God’s hand of protection (Psalm 44:3; Psalm 77:15; Exodus 6:6) and favor (Psalm 16:7-8; Psalm 110:1) is now against him for no apparent reason.
The memories of God’s mighty works in the past fill the psalmist’s mind.
This central section of the poem reflects on God as the holy and powerful redeemer.
the Red Sea: The Canaanites attributed divine power to the sea, but God is the one who made the sea and uses it for his own purposes.
The prologue is an invitation to learn wisdom.
This wisdom psalm exhorts the people to learn wisdom and faithfully pass it on.
The psalmist recites Israel’s story (Psalm 78:5-72) in a parable in order to teach wisdom and insight. • Jesus quoted this verse to explain why he taught in parables (Matthew 13:35).
This story of what God has done should be told from generation to generation (see Deuteronomy 6:20-25; Proverbs 4:1-4).
The telling of the story should motivate God’s people to obey what he commanded (Deuteronomy 6:4-9).

God holds each generation responsible for its own response, which should be to maintain faith and hope (see Psalm 9:18; Psalm 27:14) and avoid being stubborn, rebellious, and unfaithful (see Deuteronomy 9:6-7; Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Deuteronomy 31:27).

Ephraim, the second son of Joseph, received a special blessing from Jacob (Genesis 48:15-20; Genesis 49:22-26; Deuteronomy 33:13-17). The land that his descendants received included fertile valleys and strategic roads (Judges 8:2). However, the people of Ephraim did not live in obedience to God’s gracious covenant.
The miracles are the ten plagues against Egypt that God performed during Israel’s captivity (Exodus 7:1–12:51).
The focus shifts from Ephraim (Psalm 78:9-11) to Israel as a whole as the psalmist reflects on God’s power in Egypt (see Psalm 81:4-7) and in the wilderness.
God divided the sea when Israel crossed through the Red Sea (see Exodus 14:1–15:27).
God used a cloud and a pillar of fire to guide and protect Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21-22).
Israel rebelled in the wilderness despite God’s abundant provision.
Abundance comes through the doors of heaven (Genesis 8:2; 2 Kgs 7:2; Malachi 3:10). • Israel ate manna for forty years in the wilderness (Exodus 16:31-36; John 6:31).
God powerfully satisfied the people’s desires, but they did not respond with gratitude or faith. Therefore, God exercised his justice.
Israel’s rebellion resulted in God’s judgment, but even their short-lived and insincere repentance motivated God to exercise forbearance.
An entire generation died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:22-23, Numbers 14:28-35).
They repented: This demonstration of zeal was not sincere.
Israel’s continued existence, in spite of the people’s rebellion and unbelief (Psalm 78:7-8), was due to God’s compassion.
The Israelites remembered the right doctrine (Psalm 9:9; Psalm 91:1), but they did not allow God to change their hearts (Leviticus 26:41).
The Israelites rebelled even though the Lord had rescued them from powerful plagues.

Israel’s rebellion desecrated the Promised Land. The people built shrines to false gods and worshiped idols (Psalm 78:58) during the period of the judges (e.g., Judges 2:11; Judges 3:7, Judges 3:17-18).
God abandoned his dwelling at Shiloh because of the people’s idol worship (1 Sam 4:11; Jeremiah 7:12).
The tribe of Ephraim was not completely rejected, but God favored Judah (Psalm 78:68).
In the choice of Mount Zion instead of Shiloh as God’s sanctuary on earth, God moved from the north to the south (see Psalm 69:1-36).
The God who had turned against his own people (Psalm 78:62) chose David, a shepherd (Genesis 46:34; 1 Sam 16:10-11), to become their shepherd (Psalm 78:52; cp. Psalm 23:1).
your special possession: This phrase might refer to the land, the Temple (see Psalm 61:5), or the people (see Psalm 79:2; Psalm 78:71).
The poet laments the desecration of the Temple and the success of the enemy.

This lament describes the occasion of Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC. The early history of Israel’s rebellions described in Psalm 78:1-72 provoked God’s wrath, resulting in the desolation of Zion described here as the defilement of the Temple and the disgraced bodies that littered the landscape. The psalmist then prays for forgiveness and rescue (Psalm 79:8-9), as well as for God to pay back the nation’s enemies (Psalm 79:12-13). Other psalms lamenting the Exile include Psalm 42:1–44:26, Psalm 102:1-28, Psalm 107:1-43, Psalm 126:1-6, Psalm 137:1-9.
The intensity of God’s judgment surprises the people; they cry out in despair for compassion, forgiveness, and relief. Verses Psalm 6:1–7:17 are repeated almost verbatim in Jeremiah 10:25.
The repentant among God’s people ask him to vent his anger not on them but on their wicked and unrepentant enemies.
The people’s accumulation of past sins contributed to the Exile (2 Kgs 17:7-23; 24:3-4); however, the people perished because of their own sins (Jeremiah 31:30; Ezekiel 18:20).
The people ask God to rescue them. Although Israel’s sins caused the tragedy, the pagan nations must also be held responsible for the bloodshed.

The Exile resulted in national suffering and in individual searching for the Lord. • pay back: See Psalm 1:6; Psalm 94:2; Jeremiah 32:18. • The expression seven times signifies something complete. • Israel’s neighbors included Edom, Moab, and Ammon (see Psalm 137:7; 2 Kgs 24:2; Obadiah 1:1-21).
Psalm 80:1 The tune “Lilies of the Covenant” is unknown today.
God is the Shepherd of Israel: See also Psalm 23:1; Psalm 28:9; Psalm 78:52-53. • radiant glory . . . power: These expressions (Psalm 145:11) refer to God’s manifest presence.
The psalmist urgently calls upon the Lord to act.

This psalm of lament might originate with the remnant of the northern kingdom after its fall in 722 BC. The people call on God as their Shepherd and as the God of Heaven’s Armies in the hope that he will return to them and restore them. They remember the Exodus and their special relationship with the Lord and conclude with an expression of renewed commitment to him (Psalm 80:18).
This verse is repeated (with an increasing crescendo) in Psalm 80:7, Psalm 80:19.
The people cry out for rescue from the shame of their recent defeat. The enemy’s victory is less devastating, however, than the knowledge that they themselves are objects of God’s wrath.

Israel had been a prosperous grapevine (Genesis 1:28; Galatians 5:22-23) that God transplanted into the land of Canaan at the time of the conquest. However, the people forgot the source of their prosperity and chose to do evil (Isaiah 5:1-7; Hosea 10:1).
Israel has a glorious past, beginning with its redemption from Egypt.
Solomon’s kingdom had extended west to the Mediterranean Sea and east to the Euphrates River (see Psalm 72:8-9; Psalm 89:25; 1 Kgs 4:21).
broken down our walls: God no longer defended Israel (Isaiah 5:5).
The surrounding nations were ceremonially unclean, like a wild boar or vicious wild animals.
Israel was the son that God had brought out of Egypt (see Hosea 11:1) and planted in the Holy Land.
The community prays for God to change their desperate situation and restore them. They are still the Lord’s chosen people.
The son of your choice was probably the northern kingdom of Israel, although it might allude to the king of David’s dynasty (Psalm 110:1).
As a prelude to the message of warning, the psalmist invites Israel to contemplate their God in song and dance.
This warning message invites Israel to worship only the Lord and to enjoy the fullness of his blessing.

An Israelite tambourine was a hand drum—a round frame covered with a skin, used as a percussion instrument during festivities, often to accompany dancing (Psalm 68:25; Psalm 149:3; Psalm 150:4). • The sweet lyre and the harp, both stringed instruments, are the instruments most frequently mentioned in the psalms (e.g., Psalm 33:2; Psalm 57:8; Psalm 71:22; Psalm 150:3).
The ram’s horn mustered armies and announced special holy days (Psalm 47:5; Psalm 98:6). • new moon: The first day of the lunar month marked a festival.
The festival, a time to celebrate and listen to the Lord, took place at God’s appointed time.
for Israel: Literally for Joseph. The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh (the sons of Joseph) are used here to refer to the entire nation of Israel.
The Lord heard Israel’s cry in Egypt and rescued them from oppressive slavery.
God pleads with his people to remember the covenant and the Ten Commandments.
God emphasizes that he and no one else rescued Israel. • The nation should open its mouth wide to take in God’s word (cp. Deuteronomy 8:3; Ezekiel 3:1).
The Lord helps Israel to understand that their failure was not because of his weakness.

God wants to give his children his goodness, but only if they listen (Isaiah 1:18-19; Isaiah 28:12; Isaiah 48:18-19; see Deuteronomy 6:3). • God promises to subdue the enemies (Deuteronomy 9:3) of those who walk the paths of obedience and loyalty. He will also richly feed his people (Isaiah 1:19).
God presides and stands ready to render judgment (see Isaiah 3:13). • heaven’s court: See Job 1:6.
God condemns those who mistreat the helpless.
Since justice marks God’s reign (Psalm 89:4), he opposes favoring the wicked. So the psalmist is perplexed and cries out to God for justice (Psalm 82:3-4, Psalm 82:8).
The unjust oppressors cannot bring or restore order. They wander about in darkness, unmoved by circumstances even when the whole world order falls apart around them (cp. Psalm 11:3).
The gods (see study notes on 29:1-2; 58:1), like mere mortals, cannot escape the judgment common to human rulers. Jesus quoted from this passage in John 10:34.
The nations belong to God; he will take over the realms formerly ruled by local deities and give them to his people, just as he did with the Promised Land.
The enemy has successfully intimidated God’s people, so the poet prays that the Lord will hear and act.

This community lament asks God for rescue and victory. The terse poetry suggests difficult times. A powerful coalition desires to destroy Israel (Psalm 83:1-4) and allies itself against God (Psalm 83:5-8). Recalling the fate of others who came against Israel (Psalm 83:9-12), the psalmist prays that the same will happen to these enemies (Psalm 83:13-16) so that God will receive honor among them (Psalm 83:17-18). It is unclear whether this psalm arose out of a specific historical instance of opposition by these nations, or if it is a poetic collage of nations representing Israel’s enemies.
signed a treaty: The allies agreed to fight against God and his people. The nations that are named in the alliance were situated around Israel and Judah.

The Edomites, descendants of Esau, were located to the southeast of Judah (see Genesis 25:30; Genesis 32:3; Genesis 36:1-8). • Ishmaelites were desert-dwelling descendants of Hagar. • Moabites and Ammonites descended from Lot; both were located to the east of Israel and Judah. • The Hagrites were possibly located north of the Ammonites (1 Chr 5:10).

The Gebalites probably came from Gebal/Byblos on the coast of Lebanon. • The Amalekites were located south of Israel in the Negev. • Philistia was southwest of Judah, by the Mediterranean Sea. • Tyre was a port city on the Mediterranean, northwest of Israel.
Assyria was northeast of Israel and north of the Persian Gulf. • The descendants of Lot were the Moabites and the Ammonites (Psalm 83:6-7).
The Midianites, ruled by Zebah and Zalmunna and led by Oreb and Zeeb, were Israel’s enemy in the days of Gideon (Judges 7:1–8:5). Barak’s coalition defeated Sisera and Jabin (Judges 4:1-24).
The psalmist prays that God will miraculously destroy the new coalition as he did three other enemies; doing so would bring him glory.
The coalition’s motivation for wiping out Israel was to acquire the land (see Jeremiah 3:19).
tumbleweed . . . chaff: This dry plant material easily blows away (see Isaiah 17:13).
fire . . . fierce storm . . . tempest: These are images of God’s manifestation in judgment (see Isaiah 29:6).
The psalmist is far from the Temple. He turns toward it in hopeful reflection.

The psalmist expresses his deep spiritual longing for God’s presence. He faints with longing as he reflects on the Temple and on pilgrims making the journey to Jerusalem (Psalm 84:1-7). He prays for himself and for the community (Psalm 84:8-9). The conclusion of the psalm (Psalm 84:10-12) clarifies that the Temple represents God—the psalmist truly longs for God’s presence. He knows that God’s goodness is greater than life and that only God can give his people favor and honor (Psalm 84:10-11).
The poet envies the birds that have nesting places in and around the Temple.
The priests and Temple personnel lived in the Temple.
Travelers needed strength to meet the challenges of pilgrimage by foot along unpaved paths, in all kinds of weather and with the possibility of assaults.

The pilgrimage to Jerusalem reenacted the Exodus, when God marvelously provided for his people (see Psalm 78:15-16; Psalm 105:41). The psalmist imagines the pains of travel turning to the joy of arrival.

The Valley of Weeping probably refers to the anguish that lonely pilgrims endured (see Psalm 23:4), rather than to an actual location. • refreshing springs . . . autumn rains: Even when pilgrims feel totally exhausted, the prospect of drawing near to the Lord renews their spirits (cp. Isaiah 35:6-10; Isaiah 41:18-20; Isaiah 43:17-20; Isaiah 49:10).
Both kings and priests were anointed to dedicate them for service (see Psalm 132:17; Exodus 28:41; 1 Sam 9:16; 16:1-13; cp. Isaiah 61:1; Acts 10:38).
The psalmist viewed being in God’s presence as much better than being anywhere else.
Some people worshiped the sun as a god, but the true God provides all that anyone needs.
God restored the fortunes of Israel by bringing the nation back from exile (see Psalm 14:7; Psalm 126:1).
Though the psalmist gratefully acknowledges God’s goodness, he also asks God whether his wrath will last forever.

The psalmist leads the postexilic community in lament and prayer for full redemption. He ponders God’s past rescue of Israel from exile (Psalm 85:1-3), longs for greater evidence of God’s goodness, and leads the community in prayer for full restoration (Psalm 85:4-7). God responds with a message of peace (Psalm 85:8-9), and the psalm concludes with a lyrical outburst at the grandeur of God’s salvation (Psalm 85:10-13).
When God forgave the guilt of their sins, he gave the people the possibility of fellowship with him (see Psalm 32:5).
This prayer for renewal is based on God’s unfailing love for his people.

When God the Lord speaks, his faithful people listen. He promises them peace, meaning wholeness and well-being (see Psalm 37:11). They fear the Lord and know that he and his salvation are near to them. • The Lord does not tolerate foolish ways, such as those that resulted in the Exile.

In the glorious world of renewal and salvation, all the qualities of God’s care—love, truth, righteousness, and peace—come together and transform the created order into something new (see Isaiah 32:15-20).
Righteousness is like a messenger preparing the world for God’s coming in response to the prayers of his people (Psalm 85:4-7; Psalm 89:14).
Psalm 86:1 This is the only psalm connected with David in Book Three.
God’s devoted servant prays for mercy. The psalmist sees himself as a member of the covenant community and as a citizen of the world.

The psalmist invokes God’s help and praises his character in a lament prompted by the presence of evil (Psalm 86:14, Psalm 86:17). All people will worship the gracious and almighty God (Psalm 86:8-10). To this end, the poet commits himself to a lifestyle of ethical integrity (Psalm 86:11) and praising the Lord (Psalm 86:12-13). The last stanza contrasts the qualities of evil people with those of the Lord (Psalm 86:14-17).
The psalmist recounts the catalog of divine perfections (Exodus 34:6-7), especially God’s willingness to forgive sin (see Psalm 32:5; Psalm 85:2; Psalm 145:7-10).
The psalmist appeals to God to remain true to his character, which is the basis for hope.
All the nations must submit themselves to the Lord and worship him (Psalm 45:17; Psalm 117:1; Psalm 148:7-11).
The poet responds to the Lord by seeking faithful instruction in the truth. • An individual with purity of heart has integrity and wholeness (see Psalm 73:1).
In anticipation of God’s rescue, the psalmist praises him and trusts in his goodness.
The arrogant exist both inside and outside the community. The psalmist asks for a vision of God’s character; God is so great that just a glimpse of his goodness will shut the mouths of the wicked.

God has mercy on his people (Psalm 51:1); he is gracious (Psalm 25:6), slow to get angry (Psalm 103:8; Psalm 145:8), and filled with unfailing love and faithfulness (Hebrew khesed and ’emeth; Psalm 143:1). This verse repeats a theme first expressed in Exodus 34:7; Numbers 14:18 (cp. Psalm 103:8; Psalm 145:8; Nehemiah 9:17; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2).
Jerusalem was Israel’s capital and the location of the Temple, God’s earthly palace (see Psalm 84:1-12).
This psalm envisions Jerusalem as the city of God where all the nations are citizens.

As great as Zion is, it will be even greater when it becomes an international city where believers from all the nations have citizenship. • God keeps a record of all who confess him as their Lord (Daniel 7:10; Revelation 13:8).
Jerusalem becomes the international city where all God’s children are citizens.

Psalm 88:1 Heman the Ezrahite might be a sage from Solomon’s time (1 Kgs 4:31), a descendant of Judah (1 Chr 2:6), or a member of the Levitical family charged with singing at the Temple (1 Chr 15:17; 2 Chr 5:12).
The psalmist calls on the Lord for salvation.

In this lament, the psalmist sees himself as cast out from God’s presence. At first, he calls on the Lord. When he finds no relief from his suffering, he presents three charges against God (Psalm 88:6-7, Psalm 88:8-12, Psalm 88:13-17).

In his first charge, the psalmist blames the Lord for his demise. God’s overpowering anger did not make sense. • The phrase the darkest depths implies the place of the dead (Psalm 143:3; see Lamentations 3:6) or the depths of the sea (Psalm 68:22; Psalm 69:1-2).

In his second charge, the psalmist claims that God has isolated him and caused his loneliness (cp. Psalm 31:11; Psalm 38:11). Loneliness was a curse in a culture where relationships were more important than personal achievement.
In his third charge, the psalmist accuses the Lord of rejecting him. The force and apparent cruelty of the psalmist’s suffering overwhelm him.
The psalmist restates his second and first charges.
God’s unfailing love gives reason to celebrate forever.

Book Three (Psalm 73:1–89:52) begins and ends with weighty questions.
