Though Psalm 89:1-52 begins with a praise-filled account of how the Lord exalted the throne of David (Psalm 89:1-37), the psalmist protests the Lord’s apparent rejection of his covenant with David (Psalm 89:38-51; see 2 Sam 7:8-16).
The Lord has sworn by his own holiness (Psalm 89:35; see Psalm 110:4).
The psalmist restates God’s covenant with David (see also Psalm 89:19-37).
Praise for God’s greatness (see Psalm 8:1) comes from the inhabitants of heaven who witness his faithfulness.
God is the absolute standard of faithfulness, commitment, and order. The angelic beings and the heavens testify to his constancy.
mightiest angel: Literally son of God (see study note on 29:1-2).

The Lord rules over all parts of the created order, including evil. • You scattered your enemies: The Lord will crush (Luke 1:51) evil powers that oppose him (Psalm 2:1-3). • with your mighty arm: This phrase represents God’s strength (Psalm 89:13).
In this hymn, the psalmist celebrates God’s comprehensive and powerful sovereignty over nature.
Mount Tabor was in northern Israel. Mount Hermon formed the extreme northern border of the nation.
God rules wisely over creation. The qualities of righteousness, justice, and faithfulness fit the profile of a wise ruler. The happy people who live under his rule enjoy his protection.
Those who are wise worship God, walk in his light, rejoice in their relationship with him, and exult in his character.
The Lord protects his people with the same power by which he established the created order.
The Lord chose David as his son and as king of Israel (see Psalm 2:4-6; 2 Sam 7:8-16) to provide protection for his people.
I have anointed him: This is the verb from which anointed one (Hebrew mashiakh, “messiah”) is derived.
The Lord adopted David as his son, appointed him as his commander over the nations, and promised to support him forever. Verse 26 recalls a verse from David’s song of praise (2 Sam 22:47).
David would be the most eminent of earthly kings. The Hebrew word translated mightiest is the same as the designation for God as “Most High” (‘elyon).
The Lord writes his faithfulness in heaven, on the canvas of his universe (see Psalm 89:2). He records his commitment to the dynasty of David in the same way.

The Lord disciplines but does not reject his erring children. He foresees violation of trust and subsequent punishment, but he commits himself to uphold the covenant. His fidelity to David corresponds to his faithfulness to the created order.

holiness: The Lord is wholly distinct from the created order (Psalm 22:3); his character is totally pure. He does as he pleases (Psalm 115:3), and he chooses to be faithful (Psalm 89:1; Psalm 115:1); therefore, he cannot lie.
You are angry: The harshness of God’s wrath perplexes the psalmist.
broken down the walls: The Lord’s people are completely vulnerable.
Although the Lord promised to strengthen David, he secretly strengthened David’s enemies.
The psalmist wonders if he will live to see the end of the Lord’s anger. Our lifetimes are short, like a day in the Lord’s sight (Psalm 90:4, Psalm 90:10).
The phrase your servants refers to the community loyal to the Lord.

This doxology concludes all of Book Three (Psalm 73:1–89:52); it is not intended to be read as part of Psalm 89:1-52. It stands in stark contrast to the anguish and questioning of Psalm 89:1-52. Cp. Psalm 41:13; Psalm 106:48.

Psalm 90:1 Moses led God’s people from slavery in Egypt to Mount Sinai, where he received the law and established God’s covenant with Israel. • the man of God: Moses enjoyed a special relationship with God (Deuteronomy 33:1).

The Lord becomes the home of the godly; he has provided shelter for countless generations. The word translated home is not used frequently in the Psalter. It describes a place of safety where the Lord meets his needy people and cares for them (Psalm 68:5; Psalm 71:3).

Although the Lord’s people have made their home in him for generations, their sin widens the gap between them and their infinite Lord. The Lord’s wrath against a person’s sin might last a lifetime and yet be only a taste of his displeasure with sin. This lamentable situation calls the community to seek the Lord’s light. Taking the first step means seeking restoration with the Lord on the basis of his compassion and love (Psalm 90:13-14). He alone makes his servants glad and blesses their future generations (Psalm 90:16-17).
The Lord is the eternal God. • The Lord gave birth to the earth by creating it.
Unlike God, humans are mortal and transitory.
Sinners cannot escape God’s wrath because the Lord sees their sins. Their fleeting lives are filled with afflictions.
A groan of sorrow (Ezekiel 2:10) sums up a life spent in facing the consequences of sin. • Humans cause trouble (see Psalm 10:6) and receive pain in return.

In the search for wisdom, no one can comprehend the Lord (see Isaiah 40:13). The appropriate human response to the Lord is godly fear (see Psalm 60:4). The Lord alone can teach humans to follow the path of wisdom (Psalm 25:4-6).
The phrase your servants refers to the community of those loyal to the Lord.
The psalmist prays for the Lord’s favor and restoration.
The psalmist calls upon the Lord to give the people gladness to replace their mourning (see Psalm 92:4-5).
The children represent future generations in contrast to the generations past (Psalm 90:1).
Humans waste their efforts unless the Lord makes them successful (Psalm 44:3).
The Most High is an ancient title that expresses the Lord’s exalted status as the ruler and protector of the godly (see Genesis 14:19).
The Lord is an ancient shelter (see Psalm 90:1), open to those who seek refuge in him.

This wisdom psalm expresses confidence in the Almighty God, who provides a shelter for those who take refuge in him. They receive redemption, life, and glory from the Lord, who loves and cares for those who seek him.
God protects the godly from deadly disease and even a destructive word.
The psalmist invites the godly to trust in the Lord and find protection in him.
The armor might refer to a body shield, while protection refers to a small shield worn on the arm.
The godly should not be afraid, because the Lord watches over them. These promises do not guarantee an escape from trouble, but they create an expectation of the Lord’s goodness.
The reference to disease represents any kind of affliction.
The poet again invites the godly to seek refuge in the Lord and enjoy the benefits of divine protection.

he will order his angels: Satan cited these words when he tempted Jesus (Matthew 4:6; Luke 4:10-11), but God makes this promise for those who obey him (Psalm 91:14), not for those who arrogantly test him (Matthew 4:4, Matthew 4:7).
Those who love the Lord will obey him (Deuteronomy 30:20; 1 Jn 5:3) and seek his protection (Psalm 91:1; Psalm 145:18).
The godly can trust the Lord’s protection and provision.

The Lord promises to answer the prayers of his people. • The Psalter often speaks of people honoring the Lord (Psalm 50:15); here, God promises to honor the godly who risk everything for his sake (Psalm 62:7; Psalm 71:21; Psalm 84:11).
A long life on earth represents just a small part of the Lord’s goodness and eternal friendship (Psalm 23:6).

Psalm 92:1 on the Sabbath Day: Jewish tradition assigned one psalm to each day of the week: Sunday (Psalm 24:1-10), Monday (Psalm 48:1-14), Tuesday (Psalm 82:1-8), Wednesday (Psalm 94:1-23), Thursday (Psalm 81:1-16), Friday (Psalm 93:1-5), and the Sabbath (Psalm 92:1-15). This is the only psalm that indicates this use in its title.
The psalmist offers praise and thanksgiving for God’s unfailing love and faithfulness.

Thanksgiving and praise open this psalm. The Lord—the Most High—is faithful and just in discerning between the godly and the wicked. The godly will enjoy a glorious, vigorous future, while the wicked will perish. The wise see and understand the Lord’s works as they reveal his justice (Psalm 92:6-7, Psalm 92:11, Psalm 92:15). The wicked, like grass, are quickly destroyed (Psalm 92:7-10).
The Lord acts and the psalmist responds in praise (Psalm 92:4). God’s actions spring from his thoughts (Psalm 92:5).
Fools perish because they do not understand the Lord’s marvelous works and eternal plans.
The Lord’s thoughts do not make sense to the simpleton or the fool, the immoral person who desires no wisdom (Proverbs 1:22; Proverbs 10:23).
Even when the ungodly seem to grow luxuriantly (Psalm 73:3-5), they have no future (Psalm 92:9; see Psalm 1:6; Psalm 90:5-6; Isaiah 40:6-8).

The transcendent Lord stays above the world of human experience. From this exalted place, he rules and judges (Psalm 7:7), celebrates his victories (Psalm 68:18; see Psalm 47:1-9), comes to rescue the needy (Psalm 102:19), brings an end to the wicked (Psalm 92:7-8), and receives praise (Psalm 148:1).
The glory of the Lord provides the reason for the poet’s renewed strength and glory, and for the imminent defeat of the enemy.
as strong as a wild ox: The Lord allows the psalmist to share his exaltation (Psalm 92:8), thus ensuring victory.
The psalmist understands the Lord’s mighty acts. He shares in the glory of the wise of heart.

Carvings of palm trees (1 Kgs 6:29, 32, 35; 7:36) adorned the Temple, and builders made rich use of cedars (1 Kgs 5:6). The trees represent the godly, who are planted in the very courts of the Temple.
The Temple area consisted of the Lord’s own house and the courts that surrounded it.
There is no evil in him! The Lord is consistently just; he rightly judges everyone (see Zephaniah 3:5).
robed in majesty: The Lord stands victorious both before and after battle (see Psalm 45:3).
The everlasting Lord gloriously establishes his kingship (cp. Psalm 47:1-9, Psalm 99:1–100:5).

These psalms challenge the doubts created by the Exile (see Psalm 89:1-52) and answer the questions asked in Psalm 90:11, Psalm 90:13. The Lord has established a kingdom (Psalm 93:1-5) that is characterized by the punishment of the wicked (Psalm 94:1-23), reverent obedience among his people (Psalm 95:1-11), justice for the poor (Psalm 96:1-13), celebration in Zion (Psalm 97:1-12), salvation for Israel (Psalm 98:1-9), holiness (Psalm 99:1-9), and praise (Psalm 100:1-5).
God’s victory over natural chaos gives the psalmist confidence that the Lord will also defeat his present enemies (cp. Jeremiah 46:8; Jeremiah 47:2).
Through his stable rule and royal laws, the Lord orders the world. • Your reign (literally your house): The house from which God reigns might be the Lord’s heavenly palace or the earthly Temple.
After the community falls victim to the wicked (Psalm 94:5-7), they pray that the Lord will render justice (see Psalm 7:11; Psalm 9:12).

This plea for the Lord’s justice includes both communal and individual expressions of lament (Psalm 94:1-7, Psalm 94:16-23). The psalmist gives voice to the pain and suffering caused by the wicked, but he also depicts the comfort and stability of the Lord’s protection. He calls on the Lord to avenge the needy against the arrogant and foolish, he rebukes such people for their folly (Psalm 94:8-11), and he pronounces a blessing on the wise (Psalm 94:12-15).
Just as the Lord’s enemies rise up against him and his people (Psalm 3:7; Psalm 93:3), he must arise and make retribution against the enemy (see Psalm 79:12; Isaiah 65:6).
widows . . . foreigners . . . orphans: The Lord’s law protects needy people (Deuteronomy 24:17; Deuteronomy 27:19), but they remain vulnerable in society.
The wicked think that they can get away with their vile acts and speech, foolishly assuming that God isn’t looking or doesn’t care.
The psalmist rebukes human folly.
It is preposterous that those with ears and eyes would imagine their Creator to be deaf and blind.

punishes: This word also carries the idea of “warns” (Psalm 2:10), “disciplines” (Psalm 6:1; Psalm 94:12), or “instructs” (Psalm 16:7). The Lord disciplines his people to purify their character (Proverbs 3:11-12; Hebrews 12:6-11). He punishes his enemies by giving them what they deserve (Psalm 1:6; Romans 6:23).
While the Lord’s thoughts are deep, people’s thoughts are worthless (cp. Psalm 92:5; 1 Cor 3:20).
True to his nature, the Lord rewards those who live by his wise instruction and makes them happy according to his promises.
God’s relief includes his comfort and rescue.
Even when it seems that he has, the Lord will not reject his people.
Only God has the power to stand up to the wicked (see Psalm 2:2).
The psalmist’s prayer resumes (see Psalm 94:1-7) with a desperate cry for the Lord’s justice; it concludes with the hopeful expectation that evil will end.
The psalmist’s experience of slipping contrasts with God’s promise to stand with him (Psalm 94:12-13; see Psalm 15:5; Psalm 93:1).

This call to worship urges the people to respond to the Lord, the Shepherd, and to follow him faithfully. The previous generation, who refused to obey, did not receive the blessings of the Promised Land.
above all gods: The psalmist refutes idolatry and paganism (Psalm 96:4-6; Psalm 135:15-18; see also Isaiah 46:5-7).
The Lord is the great King over the whole universe.
The whole created order owes its existence to the sovereign Lord alone—not to various gods.

The great King cares for his people as a shepherd cares for his flock (Isaiah 40:11). • The Lord our maker, the Creator of heaven and earth, also made a people for himself (Isaiah 45:9-12; Isaiah 51:12-16).
To harden your hearts means to be stubborn and resist the Lord’s grace (see Numbers 20:2-13; see also Matthew 13:3-23; John 12:37-43; Ephesians 4:17-32; Hebrews 3:6-19; Hebrews 4:6-11).
If people want to enter into the Lord’s rest, they need to respond immediately (see Hebrews 3:7–4:11).
Israel’s ancestors . . . saw the wonders of the Lord, but they foolishly did not try to grasp their significance (see Psalm 92:5-6).

The generation of Israel that wandered in the wilderness for forty years failed to enter the place of rest that Israel enjoyed after the conquest of the land (1 Kgs 8:56; see Deuteronomy 12:9). The Lord promised them the land and gave it to them (Isaiah 28:12), but they did not obey him (Isaiah 28:1). The warning reminds every generation of the need to obey in faith. • The rest that God provides includes peace, provision, and protection (Psalm 132:14-18). The author of Hebrews challenged a new generation to enter the rest provided by Jesus Christ (Hebrews 3:7–4:13).
Three psalms open with the exhortation to sing a new song (Psalm 96:1-13, Psalm 98:1-9, Psalm 149:1-9); the song celebrates the Lord’s universal kingship (see Psalm 33:3).

This psalm establishes the Lord’s universal kingship (see Psalm 93:1-5) and prepares for the coming of the Lord to bring justice and righteousness into the world. The psalmist invites everyone to worship the Lord (Psalm 96:1-3), the glorious Creator of all the earth (Psalm 96:4-6), because worship is due to him alone (Psalm 96:7-9). The universe joins in praise as the righteous Judge establishes a new order (Psalm 96:10-13). • This psalm (along with Psalm 105:1-15; Psalm 106:1, Psalm 106:47-48) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1 Chr 16:1-43.

Great is the Lord! . . . most worthy of praise: With this refrain, the poet exalts the Lord over all the gods (Psalm 95:3) and nations (Psalm 99:2). He inspires awe more than anyone or anything else (Psalm 76:7, Psalm 76:12; Psalm 89:7; Psalm 99:3; Psalm 111:9). He is beyond human possession or comprehension. The story of what he does to redeem his people causes them to praise him.
The gods of the nations are as nothing before the glorious and majestic Creator of the earth.
The Lord made the heavens, an even greater task than creating the earth. The idols, made by human hands (Psalm 115:4), created nothing.
Honor and majesty: The Lord is glorious (Psalm 96:6; Psalm 104:1; Psalm 148:13), and so are his works in nature (Psalm 8:1) and in redemption (Psalm 111:3; Psalm 145:5).

nations of the world (literally families of the nations): Families and clans represent subdivisions of the nations (see Genesis 12:3). • The nations must respond to the Lord’s glory (Psalm 8:1; Psalm 19:1-4; Psalm 24:7).

The courts of God’s sanctuary were usually off-limits to non-Jewish people. In this psalm the nations of the world—the non-Jews—are invited in (Psalm 65:4; Psalm 84:2, Psalm 84:10; Psalm 100:4; Psalm 116:19; Psalm 135:2; Isaiah 1:12).
Worshipers should tremble in awe (Psalm 96:4; see Psalm 18:7-15; Psalm 97:4) at the splendor of the Lord’s majesty and holiness (Hebrews 12:25).

The Lord’s coming means the end of injustice. He rules fairly (Psalm 9:8; Psalm 96:13; Psalm 98:9) and inaugurates an era of harmony and order not experienced since Eden. • The Lord’s reign over the world is founded on the strong pillars of “righteousness and justice” (Psalm 89:14), so it cannot be shaken (cp. Psalm 11:3).
The psalmist exhorts the created order to respond with joy to the news of the Lord’s coming. Cp. a similar theme in Psalm 98:7-9.
All of nature will experience renewal in God’s presence (Psalm 65:13; Psalm 72:6, Psalm 72:16; Isaiah 44:23; Isaiah 55:12; Romans 8:21-22).
The farthest coastlands represent the most remote parts of the world.

God is greatly exalted over the gods and over all the earth. Awe-inspiring phenomena accompany his coming. Even the created order is visibly affected and the wicked perish, but the people of Zion love his coming and rejoice.
Dark clouds . . . Fire . . . lightning: This language shows that the Lord is coming in judgment.
The created order stirs at the coming of its King. He alone deserves worship.

As the Lord enters the world, the testimony of his righteousness resounds from above (Psalm 50:6). • Every nation will view the open display of the Lord’s glory (see Psalm 8:1; Psalm 19:1-4; Psalm 24:7; Isaiah 40:5).
At the Lord’s coming, when every god must bow to him, those who worship other gods will face their own folly (see Psalm 95:3-5).
Jerusalem rejoices at the news of the Lord’s coming, for he brings justice and rescues the upright of heart.

The godly people of integrity (see Proverbs 2:7, Proverbs 2:21; Proverbs 3:32; Proverbs 11:6, Proverbs 11:11; Proverbs 14:2), whose hearts are right, maintain a relationship with the Lord and with others (Psalm 94:15; Psalm 125:4). The wicked plan the downfall of the godly (Psalm 11:2), but the Lord rescues them (Psalm 11:1; Psalm 36:10). Then the sorrows of the godly turn to joy and praise (Psalm 32:11; Psalm 64:10; Psalm 111:1; Psalm 119:7).

This psalm celebrates the Lord’s kingship. The Lord is Israel’s true King, its champion and savior. His people sing a new song celebrating his victorious power and faithfulness to them. The Lord displays his righteous rule to all the nations throughout the earth, which will culminate in a worldwide kingdom of justice (Psalm 98:2, Psalm 98:9). Consequently, all the earth must worship and rejoice together because the Lord is coming (Psalm 98:4-6).
The Lord makes known his righteousness and faithfulness (see also Isaiah 52:10).
The psalmist invites the whole earth to worship the King (see Psalm 96:1).
The Temple musicians used trumpets to call people together for meetings (cp. Psalm 81:3).
The created order is personified as rejoicing at the coming of the righteous Judge (see Psalm 93:3-4; Psalm 96:11-13).
It is fitting to tremble and quake in response to the Lord’s holiness (see Psalm 96:9). • The throne between the cherubim refers to the cover of the Ark of the Covenant (Exodus 25:17-22).

The Lord is the holy and righteous King (Isaiah 6:1-5). Mount Zion, the location of the Lord’s Temple, metaphorically stands as the highest point on earth (Psalm 113:4; Isaiah 2:2; Isaiah 6:1). From this summit, the Great King (Psalm 47:2) can see, rule over, and receive praise from all nations and peoples.
The psalmist calls the nations to worship the Lord, the king of the earth who rules from Zion.
The qualities of the Lord’s rule include strength, justice, love, fairness, and righteousness (see Psalm 93:4; Psalm 97:2, Psalm 97:6-7, Psalm 97:12; Psalm 98:2-3, Psalm 98:9; Psalm 138:6).
Moses and Samuel were great models and leaders who had prayed on behalf of the Lord’s people (Exodus 32:31-32; 1 Sam 12:23).
God showed favor by responding to his people in the past, while holding sinners accountable.
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron from the pillar of cloud (Exodus 33:9; Numbers 12:5-6), and for a time, the people responded to the revelation.
This psalm calls all nations to come to Jerusalem to worship the Lord and acknowledge his goodness to Israel.
The Lord is the one who determines who his people are. • the sheep of his pasture: God will guide and protect his people (Psalm 23:1, Psalm 23:4).
Gates and courts were part of the Temple in Jerusalem.
This hymn expresses a commitment to live with integrity and to avoid evil. Jesus meets this ideal.

in my own home (literally in my house): This commitment to integrity might refer to private life at home. Some interpreters view my house as referring to the king’s palace; the commitment would then refer to the policies of his administration. • Leading a life of integrity means choosing a wise lifestyle.
The psalmist hates what the Lord hates (Proverbs 6:16-19; see Psalm 5:5; Psalm 11:4-5). • Perverse ideas come from corrupt human hearts (cp. Psalm 18:26).
The psalmist surrounds himself with people who are also committed to integrity (Psalm 101:2).
The psalmist commits himself to ridding his house and the city of the Lord—representing the entire kingdom—of all evil.
The psalmist appeals to the Lord not to turn away (or hide your face). Israel experienced his turning his face away during their exile.
A frail and afflicted human being prays for the Lord’s compassion on Jerusalem and for his presence with its inhabitants.
Smoke is an image of transitory life (Psalm 37:20; Psalm 68:2). • The psalmist’s bones represent his whole being (see Psalm 6:2; Psalm 34:19-22).
Like dried grass, the psalmist senses his life ebbing away.
skin and bones: The psalmist has wasted away because of his anguish (see Psalm 102:9; Psalm 109:24).
The owl was associated with ruin and desolation (Isaiah 34:11, Isaiah 34:15).
The psalmist cannot sleep (see Psalm 63:6-8). Like a bird on the roof, he feels isolated from both friends (see Psalm 88:8) and enemies.
The psalmist blames the Lord for his troubles.
The psalmist’s existence seems empty and transitory (Psalm 102:4; Psalm 109:23; Psalm 144:4).
forever . . . to every generation: The frailty of humans (Psalm 102:3-11) contrasts with the permanence of the Lord.
The topic changes from the psalmist’s miseries to the Lord’s glory. A vision of the Lord’s compassionate kingship gives him confidence in Zion’s future.
Now is the time for the Lord to restore Jerusalem from exile (see Psalm 75:2; Jeremiah 29:10; Daniel 9:1-19).

When the Lord arises (Psalm 102:13), the nations will tremble with fear because they will see his glory (see Psalm 8:1; Psalm 19:1-4; Psalm 24:7). The rebuilding of Zion and the Temple portray God’s glory and fulfill this promise. An even greater fulfillment will come with the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21:1-27).
The people of Israel were destitute (or naked) during the Exile.
Let this be recorded: The written record stands as a memorial to the Lord’s goodness.
The Lord will have mercy; Jews and Gentiles alike will worship him.
The heavenly sanctuary refers to God’s holy place on high (see Psalm 92:8-10).
The multitudes—both Jews and Gentiles—will join in the worship of the Lord (see Psalm 96:7, Psalm 96:9; Psalm 106:48; Isaiah 2:2-4; Isaiah 43:10-13; Isaiah 57:15; Isaiah 60:3-7).
Although the psalmist suffers in the present, he bases his hope for the future on the Lord’s past faithfulness.
The psalmist draws a contrast between his days (Psalm 102:23) and God’s years (cp. Psalm 90:4).

In contrast with the permanence of the Creator, the created order will wear out like a piece of clothing (see Isaiah 40:28). • The writer to the Hebrews describes this passage as having been addressed to Jesus, the Son (Hebrews 1:10-12).
The Lord’s presence provides the basis for the security and happiness of his people (Psalm 23:6).
Let all that I am praise the Lord: Psalm 103:1-22 and Psalm 104:1-35 each open and close with this commitment (Psalm 103:1-2, Psalm 103:22; Psalm 104:1, Psalm 104:35; see also Psalm 146:1).
The psalmist offers praise for the Lord’s goodness.
This psalm celebrates the Lord’s perfection, compassion, forgiveness, and goodness.
The Lord revealed himself to Moses in distinctive ways that ensured his relationship with his people (see Exodus 34:6-7; Numbers 14:18).
If the Lord were to constantly accuse or remain angry forever, no one would be left (see Isaiah 54:7-8; Isaiah 57:16).
The Lord’s love and forgiveness are infinite and complete.

The Lord is like a father to his children: This analogy forms the basis for Jesus’ teaching about God’s fatherhood (see Matthew 5:43-48; Matthew 6:1; Matthew 10:19-20; Matthew 12:50; Luke 6:36; Luke 12:29-32; John 8:31-59; John 15:1-8; see also 2 Sam 7:14; Jeremiah 3:19; Jeremiah 31:9; Malachi 1:6; 2 Cor 6:16-18).
The Lord compassionately cares for frail humans (see Psalm 37:2; Psalm 90:5; Psalm 92:7; Psalm 102:4; Isaiah 40:6-8).
the love of the Lord remains forever: The Lord’s kingdom is everlasting, so he commits himself to his people across many generations.
To obey God means to be faithful and loyal to him.
The psalmist exhorts the Lord’s angels, his servants and messengers, to praise the Lord.
God’s kingdom extends over all things, so all things are called to praise the Lord. • The concluding phrase takes us back to Psalm 103:1-2.

Let all that I am praise the Lord: Psalm 103:1-22 and Psalm 104:1-35 each open and close with this commitment to praise (Psalm 103:1-2, Psalm 103:22; Psalm 104:1, Psalm 104:35). • how great you are! This acclamation expresses praise for rescue (see also Psalm 35:27; Psalm 40:16; Psalm 70:4).

This creation hymn (see also Psalm 8:1-9, Psalm 33:1-22, Psalm 145:1-21) exalts God’s goodness and majesty. The psalmist reflects on the present world, the original creation, and a future new creation. He sees both creations as marvelously and wisely made (cp. Psalm 139:14), as the work of the Lord’s Spirit (Psalm 104:30; Genesis 1:2; 2 Cor 3:6).
The psalmist interacts with two of the days of creation (see Genesis 1:1-8), when God created the heavens and light.
This poetic portrayal envisions the clouds as beams that support heaven.

Wind and lightning are seen as divine messengers. The Lord uses weather phenomena as he desires (Psalm 77:17-18; Psalm 78:26; Psalm 135:7; Psalm 148:5-6). • The psalmist interacts with day three of creation (Genesis 1:9-13). The Lord is master of water and earth.
At first, water covered the earth.
The Lord created dry ground on day three of creation (Genesis 1:9-13).
The earth originates in God’s will.

The Lord set a firm boundary for the seas to protect the land. God’s sovereignty over sea and land was an argument against the existence of Baal, whom the Canaanites celebrated as victorious over the waters (see Psalm 29:1-11).

The Lord reigns over all bodies of water, including those on land. He replaced chaotic waters with order and abundance, and the earth became a splendid place for animals and humans, with water refreshing the ground, the birds, and the animals.
The psalmist celebrates animal, plant, and human life, as well as the Lord’s abundant provision for all of it (Genesis 1:9-30).
people to use: People are the managers of the created order, and they receive nourishment from the work of their hands.
While both can be misused (cp. Proverbs 21:17), the Lord provides wine and olive oil as gifts to enhance life. Life is sustained by basic food, represented by bread.
The storks migrated from northern Europe and resided in Palestine during the winter. • hyraxes: These animals are about the size of a rabbit and live in rocky places.

the moon to mark the seasons: Ancient Israel based its calendar on the cycles of the moon. • the sun knows when to set: This is a poetic description from the perspective of normal observation. The sun goes down at a regular time every evening.
The psalmist rejoices in the order of night and day, marking day four of creation (Genesis 1:14-19). This cycle gives all creatures an opportunity to live.
Cycles of darkness and dawn mark the days on earth.
The Lord’s works testify to his wisdom. All parts fit together—land and sea, night and day, land creatures and sea creatures. The Lord’s wisdom makes life orderly and wonderful.
The ocean, . . . teeming with life of every kind (see Genesis 1:20-21), exemplifies the Lord’s creative activities.

ships sailing: Commercial vessels engaged in sea trade were one of the wonders of the ancient Near East (see Isaiah 2:16; Isaiah 23:1, Isaiah 23:3). • Leviathan: The psalmist says that this feared creature is nothing but the Lord’s pet.
All life depends on the gracious sustenance of the Lord of life and death (cp. Matthew 6:11).

When you give them your breath: Life on earth is only possible as the Lord’s gift, symbolized by his breath (Hebrew ruakh, “breath, wind, spirit”). The Lord’s Spirit is the agent of renewal (Isaiah 32:15-20).
The Lord reveals his presence in the created order (see Psalm 8:1; Psalm 19:1-4; Psalm 24:7) and takes pleasure in his new creation (see Isaiah 65:19).
The psalmist moves from describing the known creation to anticipating the new creation, when the Lord will renew the created order into a world without sinners.
The trembling earth and the smoking mountains represent the Lord’s coming in judgment against sinners and salvation for his faithful people (see Psalm 18:7-15).
The Lord will remove all forms of evil that defile his creation. • The concluding phrase takes us back to Psalm 104:1 (see also Psalm 103:1-2, Psalm 103:22; Psalm 146:1).

The poet begins with the exhortation Give thanks (see also Psalm 106:1; Psalm 107:1; Psalm 118:1; Psalm 136:1). The other psalms continue with the refrain “for he is good!” The rest of Psalm 105:1-45 tells of God’s goodness.

This hymn praises the Lord’s faithfulness to Abraham and his descendants in all their journeys—from Ur to Canaan (Psalm 105:12), to Egypt (Psalm 105:17, Psalm 105:23), through the wilderness (Psalm 105:37, Psalm 105:41), and back to Canaan (Psalm 105:44). All of this fulfilled the Lord’s promise to Abraham (Psalm 105:9, Psalm 105:42), which was the basis for Israel’s very existence. Joseph, whose suffering was changed into glory, is a paradigm of encouragement for Israel (Psalm 105:16-25). • Psalm 105:1-15 (along with 96; Psalm 106:1, Psalm 106:47-48) is included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1 Chr 16.

The story of Israel is based on the Lord’s commitment to Abraham. Even when a question arises about the future of God’s covenant with David (Psalm 89:1-52), God’s covenant with Abraham stands, as does the spiritual bond between God and Israel, Abraham’s descendants.
The covenant is the Lord’s irrevocable oath to be the Father of Abraham and his descendants (see Genesis 12:1-9; Genesis 15:1-21).
God promised the land of Canaan to Abraham’s descendants as their special possession, where they could live as God’s people (Psalm 105:44-45; Genesis 12:7; Genesis 15:7-21).
The Lord protected Israel’s patriarchs.
Abraham was one of the nation’s prophets (Genesis 20:7).
These verses tell the story of Joseph (see Genesis 37:1–41:57).
tested Joseph’s character: See Genesis 39:6-12.
Egypt (Hebrew mitsrayim) is called the land of Ham.
These verses tell the story of Israel’s affliction in Egypt (see Exodus 1:1-14).
The psalmist recounts the story of Moses and the plagues in Egypt (Exodus 7:20–12:30).
not one . . . stumbled: The Lord protected all of his people (cp. Psalm 9:3).

The Exodus and the conquest of Canaan fulfilled God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Psalm 105:9-10). Unlike Psalm 78:1-72, the poet recites the Lord’s goodness without commenting on Israel’s history of rebellion (cp. Psalm 106:1-48).
The Lord’s presence was as evident to all as a fire in the darkness (Exodus 13:22).
The story of redemption is also the story of the Lord’s faithfulness.
Canaan was a land of pagan nations (see Psalm 111:6). The psalmist might also be reflecting on God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 24:60) regarding the lands given to Isaac (Genesis 26:3).
The Lord planned for Israel to testify about him by obeying him; Israel was to be his model people.
Praise the Lord! This refrain (Hebrew haleluyah) characterizes four small subgroups in the psalms: Psalm 104:1–106:48, Psalm 111:1–113:9, Psalm 115:1–117:2, Psalm 146:1–150:6.

The Israelite community in exile confessed the Lord’s goodness and justice and their own historic sinfulness. From the humble state of exile, they pleaded for redemption and restoration, asking to be gathered back from all the places the Lord had scattered them in his wrath. The psalm does not end in despair but with the memory of the Lord’s former mercy and the hope that his mercy will be renewed (Psalm 106:44-48). Israel failed, but the Lord is constant. • Verses 1, Psalm 47:1–48:14 (along with Psalm 96:1-13; Psalm 105:1-15) are included in David’s song of praise recorded in 1 Chr 16:1-43.
Wise people who practice justice and righteousness receive encouragement to proclaim the Lord’s great acts.
The poet prays individually for the Lord’s favor before leading the community confession that follows.

The story of Israel’s redemption encompasses their sinful response from the days of the ancestors to the present (Psalm 106:43). The themes of sin and divine wrath both open and close Book Four (Psalm 90:1-9; Psalm 106:6, Psalm 106:23, Psalm 106:43).
The community joins together to confess their sins and their ancestors’ many acts of unbelief.
Red Sea: See Exodus 14:15-31.
They wouldn’t wait: God’s impatient people did not trust him to work according to his will (e.g., see Exodus 15:24; Exodus 16:2-3; Exodus 17:1-3; Numbers 14:26-45; Numbers 21:4-9).
he sent a plague: See Exodus 32:35; Numbers 11:33.
The people became jealous because they presumed to have the same privileges as God’s appointed priests (see Numbers 16:1-35). • the earth opened up: See Numbers 16:28-33.
they bowed before an image: The people forgot their Savior and committed the sin of idolatry (see Exodus 32:1-6).
The land of Ham here means Egypt (Psalm 106:21).
The people disobeyed God’s command when they refused to enter the pleasant land (the Promised Land; see Jeremiah 3:19). • they wouldn’t believe his promise: See Numbers 13:25–14:12.

God’s judgment when Israel refused to obey was death and exile (Numbers 14:26-30). The occasion for these severe judgments seems to have been disobeying God’s word (Psalm 106:24-25) and provoking the Lord’s wrath (Psalm 106:28-46).
the worship of Baal at Peor: See Numbers 25:3; Deuteronomy 4:3.
Israel’s idolatry outside of the land came with them into the land. Their nature did not change; they continued to provoke the Lord to anger by their actions.
Phinehas, who executed a flagrantly apostate Israelite man (Numbers 25:3-8), is an even better model of a righteous man than Moses, who failed at Meribah (Numbers 20:11-13).

Israel continued to disobey the word of the Lord while living in the Promised Land. Rather than destroying the nations, Israel accepted them and their ways (see Judges 2:1-3, Judges 2:11-15; Judges 3:5-6).
Pagan gods were demons (see Deuteronomy 32:17).
Idolatry, like adultery, defiles God’s people (see Leviticus 18:24; Hosea 5:3).
God abhorred Israel’s sin, as he does all sin.
The psalmist returns to the Babylonian exile (Psalm 106:26-27). The Lord judged Israel severely, but he also restrained his wrath, remembering the covenant he had made with Abraham.
When Israel was finally destroyed, the destruction was not complete. The Lord pitied them, so he left a remnant.
He remembered . . . and relented: Unlike Israel, the Lord is faithful to his covenant (Psalm 105:8).
As harsh as the Exile was, the Lord still protected his people (see 2 Kgs 25:27-29).
Gather us back: The community prays for restoration from exile (see Psalm 102:19-22; Psalm 107:3; see also Isaiah 11:12; Isaiah 40:11; Isaiah 43:5; Isaiah 54:7; Isaiah 56:8; Isaiah 66:18).

This doxology concludes Book Four (cp. Psalm 41:13; Psalm 89:52). • from everlasting to everlasting! The reference to God’s eternal nature links to the opening of Book Four (Psalm 90:1-2). • Let all the people say, “Amen!”: The Hebrew word ’amen means “It is true.” The godly accept the Lord’s will in exile and his promise to be their God.

This psalm is a hymn of praise to God the Redeemer. After an introduction exhorting the redeemed to praise God for his goodness (Psalm 107:1-3), the psalmist brings together four case studies of people whom the Lord redeemed from adversity (Psalm 107:4-32). He then sums up the Lord’s sovereignty (Psalm 107:33-42) and concludes with an invitation to discern God’s unfailing love in all areas of life (Psalm 107:43).
The redeemed might be all who came out of exile.
exiles: People came from all nations where the people of Israel and Judah had been scattered.
Those who were lost in the wilderness thank God for his rescue. The wilderness might be a metaphor for leaving the path of wisdom (Psalm 1:1; Proverbs 4:10-15).
The psalmist does not specify the occasion of his trouble and distress. The generic nature of the adversity permits readers in a variety of circumstances to identify with the laments.
God led them like a shepherd (see Psalm 23:1). • Verse 8 is a refrain that is repeated in Psalm 107:15, Psalm 107:21, Psalm 107:31.
The psalmist calls for thanksgiving and praise from people in despair over the consequences of their rebellion.
God’s counsel includes his instruction and will.
Exhausted by their hard labor (Lamentations 5:13), the people fell. While this might be expected of the wicked (Psalm 9:3; Psalm 27:2), it was unlike the Israelites’ flight from Egypt (Psalm 105:37).
Fools who received what they deserved but were rescued from death offer thanksgiving to the Lord.
The Lord creates (Genesis 1:3) and sustains the universe (Hebrews 1:3) simply by speaking (Psalm 147:18); when he speaks, people are also healed (Matthew 8:8).
Sailors give thanks to the Lord when he saves them from the chaos and peril of the sea.
The same God who speaks and brings about the sailors’ distress can also calm the storm with just a word (cp. Jonah 1:4; Matthew 8:26).
This call for public praise expands the refrains in Psalm 107:21-22 and Psalm 107:31.
The Lord can choose to make the earth fertile or barren (Psalm 74:15; Isaiah 35:6-7).
These two sections (Psalm 107:33-38, Psalm 107:39-42) expand the theme of the Lord’s sovereignty over things that humans cannot control.
God’s presence can be seen in the abundance of his people’s families and herds (Psalm 127:3; Psalm 133:3; cp. Psalm 109:8).
People often become impoverished when their rulers practice oppression.
In his contempt for human rulers, the Lord rectifies their corruption on earth.
The large families of the poor are evidence of God’s blessing.
Justice prevails in God’s world (Psalm 1:6), and Israel’s history demonstrates God’s faithful love.
This psalm combines two excerpts from David’s other psalms (cp. Psalm 57:5, Psalm 57:7-11; Psalm 60:5-12).
The psalmist sees no evidence that God cares (see Psalm 28:1).

The psalmist begins this lament with a general charge against his accusers: They do evil in return for good (Psalm 109:1-5). At the end of the psalm, he turns to the Lord in prayer, asking for his protection (Psalm 109:21-25) and vengeance (Psalm 109:26-31).
The psalmist’s acts of kindness and godliness (see Psalm 35:12-14) have only met with stubborn opposition and expressions of hatred.
The NLT translates these verses as the words of the psalmist’s accusers; Hebrew lacks They say, which makes it unclear who is speaking.
The wicked person apparently held a position of leadership. Peter referred to this psalm in regard to Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:20-26).
Family members of those guilty of capital crimes often died with the perpetrator (Numbers 16:1-33; Joshua 7:1-25) or had their property confiscated (1 Kgs 21:13-16).
If one’s family name was blotted out, it meant there was no offspring to carry on the family name or remember its history (see Proverbs 10:7).

Children inherit the sinful nature of their parents (Psalm 51:5; Exodus 20:5; Ephesians 2:3). The speaker wants the Lord to punish the perpetrator for the guilt of family members who went before him (cp. Matthew 23:35-36).
The defendant committed capital crimes and did not exercise even basic decency.
Cursing is the accused person’s whole way of life.
The psalmist appeals to the principle of retribution (see Psalm 94:23).
The Lord’s reputation is at stake. If the wicked triumph, others could think that the Lord is also wicked and be drawn to that wickedness (Psalm 1:1).
Vulnerable and miserable, the psalmist appeals to his Lord for help. The accusations have killed his inner spirit and even his physical stamina.
A shadow at dusk suggests a transitory, empty existence (Psalm 102:11; Psalm 144:4); a single locust could easily be brushed off one’s clothing.
These verses form a prayer for God’s presence and for vindication. The psalmist wants everyone to see that he is vindicated by the Lord, not by any human agent.
The Lord’s servant demonstrates loyalty and obedience.
The psalmist had been accused of being clothed with curses (Psalm 109:18); now he asks that his accusers be clothed with disgrace and humiliation.

The king of Israel had the great privilege of being the Lord’s adopted son (Psalm 2:1-12; 1 Chr 22:10), but he fell (Psalm 89:1-52). This decree restores and heightens his position. • The Lord: Hebrew Yahweh, the name of God (see Exodus 3:6-14; Exodus 6:2-8; Exodus 20:2). • my Lord (Hebrew ’adoni) means “my master” or “my superior.” The psalmist viewed God’s messianic ruler as his superior. The New Testament frequently cites this psalm to validate Jesus’ claim to be the Messiah (Matthew 22:44-45; Mark 12:36-37; Luke 20:42-44; Acts 2:34-35; Hebrews 1:13). • The Lord’s right hand represents his authority, strength, presence, and benefits. The Lord chose the descendant of David and raised him up to be close to him (Psalm 80:17). Jesus claimed this position for himself (Matthew 26:64; Mark 14:62; Mark 16:19; Luke 22:69), and the apostles announced that Jesus, having ascended to heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father (Acts 2:33; Acts 5:31; Acts 7:55-56; Romans 8:34; Ephesians 1:20; Colossians 3:1; Hebrews 1:3; Hebrews 8:1; Hebrews 10:12; Hebrews 12:2). • Ancient Near Eastern kings were sometimes portrayed as placing their feet on the backs of their conquered enemies as on a footstool (see Hebrews 10:12-13).

Jesus and the apostles cite this psalm to explain Jesus’ unique ministry and status as the Messiah (Matthew 22:43-45; Acts 2:32-36). It reaffirms God’s covenant with David and gives hope for the future (see 2 Sam 7:8-16).
The kingdom will expand and increase, beginning from Jerusalem, until all enemies are conquered.

The Lord had made an unbreakable oath and covenant, so his apparent rejection of David’s dynasty (Psalm 89:38) in the Exile had led to a crisis. The placement of Psalm 110:1-7 in Book Five reaffirms the future of the dynasty: David’s descendant must conform to God’s standard of integrity (Psalm 101:1-8). His ministry will be transformed as he serves under God’s kingship (Psalm 93:1–100:5). • You are a priest forever: The role of God’s messianic ruler changes. The priestly kingship of David and his descendants extended to serving as patrons of the Temple. David had the Ark brought to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6:15) and arranged for the Temple service (1 Chr 6:31-48; 15:11-26; 16:4-42; 23:4-32; 25:1). Solomon supervised the Temple construction (1 Kgs 5:1–7:51). Even so, Israel’s kingship was separate from its priesthood. In the messianic kingdom, the king would also minister as priest, as Melchizedek, king of Salem (Genesis 14:18), had done. The New Testament develops the ministry of Jesus Christ as a fulfillment of this new order (see Hebrews 5:6-10; Hebrews 6:20–7:25).

at your right hand: This position brings help and protection (see Psalm 16:7-8; Psalm 108:13). • The Lord will strike down rebellious kings. Rebellion against the Lord is a capital offense (Psalm 2:1-12; Romans 6:23).
The new priestly role of David’s descendant does not rescind his old role as conquering ruler. He must still bring the nations under his rule (Psalm 110:2-3; see Psalm 2:1-12).
God’s messianic ruler obtains victory as a vigorous person, as if he had received nourishment from brooks along the way (Psalm 110:3).

The godly praise God and delight themselves in his great works. His mighty acts reflect his righteousness, grace, and compassion (see Psalm 116:5-7). All who submit themselves to him experience his glory.

This wisdom psalm contains many references to the works of the Lord that reveal his character. God is righteous, gracious, compassionate, faithful, just, trustworthy, upright, holy, and awe-inspiring (Psalm 111:3, Psalm 111:4, Psalm 111:7, Psalm 111:8, Psalm 111:9). God’s character gives hope in the covenant relationship (Psalm 111:5). He rescued Israel from Egypt (Psalm 111:9), gave them the land (Psalm 111:6), and provides for his people (Psalm 111:5). However, God demands that the beneficiaries of this relationship also be people of righteousness and integrity.
The refrain Praise the Lord! (Hebrew haleluyah) characterizes this group of psalms.
God takes care of his people’s needs, even providing food. He remembers his covenant with Abraham (see Psalm 105:8-11).

Giving Israel the lands of other nations was just and good because the Lord was executing his justice on those he dispossessed and showing grace to the Israelites. However, if the Israelites do not live faithfully and with integrity, they will also be dispossessed. The Lord’s people must reflect his character.
The people of the Exodus generation went free because of God’s grace.
True wisdom is the source of life (Proverbs 3:18; Proverbs 9:11; Ecclesiastes 7:12); it begins with the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 9:10).
The fear of the Lord leads to a life of wisdom that honors God and blesses the family and community. The godly joyfully imitate God; their obedience is not slavish.
This psalm reiterates the themes of wisdom and the fear of the Lord (Psalm 111:1-10). The wise have reason to be happy (Psalm 112:1-5) and vigorous (Psalm 112:6-10).
successful: All will know the children of godly people (see Psalm 127:4) because the godly leave a legacy for their children (see Psalm 1:3; cp. Matthew 6:20).

The godly imitate God by being generous, compassionate, and righteous (Psalm 51:1; Psalm 111:1-10; 2 Cor 9:9). They lend money to the poor without charging interest (Psalm 15:5; Psalm 112:9; Exodus 22:25).
The honesty and compassion of the wise keeps them from stumbling (Psalm 15:5; Psalm 37:23-24), ensuring that they will be long remembered (Proverbs 10:7).
Because the godly joyfully expect God to prevail and rescue them, they face their foes triumphantly (Psalm 59:10; Psalm 112:4; Psalm 118:7).
Paul quotes this verse in his instructions about generous giving (2 Cor 9:9).

The wicked . . . grind their teeth in anger out of their bitter envy (Psalm 35:16; Psalm 37:12). The vigor and reputation of the godly cause conflict with those who want them dead. • The wicked will slink away out of fear and shame.
The name of the Lord (Hebrew Yahweh; see Exodus 3:15) reveals his being, character, and reputation. He is exalted in time (now and forever) and in space (from east to west).

This hymn of praise exalts the greatness of the Lord’s name and glory. God is greatly exalted and glorious in heaven (Psalm 113:4); he also stoops down to take care of the lowly and needy on earth (Psalm 113:5-9).

These psalms form what is known as the “Egyptian Hallel” (hallel means “praise”) because Jews use the collection in the celebration of Passover, which was instituted at the beginning of the exodus from Egypt. Psalm 113:1–114:8 are recited before the Passover meal and Psalm 115:1–118:29 afterward.
The Lord’s glory reaches to the heavens (Psalm 57:5, Psalm 57:11; Psalm 99:2; Psalm 108:5; Psalm 138:6; Isaiah 6:1; Isaiah 57:15) and throughout the world of human relationships.
The incomparable Lord intimately involves himself in caring for people on earth.
The Lord stoops to the world’s level to be directly involved with his people (see Psalm 138:6; Philippians 2:6-8).
These phrases are a quotation from Hannah’s prayer of praise (1 Sam 2:8-9a).

A childless woman was customarily treated with disdain (Genesis 16:4); the Lord has the power to make her a happy mother, as he made Sarah (Genesis 21:2), Rebekah (Genesis 25:21), Rachel (Genesis 30:23), and Hannah (1 Sam 1:20). • God’s greatness and goodness provide ample reason to praise him.

At the time of Israel’s exodus from Egypt and their entrance into the Promised Land, Israel was one holy kingdom (Exodus 19:5-6). • The separate references to the land of Judah and Israel indicate that the psalm was composed after the kingdom was divided (1 Kgs 12:16-17; cp. 1 Sam 11:8; 1 Kgs 1:35), and probably after the Exile. The land of Judah became God’s sanctuary because the people worshiped God; his Tabernacle and later his Temple were located there.

This lyrical celebration of the Lord’s power in nature recalls Israel’s beginning as a nation at the Exodus (Psalm 114:1-2) and upon their entry to the Promised Land (Psalm 114:3-6). It promotes reverence for the God of Jacob (Psalm 114:7-8).

hurried out of their way! The waters divided for Israel to escape Egypt (Psalm 77:17-18; Exodus 14:1-31). • The Jordan River turned away when Israel arrived to cross over (see Joshua 3:1-17). • skipped like rams: God’s presence caused the mountains to quake (Exodus 19:16-20).
The Lord miraculously provided for his people in hard times after the Exile, just as he had done in the wilderness after the Exodus.
The community confesses their faith that God will rescue them for the glory of his name.

In this hymn of thanksgiving for God’s blessings, the community ascribes all glory to the name of the Lord, who is the true source of hope and blessing. Meanwhile, those who trust in idols are greatly disappointed. The blessing of the Creator of heaven and earth extends to future generations (Psalm 115:14), and especially to the priesthood (Psalm 115:12).

Where is their God? People deny God’s presence or power when he does not act as they think he should (cp. Psalm 14:1; Psalm 42:3, Psalm 42:10). However, God is in the heavens—he has all power, authority, and knowledge. He does as he wishes, not what people think he should do. He works out his plans in accord with his will (Ephesians 1:11) and acts in his own time and in ways he chooses.
This entire section is repeated in Psalm 135:15-20. • Unlike the Lord (Psalm 95:3-5), idols cannot do anything; they are good for nothing.
Worshiping idols leads one astray and corrupts those who trust in them (Isaiah 44:20).

Israel . . . priests . . . you who fear the Lord: The psalmist calls on all those in the God-fearing community to commit their ways to the living God. The threefold address assures them that the Lord is their true helper and shield (cp. Psalm 118:2-4).
The groups named in Psalm 115:9-11 receive assurance of the Lord’s blessing, regardless of their social status (see Psalm 113:8).

The psalmist blesses (Psalm 107:37-38, Psalm 107:41) all who trust in and fear the Lord. The Creator will care for the families of those who fear him. • who made heaven and earth: This statement speaks of the Lord’s all-encompassing power in creation.

The heavens belong to the Lord:’s: God’s exaltation begins in heaven (Psalm 113:4), far above the gods of the nations. Of course, the earth also belongs to him (Psalm 47:9; Psalm 95:4). • The dead cannot participate in God’s blessings. The living praise God in thanksgiving for his blessings (Psalm 79:13).
I love the Lord: This unique opening expresses affection for and commitment to the Lord (see Psalm 18:1; Deuteronomy 6:5) on the basis of what the Lord has done.
The psalmist praises the Lord for answering his prayers and rescuing him from death.

This hymn of thanksgiving rejoices in God’s character and in rescue from death (Psalm 116:1-11). It gives an assurance of God’s protection in life and reminds the godly that the Lord watches over them even at death. The psalmist commits to living as God’s servant and resolves to honor him publicly (Psalm 116:12-19).
Because the Lord responds to the cry of his people (Psalm 107:41; Psalm 113:6-8), the psalmist now strongly believes in prayer.
It isn’t clear if the psalmist’s crisis was a literal near-death experience or if he was using the term figuratively.
This is the first of three times that the psalmist calls on the Lord’s name (i.e., reputation).
The gracious, righteous, and compassionate Lord (see Psalm 111:1-5) rescued and gave rest to the psalmist.
People with childlike faith readily receive his wisdom and instruction (Psalm 19:7-11; Matthew 18:3-4).
The psalmist’s near-death crisis made him more aware of life and of walking before the Lord. Though he had been in anguish, the Lord was faithful. However, people are all liars.
I walk in the Lord’s presence: The psalmist already lived with integrity, but since his experience of deep distress, he now enjoys open fellowship with the Lord (see Psalm 56:13; cp. Job 42:5).
I believed in you: Paul quotes this phrase in 2 Cor 4:13.

The Lord’s gracious gifts are so great that the psalmist can do nothing to repay his debt. Keeping his promises publicly demonstrates his gratitude. • All he has done for the psalmist includes answers to prayer, rescue, and life. • The cup of salvation overflows with God’s blessings (Psalm 23:5), unlike the cup of judgment (Psalm 75:8). • The psalmist makes promises (“vows,” Psalm 116:18) to praise the Lord publicly (Psalm 116:17-18).
No one lives or dies outside of God’s will. Having been given a second chance at life, the poet readily commits himself to the Lord with renewed acts of public devotion.
Paul quotes this verse to show that Gentiles would eventually praise the God of Israel (Romans 15:11).
This psalm, the shortest in the Psalter, invites all . . . people of the earth to praise the Lord because of his unfailing love and enduring faithfulness.

With an exultant testimony, the psalmist gives thanks for the Lord’s goodness and encourages others to trust in his faithful love (Psalm 118:1-4, Psalm 118:29). This poem is the last of the Egyptian Hallel (Psalm 113:1–118:29).
Israel . . . Aaron’s descendants . . . all who fear the Lord: These three groups represent the whole of the covenant community (cp. Psalm 115:9-11; Psalm 135:19-20).
The Lord alone is the psalmist’s helper.
The Lord is for me: Cp. Romans 8:31; Hebrews 13:6. • God’s presence cancels out the need to fear mere people (Psalm 56:11). The psalmist joyfully expects God’s rescue (Psalm 59:10; Psalm 112:8).
Trusting in the Lord is better than placing confidence in even the most powerful human leaders (Psalm 118:6; Psalm 146:3).

Strength comes in the name of the Lord, declared by the threefold mention of the attackers, the Lord’s name, and victory. • Even when hostile people blazed . . . like a crackling fire, the Lord caused them to subside like burning thorns (see Isaiah 9:18; Isaiah 10:17).
The psalmist celebrates the victory of the Lord’s strong right arm, which kept him from death.
God has restored the psalmist from death to life, so he praises the Lord publicly (cp. Psalm 116:6, Psalm 116:12-19).

The cornerstone (or keystone) of a building or an arch gives the structure its shape and foundation. It is the most important of all the stones. The Lord chooses and places this stone for his sanctuary (Isaiah 28:16). Jesus referred to himself as this cornerstone (Matthew 21:42; Mark 12:10-11; Luke 20:17; see Acts 4:11; Ephesians 2:20; 1 Pet 2:6-7).
The psalmist sees his own salvation as the beginning of a new day in which the Lord will do great things.
This is the day the Lord has made: The day of the Lord’s victory has already arrived, although its completion awaits another day (Psalm 118:25).
The psalmist concludes with prayer and thanksgiving, anticipating an even greater revelation of God’s victory and rescue.

The one who comes in the name of the Lord brings the Lord’s complete victory (see Psalm 118:10-12). • During Jesus’ triumphant entry into Jerusalem, the crowds called out various blessings, including phrases taken from this verse (Matthew 21:9; Mark 11:9; Luke 19:38; John 12:13). Jesus himself quoted this passage as he wept over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:39; Luke 13:35).

The wise are happy. They are people of integrity (see Psalm 84:11) who follow the path of divine instruction. They obey God’s revelation and search for it with all their hearts (see Psalm 27:7; Psalm 119:10, Psalm 119:45, Psalm 119:94, Psalm 119:155), and they reject all forms of evil. Cp. Psalm 1:1-2.
Aleph (א): God, the author of these instructions, commands that his followers live by them. The psalmist prays to be given the grace to live by that revelation.

This psalm combines elements of wisdom, lament, praise, thanksgiving, and confession. Eight Hebrew words are used frequently, translated as “instructions,” “laws,” “words,” “regulations,” “statutes,” “commands,” “decrees,” “commandments,” and “promises.” Together, these words encourage love for and obedience to God’s instructions, as found in the Scriptures (see 2 Tim 3:14-17). The expression of deep commitment to these instructions unifies the psalm.
To keep God’s commandments means to guard them by obeying them.

A young person tends toward foolishness (Proverbs 22:15) and can easily make mistakes that destroy his life (Proverbs 7:6-23). Youth is also the best time to develop personal discipline and pursue wisdom (see Psalm 34:11; Proverbs 1:4). • To stay pure means to remain uncorrupted by wickedness and sin and to develop the integrity of life defined in Psalm 15:1-5.
Beth (ב): The psalmist is determined to pursue purity and encourages the cultivation of wisdom through God’s principles (Psalm 119:9) and instructions (Psalm 119:10-16).
The student asks God the teacher to discipline him so that he will not wander.
God’s wisdom is far greater than any riches humans seek (Psalm 119:72, Psalm 119:127; Proverbs 3:14-15).
The way of wisdom includes meditating on God’s ways (see Psalm 119:1, Psalm 119:3). The wise reflect on the implications of God’s word.

The psalmist seeks to please the Lord with a full and obedient life of praise (Psalm 118:17; Psalm 119:25, Psalm 119:77, Psalm 119:116, Psalm 119:144, Psalm 119:175). Only the Lord can remove his adversaries and enable him to see the wonderful truths found in God’s instructions.
Gimel (ג): Like a foreigner in hostile territory, God’s servant needs God’s guidance.
The arrogant are probably those who mock the psalmist (Psalm 119:22-23).
Those who meditate on God’s instructions receive wise advice from them.

Daleth (ד): Though the poet feels anguish and sorrow, he entreats the Lord to revive him because he wants to obey the Lord. Suffering and death may result from the Lord’s chastening (Psalm 118:17-18; Psalm 119:67, Psalm 119:71, Psalm 119:75), but his instruction revives the weary soul (see Psalm 119:12).
lying to myself: Self-deception is a fruit of sinful human nature (Jeremiah 17:9); it leads to folly. • Access to God’s word is a privilege, not a right.
He (ה): As a student, the poet asks his teacher, God, to renew life and to transform disgrace into righteousness.
The love for money can lead to sin (cp. Exodus 18:21; 1 Tim 3:1-5; 6:10).
The psalmist asks to be saved from enemies who speak harshly (see Psalm 42:10; Psalm 44:16; Psalm 89:50-51; Psalm 102:8).
Waw (ו): The psalmist prays that God’s word would continue to be the source of his love and salvation.
The psalmist is determined to obey the Lord.
The psalmist finds delight in God’s word in spite of pain (Psalm 119:92, Psalm 119:143).
Zayin (ז): The psalmist asks God to remember his word as the psalmist also remembers God’s word and his name. Remembrance expresses devotion.
The age-old regulations are the Torah (God’s “instructions” or “law”), a term that refers to the books of Genesis—Deuteronomy.
Heth (ח): The psalmist seeks God’s favor and unfailing love. Although surrounded by evildoers, he remains a loyal servant of the Lord.
Evil people try to drag him into sin, but the psalmist’s memory of God’s word keeps him standing firm (see Psalm 119:16).
God’s goodness fills the earth; the whole created order provides evidence of his goodness (see Isaiah 6:3; Isaiah 11:9).

Good judgment and knowledge come from wisdom (Psalm 111:10). • The psalmist admits that he used to wander off like a stray sheep (Psalm 119:176). • you disciplined me: See Psalm 119:25-29. • You are good and do only good: God’s character is perfect (Psalm 97:2; James 1:17; 1 Jn 1:5).
Teth (ט): The psalmist describes himself as a penitent sinner who gratefully accepts the Lord’s discipline.
As God’s child, the psalmist asks for divine wisdom.

Yodh (י): In this prayer for comfort and compassion, the psalmist commits himself to his Creator, who has afflicted him. He wants God to pay back his enemies for the wrongs they have done. He also prays to receive the gift of life. He not only prays for himself but also considers the whole community of the godly, asking that God’s answers to prayer would encourage them.
Kaph (כ): The psalmist is worn out from waiting for the Lord, but his hope is in God’s future rescue.
God’s word is trustworthy, in contrast to the deceptions of the enemies who hunt the psalmist down without cause (see Psalm 119:78).
Lamedh (ל): The stability of God’s wisdom gives understanding. God’s word provides order and a framework for living, even when under pressure from adversaries.
The wicked intended to kill the psalmist, but destruction (Psalm 1:6) was their own fate.
Even perfection has its limits: Humans cannot fully understand God’s ways (see Ecclesiastes 3:11).
make me wiser: God’s word provides wisdom and perspective. God is the true source of wisdom.
Mem (מ): The instruction and wisdom of God through his word are far superior to the best that human teachers can offer.

Wisdom is preferable to even the finest food (Psalm 19:10; Psalm 81:16). • The psalmist had already rejected the delusion offered by the way of folly (see Psalm 119:18, Psalm 119:78, Psalm 119:86, Psalm 119:163).
The Lord’s word is a lamp that provides perspective, hope, and guidance in darkness (Psalm 18:25-29; Psalm 119:130). Even more, this light gives life (Proverbs 6:23).
Nun (נ): The psalmist’s devotion to God’s word comes from within his being (Psalm 119:112) and guides his external life.
offering of praise: This Hebrew expression is unique in the Old Testament (cp. Psalm 50:23). • The psalmist is vulnerable to his opponents because of his commitment to a wise life.
The godly hate the wicked and their deeds (Psalm 5:4-6; cp. Ezekiel 33:11).
Samekh (ס): The psalmist declares his hatred of evil and his love for God and his ways.
Ayin (ע): The servant of the Lord strains to endure the evil around him. He boldly petitions the Lord to rescue him immediately!
Simply possessing God’s law does not provide any benefits. The psalmist knows that only as the Lord gives discernment will he understand it.
Pe (פ): The psalmist prays earnestly for God to speak to him as he suffers from his adversities.
Tsadhe (צ): God is righteous, and his word is right and just, especially in contrast to the deceptions of the wicked.
The psalmist’s indignation (cp. Psalm 69:9) comes from seeing the wicked disregard God’s word.
The psalmist is greatly troubled by his oppressors (see Psalm 119:143; cp. Isaiah 53:1-12).
I pray and I cry out translate the same Hebrew verb. • I rise early and I stay awake translate the same Hebrew verb.
Qoph (ק): The psalmist prays to the Lord at night. Although God appears to be distant, he is nearby.
Coming to attack me (or are coming near to me) is a Hebrew wordplay on but you are near. The wicked remain far from God’s instructions, whereas the psalmist stays near, so he does not need to fear.
Resh (ר): This petition for life can be found throughout Psalm 119:1-176, but it is concentrated in this stanza.
my heart trembles . . . I rejoice: Fear, trembling, and joy mark the psalmist’s devotion to God. • God’s word is a treasure. • In the Old Testament, seven signifies wholeness.
Shin (ש): The psalmist looks beyond his adversaries to the peace of God. This perspective allows him to praise God throughout the day.
Taw (ת): God’s servant petitions the Lord one final time; he still feels like a lost sheep.
God, the Great Shepherd, seeks out his lost sheep (Psalm 23:1; Luke 15:4-6).
The psalmist is surrounded by liars, so he makes his lament to the Lord, the only one who can help him.

This short, individual lament expresses the psalmist’s trust that the Lord will deal with deceptive evildoers. It also laments living as a stranger among hateful liars. The psalmist’s picture of his life in a foreign land might have been a reality as he set out for Jerusalem, or it might depict his feelings and concerns as he begins his pilgrimage. Overwhelmed with injustice, he trusts God and looks forward to arriving in the Lord’s presence.

These short, appealing songs were sung during pilgrims’ journeys to Jerusalem for the national festivals three times per year (Deuteronomy 16:16). The title of these psalms includes the Hebrew word for stairs, which some take to mean “ascending to Jerusalem.” These psalms (sometimes called the Songs of Ascents) take the reader on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to praise God for his goodness to Israel throughout history.

The psalmist dialogues with the liars who surround him. He feels reassured that the Lord will judge them. • The Divine Warrior (see Psalm 7:12-13; Psalm 11:4-6) will throw sharp arrows and glowing coals on the liars.

Meshech was a Japhethite territory far to the north of Canaan. Kedar was an Ishmaelite territory in Arabia. Violent people lived in both locations. Meshech was the home of a famous slave trade (Ezekiel 27:13; cp. Exodus 21:16) and Kedar of renowned warriors (Isaiah 21:16-17). These places can be understood as representative of the apostate, violent land where the psalmist suffered.
The psalmist feels the anguish of alienation, isolation, and perpetual conflict.
peace: See Psalm 37:11; Psalm 122:6-9; Psalm 125:5; Psalm 128:6.

The mountains were known for their idolatrous worship (Deuteronomy 12:2), and Israel was enticed to the hilltop shrines (Hosea 4:13). This verse can be understood as a rhetorical question expecting a negative answer: The gods of the hilltop shrines cannot rescue anyone. Others understand the mountains to be a symbol of the Lord’s strength (Psalm 95:4). In that case, the question would be interpreted literally (Where does my help come from?), with the answer given in the next verse
The leader of the group of pilgrims uses word pictures to assure the group of the Lord’s presence during the journey.
God watches over his own, even and especially when they face many troubles (Psalm 12:5, Psalm 12:7; Psalm 69:29; Psalm 91:14; Psalm 146:9).

The Creator (Psalm 121:2) is the guardian of Israel. • God stands beside Israel, supporting and caring for the godly (see Psalm 16:7-8). • Both the sun and the moon were regarded as deities in the ancient Near East, but the Creator limits their power. They, too, praise the Lord (Psalm 148:3).
The central sanctuary was the house of the Lord. This phrase originally referred to the Tabernacle (Exodus 23:19; Exodus 34:26).

Jerusalem is here idealized as the city of God, the city of David, and the city of faith. A group of people on a pilgrimage joyfully arrive in the city (Psalm 122:1-2). The psalmist sings an ode to Jerusalem (Psalm 122:3-5) and prays for the city’s peace (Psalm 122:6-9).
Several psalms celebrate or look forward to being inside the gates of the city (Psalm 9:14; Psalm 87:2; Psalm 100:4; Psalm 118:19).
In the time of David and Solomon, Jerusalem was renowned as a place of security (1 Kgs 10:6-7).
Jerusalem is a metaphor for God’s heavenly dwelling. David was the archetype for God’s chosen rulers.

Each of the people of Israel belonged to one of the tribes, and all of the tribes belonged to the Lord. • To give thanks is to present an offering acceptable to the Lord (Psalm 50:14, Psalm 50:23; Psalm 100:4; Psalm 118:19). • as the law requires of Israel: See Exodus 23:17; Deuteronomy 16:16.
the thrones where judgment is given: In the eras of David and Solomon (1 Kgs 3:28), Jerusalem was the home of wisdom and justice; it would be so again (Isaiah 9:7).
Prayers for the peace of Jerusalem are motivated by love of family and God’s sanctuary.

This lament on the psalmist’s lowly position expresses vivid trust in the Lord (Psalm 123:1-2). The psalmist prays for God’s favor on the community, as the reality of evil surrounds them (Psalm 123:3-4). The poet looks beyond Jerusalem (Psalm 122:1-9) to God’s throne in heaven.
The negative rhetorical questions emphasize the positive idea that the Lord was indeed on their side.
This thanksgiving song describes what might happen if the Lord were not present with his people.
the raging waters of their fury: The enemies could have overwhelmed the Israelites and wiped them out if the Lord had not been with his people (cp. Psalm 69:15; Jeremiah 46:8).
The enemies of God’s people, like lions or bears who tear their prey with their teeth (see Psalm 57:4; Proverbs 28:15), had their mouths shut by the Lord (Daniel 6:22).
The psalmist expresses the community’s confidence in the Lord’s protection (Psalm 125:1-2) and prays for peace (Psalm 125:3-5).
surrounds: God guards and protects like a wall of fire (Zechariah 2:5).
The godly might be tempted through peer pressure and cultural domination.
People who reject the straight path of the upright are fools (Proverbs 2:12-15). God pours out his goodness on the godly (see Psalm 122:6-9).

The Lord brought about Israel’s restoration from exile, just as he had brought Israel out of Egypt (Psalm 114:1). The restoration transformed the weeping of the Lord’s people into laughter and showed the Lord’s character to the nations (Psalm 9:11; Psalm 64:9; Isaiah 12:4).
This hymn celebrates Israel’s return from exile (Psalm 126:1-3). The psalmist prays for full restoration (Psalm 126:4-6).

The prophets had spoken of the restoration as a time when the wilderness would change into the Garden of Eden (Isaiah 51:3; Ezekiel 47:1-23); the reality fell far short of paradise. Here the restoration community prays for full redemption (see Haggai 2:19). • as streams renew the desert: The seasonal rains filled the dry river beds (wadis), and the land turned green again. The prayer looks for a similar transformation of Israel’s fortunes, a fulfillment of the imagery of the “Second Exodus” in Isaiah (see “The Promise of a Second Exodus” Theme Note). • The harvest represents God’s full restoration.

Unless: These conditional sentences emphasize the positive idea that the Lord will protect the city (cp. Psalm 124:1-2). • Human effort is futile unless the Lord blesses it (see Psalm 44:3). • from early morning until late at night: This depicts an aggressive and competitive lifestyle. • God’s loved ones enjoy a quiet night’s sleep (Psalm 3:5; Psalm 4:8).
Blessing and protection come from God. Without his presence, there is no success (Psalm 127:1-2). This is particularly true for children, who are God’s gift (Psalm 127:3-5).
Children are one of God’s blessings. The words translated “children” (Hebrew banim) and “builders” (bonim, Psalm 127:1) form a wordplay. Having children builds a family.
like arrows: God uses children to protect the reputation of his people against the wicked (cp. Psalm 120:4; Psalm 7:12-13).
Enjoying the fruit of one’s labor means gaining benefit from whatever work one does.

The godly, who fear the Lord, will know true happiness (Psalm 128:1-2). The Lord is with them (see Psalm 127:1-2), building their home life (Psalm 128:3-4) and blessing them across the generations (Psalm 128:5-6).
Like vigorous young olive trees, children are saplings filled with potential. Olive oil symbolizes God’s blessing (Psalm 104:15; Numbers 18:12; Jeremiah 31:12; Haggai 2:19).

God will continually bless all who fear him (Psalm 133:3) from his dwelling in Zion (Psalm 20:2; Psalm 50:2; Psalm 110:2), no matter where they live. • grandchildren: God’s blessings extend from generation to generation for the faithful (Psalm 79:12-13; Psalm 89:1; Psalm 100:4-5; Psalm 103:17-19).
Israel’s earliest youth as a nation was during its sojourn in Egypt.
The psalmist briefly reviews Israel’s history of trouble (Psalm 129:1-2) and redemption (Psalm 129:3-4). He concludes with curses against the enemies and blessings on the godly (Psalm 129:5-6).
the Lord is good: He rescued Israel from Egypt, from many enemy attacks, and from the Babylonian exile.
Grass on a rooftop had shallow roots and would scorch easily. A crop was ignored by the harvester when the yield was low. The enemies who had sown hurt among God’s people would gain little.
A cry from the depths is from a place of deep distress (cp. Psalm 69:2, Psalm 69:14; Isaiah 51:10; Ezekiel 27:34). Out of the frailty of his being, the psalmist prays for divine favor.

Beginning with himself as a representative of the community, the psalmist cries for God’s mercy (Psalm 130:1-3) out of deep distress. He places his hope in the Lord (Psalm 130:4-6), knowing that the Lord will rescue when and as he chooses. Based on this confidence, the psalmist invites Israel to wait for the Lord (Psalm 130:7-8).
The psalmist knows that his sins make him guilty and deserving of God’s judgment.
The good news comes in God’s readiness to forgive sinners. His grace encourages people to fear him and hope in him.
God’s word imparts hope (Psalm 119:42-43, Psalm 119:49; Psalm 147:11).

Israel is invited to hope in the Lord (Psalm 9:18; Psalm 27:14; Psalm 131:3) because the Lord pays the costly price for redemption and covers whatever sin separates humans from him (see also Psalm 111:9; Exodus 6:6-8; 2 Sam 7:23-24; Isaiah 43:1-4; Titus 2:14; Hebrews 9:12; 1 Pet 1:18).

The heart represents the whole being (see Psalm 27:8). • God hates arrogance, which is a foolish way of life (Proverbs 6:16-19). • The psalmist does not trouble himself with matters that properly belong to the Lord.
Out of his contentment in the Lord, the psalmist invites Israel to seek their rest in God (Psalm 131:3).
The psalmist calmed and quieted himself, surrendering his ambitions and taming his ego (Galatians 2:20). • like a weaned child: The psalmist sees himself as a contented child.

This psalm celebrates the Lord’s faithfulness to David. When David wanted to bring the Ark into Jerusalem (Psalm 132:1-5), the Lord granted the request and made Jerusalem his earthly home (Psalm 132:6-10). The choice of Jerusalem marked God’s election of David’s line (Psalm 132:11-13), of Zion (Psalm 132:14-17), and of the priesthood (Psalm 132:9, Psalm 132:16).
Ephrathah is Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19; Genesis 48:7). • Jaar is the singular form of the plural “Jearim.” The Ark was at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years in Samuel’s time (1 Sam 7:1-2).
These verses form a recollection of David’s moving the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6:1-15) and of the Lord’s oath to David (2 Sam 7:4-16).
These verses are a quotation from Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the Temple (2 Chr 6:41-42).
The priests were to exhibit righteousness in their lives (Psalm 132:16; Malachi 2:6).

The Lord swore an oath to David (2 Sam 7:4-16): God’s promise is unconditional, but the covenant is not (If . . . then). Those who break God’s covenant can expect the discipline of God’s judgment (see Psalm 89:30-37).
The psalmist recounts the selection of Jerusalem and of the priests.

anointed one: The ruler God chose and established (see Psalm 1:1–8:9) would never cease to provide light for the Lord’s people. This light would burn continually (see 1 Kgs 11:36; 2 Kgs 8:19; cp. John 8:12; Revelation 21:23-24).
The adversaries will be humiliated, in contrast to the glorious king (Psalm 132:9, Psalm 132:16).
Brothers are related by blood, by profession, or by commitment.
The psalmist tells of the joy of consecrated relationships.
In this wisdom psalm (see Psalm 1:1-6), peaceful and harmonious relationships manifest the presence of God.
The anointing oil was the oil used to ordain and consecrate Aaron for service in his office (see Exodus 29:7). • head . . . beard . . . border of his robe: The oil consecrated Aaron completely.

The dew represents the richness of divine blessings; in Jerusalem, it comes from moist winds from the Mediterranean Sea. Mount Hermon, which is capped with snow, is a place of abundant moisture. • A blessing is God’s life-giving power, a guarantee of his provision and protection (Psalm 5:12; Psalm 41:2), secured by his presence (Psalm 21:6; Psalm 67:1). Even the other nations will ultimately be blessed (Psalm 67:1-7; Psalm 72:17). Zion is the focal point of God’s blessing (Psalm 134:3; Psalm 147:13). • God gives life everlasting to human beings.
Those who serve at night were the priests and Levites (see also Psalm 135:2).
In the last of the pilgrims’ songs (Psalm 120:1–134:3), the travelers call the Temple workers to praise the Lord. In return, they will receive a much-anticipated blessing.
God, the Creator and the Lord of history, “made heaven and earth” (Psalm 134:3). He deserves praise because, unlike idols, he redeems his people.
The synonyms Jacob and Israel include all twelve tribes. The Lord cherishes his chosen people. They are his treasure out of all the kingdoms of the world (Exodus 19:5-6).
The Lord is superior to any real or imagined supernatural being (see Psalm 95:3-5; Psalm 115:4-8).
God is sovereign over the whole created order—he does whatever pleases him him. • The phrase heaven and earth refers to all of creation.
The psalmist tells of God’s sovereignty over the weather (Psalm 29:1-11; Psalm 77:17-18; Psalm 78:26; Psalm 104:4; Psalm 147:8-9; Psalm 148:5-6).

In the tenth and culminating plague against Egypt, God destroyed the firstborn of each family. • The miraculous signs and wonders are the ten plagues (see Exodus 7:1–11:10; Deuteronomy 4:34; Nehemiah 9:10).
The Lord was sovereign over the Exodus and the conquest of the Promised Land.
The Lord’s name and character stand in contrast to idols.
Idols corrupt the thinking because they are merely things made by humans; they cannot speak, see, hear, or breathe (Isaiah 41:22-24; Isaiah 44:9, Isaiah 44:18; Romans 1:21-23).
This entire section is repeated in Psalm 115:4-11.
The groups named here comprised the covenant community (see Psalm 115:9-11).
The psalmist invites the community to praise the Lord, who is good and full of love, the true Lord of humanity. Verse 1 alludes to the poetic expression in 2 Chr 5:13.

This is the last of the Great Hallel psalms (Psalm 120:1–136:26). It distinctively repeats the refrain His faithful love endures forever in every verse. The hymn is framed by a call to praise (Psalm 136:1-3, Psalm 136:26). It proclaims the Lord as the Creator of all and the Redeemer of Israel, both in the distant (Psalm 136:10-22) and in the recent past (Psalm 136:23-24).
The psalmist recounts the early history of Israel’s redemption.
The psalmist relates the recent history of Israel’s redemption, although the circumstances are not specified.
