The Lord provides for all of his creatures.

The phrase God of heaven is an exilic and postexilic designation for the Lord; it is found in Ezra (Ezra 1:2; Ezra 5:11, Ezra 5:12; Ezra 6:9, Ezra 6:10; Ezra 7:12; etc.), Nehemiah (Nehemiah 1:5; Nehemiah 2:4, Nehemiah 2:20; etc.), and Daniel (Daniel 2:18, Daniel 2:19, Daniel 2:37, Daniel 2:44).

In response to the pain of exile (Psalm 137:1-4), the psalmist resolves to remember Jerusalem even though the memories cause him pain (Psalm 137:4-6). He also writes an astounding imprecation, or prayer for vengeance (Psalm 137:7-9).

Because the music of Jerusalem was tied to the joys of life in the Promised Land, the Exile removed any occasion for singing joyous songs. The Babylonians wanted the Judeans to sing and dance for them, but the exiles’ grief made doing so either distasteful or impossible. The songs celebrating the Lord speak of his power and goodness, but his people were filled with doubts and questions. They hung their harps in trees, perhaps signifying the death of their joy under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23).
The psalmist pledges his loyalty to Jerusalem, the city at the center of God’s reign and the location of fellowship with him.

The poet witnessed the betrayal of God’s people from Judah by the Edomites, so he curses Edom. The long rivalry between Edom and Judah came to a head during Judah’s last days, when the Edomites handed the Judeans over to the Babylonians (Obadiah 1:10-11) and rejoiced in Jerusalem’s fall. • This prayer for vengeance is shocking.
The Lord receives praise before the gods of the nations.
In this wisdom psalm, the Lord is presented as the God of gods. He rescued his people and has a perfect plan for them as individuals. The nations will join Israel in glorifying God.
In this final collection of psalms of David, praise and wisdom psalms (Psalm 138:1–139:24, Psalm 145:1-21) form a frame around five poems of lament (Psalm 140:1–144:15).

As the Lord’s glory fills the earth, the world’s population must willingly submit to him. Every king (cp. Psalm 2:1-12) will join the community of praise as they hear the Lord’s ways of truth and love.
God’s holiness and excellence are great, beyond the scope of humanity (see Psalm 99:2; Psalm 113:4; Isaiah 6:1; Isaiah 57:15).
The exalted God takes care of the humble (Psalm 138:6), especially his servant the psalmist (Psalm 138:7-8).
The psalmist expresses confidence in the Lord’s plans, which are perfect, and prays for God’s continued involvement. The psalmist sees himself as part of God’s plans (see Psalm 9:10; Psalm 139:14).
The Lord knows the psalmist well; God has examined him thoroughly, in an inescapable examination that is painful at times (Job 7:17-19).

In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist opens every aspect of his being, character, behavior, and speech to God’s examination. As hard as life is, he wants to ensure his own growth in wisdom so that he does not come under God’s judgment of the wicked (Psalm 141:5; Psalm 142:3; Psalm 143:8, Psalm 143:10; Psalm 144:3-4). Further, the poet recognizes that he cannot escape from the Lord. His sense of stress disappears when he considers the Lord’s loving care for him, even before birth (Psalm 139:13-18). He then invites the Lord to continue examining him as he walks in the path of wisdom (Psalm 139:23-24).
The phrase sit down or stand up refers to daily activities (cp. Deuteronomy 6:6-9).
The Lord’s omniscience and omnipotence provide comfort to the godly, but they imprison the hearts of the wicked (Psalm 2:3).
The Lord’s wonderful understanding lies beyond the psalmist’s ability to comprehend (see Judges 13:18).
The psalmist expresses his awe at the Lord’s omnipresence.
down to the grave: God has total access to his entire creation—even the most hard-to-reach places.

ride the wings of the morning: This poetic expression describes traveling eastward, as far as the sunrise, if that were possible. • the farthest oceans: This expression takes the traveler in the opposite direction, far to the west.
The delicate, inner parts of the body include a person’s very being. • Even when hidden in his mother’s womb, the psalmist was guided by the Lord.
How precious are your thoughts about me: God’s investigation reveals loving care. Fellowship with the Lord provides riches beyond description.

The psalmist’s sense of awe leads him to consider the wicked and to reflect on himself. The Lord, as the examiner of all people, judges the wicked for their destructive acts and speech; thus, the psalmist prays that he will not be among them.
I hate: Rejection of evil is a mark of wisdom (see Psalm 1:1; Psalm 5:4-6).
The psalmist’s prayer against the wicked leads him also to reflect on himself; he does not presume that he is righteous. This prayer has been repeated by believers over the centuries.
The path of wisdom leads to everlasting life (see Psalm 1:6; Proverbs 4:18; Proverbs 6:23).
The psalmist prays for the Lord to rescue him from wicked people.

In this individual lament, the psalmist artistically sketches God’s enemies with all their evil intents. He prays for the Lord’s protection and rescue with confidence in God’s strength and justice. He foresees the evil as being judged by fire (Psalm 140:9-11) and himself as being vindicated and dwelling in the Lord’s presence (Psalm 140:13).
sting like a snake . . . a viper: These creatures depict the wicked as very corrupt people (see Proverbs 23:32; Isaiah 14:29; Romans 3:13).
The psalmist asks for divine protection (see Psalm 121:1-8), praying that the Lord will keep him safe from the many schemes of the wicked.
The expression Sovereign Lord comes from combining the name Yahweh with the title Adonai (Master). See also Psalm 68:20; Psalm 69:6; Psalm 71:16; Psalm 73:28; Psalm 109:21; Psalm 141:8.
The psalmist prays for God’s judgment on the wicked.

The psalmist wants fire to descend on his enemies, and he wants them thrown into pits so they can never attack again. The language foreshadows the New Testament teaching on hell (Matthew 5:22, Matthew 5:29-30; Matthew 10:28; Matthew 18:9; Mark 9:43-47; Luke 12:5; James 3:6; 2 Pet 2:4).

The psalmist prays urgently for rescue. He does not have at hand either incense or an evening offering (Exodus 29:38-39), but his prayers and devotion are the reality that those elements represent (cp. Isaiah 1:13; Revelation 5:8). • Upraised hands are a posture of prayer (Psalm 28:2; Psalm 88:9; Psalm 143:6; Exodus 9:29; 1 Tim 2:8).
The psalmist prays for rescue and wisdom, and he envisions the end of evil. The principle of retribution (Psalm 141:10) unifies the psalm.

Wisdom sometimes requires protection from oneself. One could say or think things that lead to the evil path (Proverbs 13:3; Proverbs 21:23). • Wisdom opens itself to correction from godly people (see Proverbs 3:11; Proverbs 9:8; Proverbs 15:31; Proverbs 19:25).
Though overwhelmed by his persecutors (Psalm 142:6), the psalmist looks to the Lord for wisdom.
regarding his experience in the cave: Cp. Psalm 57:1.

The psalmist reaches a point of despair (see Psalm 77:3), and the Lord cares for him in his distress. The psalmist commits himself to the Lord’s wisdom (see Psalm 139:1-24) but laments his entrapment by the wicked (Psalm 5:9-10; Psalm 140:5; Psalm 141:9; Psalm 142:3).
Though he is alone, the psalmist’s trust remains in the Lord, who is his life (see Psalm 9:9; Psalm 16:5; Psalm 27:13).
Though overwhelmed by loneliness and trouble, the psalmist focuses on the Lord’s goodness and protection. He knows that the Lord alone is his Redeemer, so he offers his praise.
His experience of confinement and duress is like being in prison (see Psalm 107:10).
The psalmist prays for God’s love and mercy.

In this lament, the psalmist feels overwhelmed by constant harassment from his foes, so he turns to the Lord’s love, righteousness, and faithfulness. He remembers God’s acts in the past and yearns for the renewal of the Lord’s love. He opens himself to God’s wisdom because he knows that instruction will lead to life.
All people are guilty before God (Romans 3:20-24).
I am losing all hope: The psalmist confesses his desperation as his life slips away under oppressive and ruthless foes.
Remembering God’s acts from the past reassures the psalmist of God’s faithfulness (Psalm 42:4; Psalm 63:6; Psalm 77:3, Psalm 77:6; Psalm 119:55).
The psalmist’s thirst is a deep longing for God’s redemption (see Psalm 42:1-2).

The psalmist experiences depression. He feels that he is dying from anguish (Psalm 31:10; Psalm 119:87), exhausted (Psalm 39:10; Psalm 71:9; Psalm 119:81), fainting with longing (Psalm 84:2), and overwhelmed by the weariness of life (Psalm 90:7, Psalm 90:9).
The psalmist petitions the Lord for a renewal of his love.
The psalmist prays for wisdom (see Psalm 5:8; Psalm 25:4-6; Psalm 138:1-8; Psalm 143:10). • your gracious Spirit: The Spirit brings God’s goodness (see Psalm 23:6).
To preserve means in this case to restore from despair (Psalm 80:19; Psalm 85:6; Psalm 138:7).
A prayer for vindication and renewal of life concludes the psalm.
The psalmist’s descriptive names for the Lord reveal his deep love for him.

This lament begins with an exclamation of love for the Lord. The community then reflects on the transitory nature of life (Psalm 144:3-4). The psalmist prays for divine intervention and anticipates victory (Psalm 144:5-11). A new song (Psalm 144:9-10) and a prayer for rescue (Psalm 144:11) open up the theme of the Lord’s blessing through his provisions and protection (Psalm 144:12-15).

what are human beings? The same question in Psalm 8:4-6 elicits the answer that humans are mere mortals but are also glorious rulers. The psalmist depicts humans as having a transitory, empty existence (see Psalm 90:3, Psalm 90:7-10; Psalm 102:11; Psalm 109:23; Psalm 146:4).
The psalmist prays for God’s intervention against his enemies (cp. Psalm 18:7-19).
The psalmist compares sons and daughters to plants and pillars, which are images of strength and beauty.

This prayer for the Lord’s blessing brings the laments of Psalm 140:1–144:15 to a close. It offers a vision of God’s provision and protection (see Psalm 127:1-5), not only for the psalmist, but for his descendants and those of all the godly.
no enemy . . . no cries of alarm: These images depict peace and security.
The psalmist praises God, the Great King who reigns over all other rulers (see Psalm 47:2).

This hymn of praise is the last in this collection of the psalms of David (Psalm 138:1–145:21). Praise continues in the last five psalms (Psalm 146:1–150:6). This psalm celebrates the Lord as King of all (Psalm 145:1-3, Psalm 145:10-13). God’s actions reveal his royal qualities (Psalm 145:4-7). He cares for all creatures (Psalm 145:14-17) and for those who fear him (Psalm 145:18-20).
This litany praises God’s character and mighty deeds. Each generation will continue to testify to God’s power (Psalm 22:30).
God consistently demonstrates his character toward all his creation (see Psalm 136:25).
These verses form a description of the Lord’s kingdom.
The Lord cares for his creatures.

The Lord cares for those who love him and fear him. God-fearers love the Lord and find refuge in him (Psalm 5:11); they seek him as their only true Savior (Psalm 40:16; Psalm 70:4). They will experience a grand future (Psalm 69:36), as well as God’s peace (Psalm 119:165).
This verse is reminiscent of Psalm 103:1, Psalm 103:2, Psalm 103:22; Psalm 104:1, Psalm 104:35.

The call to praise (Psalm 146:1-2) leads into a warning against folly and false confidence (Psalm 146:3-4). The psalm concludes with a blessing for all who place their hope in the Lord (Psalm 146:5-7).
The Psalter ends with five hallelujah psalms, so named because each begins and ends with Praise the Lord! (Hebrew haleluyah).
The fourfold repetition of the name of the Lord emphasizes that only he heals, unburdens, loves, and protects.
This verse is a call to worship.
The psalmist calls for the Lord to be praised for restoring and blessing Zion, caring for the poor, displaying his power over nature, and revealing himself to his people.
The psalmist recalls the restoration of Jerusalem and the Lord’s afflicted exiles.
The Lord created the heavens. • He counts the stars: God’s people can feel secure in knowing that the Lord attends to every detail of his creation; he knows all that belongs to him.
God measures out his justice on the poor and on the wicked (Psalm 55:22; Psalm 140:12; Psalm 145:14; Psalm 146:7).
Human achievements fail to impress the God who commands nature; rather, he takes pleasure in those who fear him.
God holds sovereign power over the weather (Psalm 77:17-18; Psalm 78:26; Psalm 104:4; Psalm 148:5-6).
human might: Any physical or intellectual achievement is a gift from the Lord, just like the strength of a horse. These gifts are a reason to praise the Lord, not to boast (Jeremiah 9:23-24).
The bars of the city gates symbolize defenses against enemies. • God blessed his people by empowering them with safety, prosperity, peace, and provisions (see Psalm 133:3).
Simply by speaking his command, the Lord can change the season from unbearable winter to refreshing spring (see Psalm 147:8; Psalm 148:5-6).
words . . . decrees . . . regulations: The Lord gave powerful words to Israel so that they might obey him (Psalm 105:45).
During Jesus’ triumphant entry into Jerusalem, the crowds called out various blessings, including a phrase taken from this verse (Matthew 21:9; Mark 11:10; Luke 19:38).
This psalm calls for the whole created order to praise the Lord because he has honored his faithful people.
The created order is stable because of the Lord’s word (see Psalm 33:9).

In the ancient Near East, people viewed different gods as having control over separate aspects of nature. The Lord, however, reigns sovereign over all natural phenomena; all the parts of creation are his servants, bringing praise to him through their obedience (Psalm 77:17-18; Psalm 104:4; Psalm 135:7; Psalm 147:8, Psalm 147:15-18; Numbers 11:31).
The psalmist calls all humans to offer praise to God, regardless of status, age, or gender.

Universal praise of the Lord is fitting because he is glorious, and he has blessed his people (see Psalm 147:13; Isaiah 46:13; Ephesians 3:10). • His faithful ones are his trusting and devoted servants (Psalm 86:2).
This hymn of praise celebrates the Lord’s victory. He is the Maker of Israel (Psalm 149:1-2) and the victorious King who shares his glory with his faithful ones (Psalm 149:3-9).
God’s people, whom the world ignores and despises, will be vindicated (Matthew 19:30). The humble will experience victory over their oppressors and persecutors (see Isaiah 61:3).
Vengeance is the Lord’s business (see Psalm 2:3; Psalm 94:1; Psalm 102:20; Psalm 142:7; Psalm 146:7).
The phrase mighty heaven alludes to Genesis 1:1-31 and to God’s glorious work in filling the emptiness.
Everything that breathes is commanded to praise the Lord as he deserves. The whole Psalter describes the greatness of the Lord, so this psalm is a fitting conclusion.

The psalmist calls all people to praise God with instruments and dancing. flutes: These wind instruments are not mentioned as being used in Temple worship. • clanging cymbals: Temple musicians clapped two bronze bowls together as percussion instruments.
Praise the Lord: This refrain is a fitting conclusion to the entire book of Psalms.
